en: They choose a place for the sacrifice to the gods.
They should choose that which is the highest, so that nothing else may overtop it from the earth; for from there indeed the gods ascended to heaven. Or, the gods...

He who undergoes initiation ascends; he sacrifices on the sacrificial ground (devayajana) together with the gods. If he were to lie down upon anything other than the earth, he would be as if cast down lower. Therefore, they should choose that which is the highest. 3.1.1. [2]
That altar-ground should be level;
being level, it should be even; being even, it should not be sloping;

being not sloping, it should slope toward the east, for the east is the direction of the gods; or it may slope toward the north, for the north is the direction of humans; [but it must not slope] toward the south.
It should be somewhat elevated toward the north, for this direction indeed belongs to the ancestors. If it were sloping toward the south, the sacrificer would quickly go to yonder world;
therefore, the sacrificer lives long. Thus, it should be somewhat elevated toward the south. 3.1.1. [3]
It should not extend beyond the measure of the sacrificial ground (devayajana) in front;
for he would thereby cause his hateful rival to exceed him. It may, however, extend as much as one desires to the south or likewise to the north; this indeed is the case.
"A place for sacrifice that is so abundant that only a space sufficient for the sacrifice remains at the back—verily, the subsequent performance of sacrifice approaches him quickly.
Such was the teaching regarding the place for sacrifice.
Then Yājñavalkya said:
"We went to Vārṣṇya to choose a place for the sacrifice to the gods.

He said, 'This entire earth is indeed a divine place for sacrifice; wherever one may perform the sacrifice on it, having encircled the site with a sacrificial formula (yajuḥ), that is sufficient. 3.1.1 [5]
The officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) are indeed the sacrificial ground for the gods.
Those Brahmins who have heard the sacred lore, who are learned in the Vedas, and who are wise—when they perform the sacrifice, that itself is the unshakable [ground];
we consider it as if it were closest at hand. 3.1.1. [6]
They erect either a hall or a hut with its ridge-pole facing east;
for the east is the direction of the gods.
For the gods turned westward toward men from the front; therefore, one offers oblations to them while standing facing the east. 3.1.1 [7]

Therefore, one should not sleep with the head pointing westward, lest one sleep having stretched out toward the gods. That direction which is south belongs to the ancestors; that which is west belongs to the serpents, for it is from there that the gods departed; and that which is north is this [direction] devoid of serpents.
Therefore, for human beings, they erect a hall or a shed with its rafters pointing northward;
for the north is the direction of human beings. It has its rafters pointing eastward only for one who is consecrated, not for one who is not consecrated.
They enclose that very [structure].

"It is not because of the rain," he says; for the one who undergoes initiation approaches the gods, and he becomes one of the deities. The gods are, as it were, hidden from men, and this enclosure is, as it were, a place of concealment; therefore they enclose it. 3.1.1. [9]
Therefore, not everyone should undertake it; rather, only a Brāhmaṇa, a Rājanya, or a Vaiśya, for these are worthy of sacrifice.
He indeed should not converse with everyone.
For he who undergoes consecration (*dīkṣate*) approaches the gods; he becomes one of the deities.

Indeed, the gods do not converse with everyone—neither with a Brāhmaṇa, nor a Rājanya, nor a Vaiśya; for they alone are worthy of sacrifice. Therefore, if he should encounter a conversation with a Śūdra, he should say to one of these [three]: "Look at this one! Look at this one! This, indeed, is the proper conduct for the consecrated one (dīkṣita) in such a case. 3.1.1. [11]
Then, taking the fire-drills in his hand, he settles in the middle of the hall; having approached the central pillar at its eastern end, he recites this sacrificial formula:
"We have come to this place of sacrifice on earth where the gods [dwell]."

"All have delighted in it"—thereby it becomes acceptable to all the gods and to those Brahmins here who are learned and well-versed in the Vedas; for when those learned Brahmins look at him with their eyes, by that it becomes acceptable to them. 3.1.1 [12]
As it is said: "Wherein all the gods have delighted"—thereby it becomes beloved by all the gods.

"Crossing over with Ṛks, Sāmans, and Yajus"—for by means of Ṛks, Sāmans, and Yajus they reach the completion of the sacrifice; thus he says, "May I reach the completion of the sacrifice. [He adds] "with the increase of wealth."
"May we rejoice in abundance" (*samiṣā madema*). Abundance is indeed the increase of wealth; abundance is prosperity.
Thus he invokes this very blessing when he says, "May we rejoice in abundance. For they say of one who attains prosperity and reaches the highest state that "he rejoices in abundance.
Therefore he says, "May we rejoice in abundance. 3.1.2.1.
He should undergo initiation in the afternoon.

Before the shaving of his hair and beard, he may eat whatever he desires or whatever is available, for from that point on his food consists solely of the sacrificial vow. However, if he has no desire to eat, he may certainly abstain. 3.1.2. [2]
Then they enclose the hall on the north side.
There he places a water-jar. The barber stands by it;
there he shaves his hair and beard, trims his nails, and—indeed, there is impurity in a man wherever the waters [reach him].

The waters do not settle upon his hair and beard, nor upon his nails; therefore, when he shaves his hair and beard and cuts his nails, it is so that he may become pure for the consecration (*dīkṣā*). Regarding this, some indeed shave their entire heads, thinking, "Having all become pure, we shall undergo the consecration. But that is not so.
One should not do anything else; rather, when he shaves his hair and beard and clips his nails, at that very moment he becomes pure.
Therefore, one should indeed shave the hair and beard and clip the nails. He clips the nails first.
In the case of humans, it is first the right [hand], or first the left;
but in the case of the gods, it is thus: first the thumbs, or first the little fingers. 3.1.2.
[5] He first parts the hair at the godāna on the right side.
In human practice, one begins with the left; however, in the ritual for the gods, it is thus:
he first moistens the hair on the right side of the head with the formula, "May these divine waters be auspicious for me. He...
When he says, "May these divine waters be propitious to me," the waters are indeed a thunderbolt, for the waters are a thunderbolt;
therefore, wherever they flow, they create a depression, and wherever they settle, they burn it up. Thus, by this [formula], he pacifies that very thunderbolt;
so, being pacified, this thunderbolt does not harm him. Therefore he says, "May these divine waters be propitious to me. 3.1.2. [7]
Then he places a young blade of darbha grass between [the head and the razor], saying:
"O herb, protect him! For the razor is indeed a thunderbolt; thus this thunderbolt, the razor, does not harm him. Then he applies the razor with [the formula]: "O axe, do not harm him."
"May he not harm," [he says]. The razor is indeed a thunderbolt; thus, this thunderbolt-razor does not harm him.
Having cut [the hair], he throws it into a water-vessel.
He silently moistens the hair of the other side, silently.
He places a young blade of darbha grass between [the head and the razor], silently sets down the razor, cuts [the hair], and throws it into a water-pot.
Then he hands the razor to the barber;
he shaves the hair and beard. When he shaves the hair and beard—

Then he bathes. Man is indeed impure in that he speaks untruth; by that he is foul within. Water is pure; "having become pure, may I be consecrated," he thinks. Water is a means of purification; "purified by the purifier, may I be consecrated," he thinks. Therefore, he bathes. He bathes with [the mantra]: "May the waters, our mothers, cleanse us; may they, rich in ghee, purify us with ghee. This, indeed...

"From that which they purified with ghee, he says: 'May those who purify with ghee purify us with ghee. For they carry away all impurity (*ripra*); the goddesses indeed carry away from him all that is impure, all that is *ripra*. Therefore he says: 'For they carry away all impurity, O goddesses. 3.1.2. [12]
Then he steps out toward the northeast, saying:
"Pure and purified, I go upward from these [waters]," for indeed, pure and purified, he goes upward from these [waters].
Then he puts on the garment.
This is for the sake of wholeness; he thus bestows his own skin upon him. For this skin which belongs to the cow was originally the skin of man. 3.1.2. [14]
Those gods said:
"The cow indeed supports all this. Come, let us place this skin which is on the man onto the cow;
by means of it, she shall endure the rain, by means of it the cold, and by means of it the heat. 3.1.2 [15]
Having cut off a man, they placed that skin upon the earth; with it, he endures rain, with it, snow, and with it, the heat of the sun. 3.1.2.[16]
For man was indeed cut;

therefore, wherever a blade of grass or whatever else cuts him, from that very spot blood flows out. Upon him they placed this skin, which is his garment; therefore, there is no garment other than that of man.
For he maintains this skin; therefore they placed it upon him. Thus, one should desire to be well-clad, thinking, "May I be endowed with my own skin.
Therefore, people even desire to see one who is ill-clad if he is well-dressed, for he is indeed endowed with his own skin.
One should not be naked at the end of the cow.
"The cow indeed knows: 'I wear his skin,' and so she is afraid and trembles, thinking, 'He will take my skin away. Therefore, cows always keep close to one who is well-dressed.
Regarding that very garment of his:

The border belongs to Agni, the fringe to Vāyu, the hem to the Pitṛs, the woven pattern to the Sarpas, the warp-threads to the Viśve Devas, and the stars to the Nakṣatras; for indeed, all these gods are dependent upon this garment. Therefore, it becomes the garment of the consecrated (dīkṣita). 3.1.2. [19]

Or it may be unwashed; this is for the sake of its freshness. He should tell [the weaver] to beat it, thinking: "Whatever unclean part of it she has cut or woven here, let that become pure for him. If, however, it is unwashed...

It may be that he sprinkles it with water so that it becomes pure; furthermore, one may also undergo consecration (dīkṣā) by means of that garment which has been set aside for the bath and has not yet been washed.
He puts it on.

"Thou art the body of consecration and austerity"—for this [body] is first the body of one who has not yet been consecrated, but here it becomes the body of consecration and austerity; therefore he says, "Thou art the body of consecration and austerity. "Thee, the auspicious and beneficial, I entrust"—by this he means, "Thee, the auspicious and excellent, I entrust. "Nourishing a blessed complexion"—[he says this] because he is [previously] possessed of evil.
"He first nourishes his appearance"—that which he, being uninitiated, does not yet possess; therefore, it is auspicious here.
For this reason, he says, "nourishing an auspicious appearance.
Then he causes him to enter the hall.
He should not eat the meat of the cow or the ox; for the cow and the ox sustain this entire world. The gods said, "The cow and the ox sustain this entire world;
come, let us place whatever vigor belongs to other birds into the cow and the ox. Thus, whatever vigor belonged to other birds...
There was vigor; they placed it in the cow and the ox, and therefore the cow and the ox consume the most food.

Now, he who should eat the food of both the cow and the ox eats as if eating everything; he is like one who has reached the end [of his life]. Indeed, a wonder occurred: "He has struck down a fetus for his wife," they said; "he has committed a sin," said the wicked one.
"Therefore, one should not eat [the meat] of a cow or a bull. Regarding this, Yājñavalkya said:
"I do indeed eat it, provided that it is well-fleshed. 3.1.3.
Having poured out the water for the ritual.
He offers a cake on eleven potsherds to Agni and Viṣṇu.
Agni indeed is all the deities, for into Agni they offer to all the deities; Agni is the lower limit of the sacrifice and Viṣṇu is the upper limit.
Thus, having encompassed all these deities and having encompassed the entire sacrifice, [he performs] the consecration.

Therefore, there is a cake on eleven potsherds for Agni and Viṣṇu. Regarding this, some offer a *caru* oblation to the Ādityas; concerning that, there is a verse which seems to have been recited: "Eight sons of Aditi were born from her own body; with seven she went forth to the gods, but Mārtāṇḍa she cast away."
There were indeed eight sons of Aditi, whom the gods call the Ādityas; seven of them were born unaltered,
but she brought forth the eighth, Mārtāṇḍa, as an embryo that was indistinct, being as tall as he was broad.
"Measured by a man," so say some.
Then those gods, the Ādityas, said: "Since he was born after us, let him be just like us; come, let us [make him so]. 3.1.3 [4]
"Let us transform him," they said, and so they transformed him. As this man was thus transformed, they cut his flesh into pieces and cast it down;

from that, the elephant came into being. Therefore they say, "One should not accept an elephant as a gift, for the elephant is born from man. And he whom they thus transformed was Vivasvat Āditya; these creatures are his offspring. 3.1.3 [5]
He said: "He shall prosper among his offspring who offers this oblation of cooked rice (caru) to the Ādityas.
Indeed, he prospers who offers this oblation of cooked rice to the Ādityas; however, this [other sacrifice] to Agni and Viṣṇu is well-known.
For it, there are seventeen *sāmidhenī* verses.

He sacrifices to the deities in a whisper; there are five *prayāja* offerings and three *anuyāja* offerings; they perform the *patnīsaṃyāja* for the sake of completeness. However, he does not offer the *samiṣṭayajus*, thinking, "Lest, having put on this garment of the consecrated, I should reach the end before the sacrifice is completed," for this is indeed the end of the sacrifice.
The *samiṣṭayajus* offering (ŚB 3.1.3.7).
Then, standing in front of the hall, he anoints himself. Man is indeed a wound when he is unanointed; by this act, he becomes free from wounds.
That which he anoints is indeed the skin of the cow; for this fresh butter (navanīta) comes from the cow.
He thus endows him with his own skin; therefore, he anoints himself.
That [ointment], moreover, is fresh butter.

Clarified butter indeed belongs to the gods, and the hot decoction to men; but this [mixture] is neither clarified butter nor a hot decoction—it should be both clarified butter and a hot decoction for the sake of freshness (*ayātayāmatā*). Thus, by means of that which is fresh, he makes him fresh. 3.1.3. [9]
He anoints him from the head downwards to the feet, following the direction of the hair, with the formula: "Thou art the milk of the great ones.
"Great" (mahī) is indeed one of the names of these cows; this is their milk, therefore he says, "of the great ones."

"Thou art milk," [he says]; "Thou art the giver of splendor; give me splendor"—in this there is nothing, as it were, hidden. 3.1.3.[10] Then he anoints his eyes. "The eye is indeed a sore for man; 'May it be healed for me,' so Yājñavalkya used to say."
The eye is like a bad die; its film is indeed pus. When he anoints the two eyes, he thereby removes that [pus].
3.1.3. [11] When the gods slew the Asuras and Rakṣasas, then Cūṣṇa the Dānava fell upon them facing westward.
He entered the eyes of men; that very one is this pupil (*kanīnaka*), which shines like a little boy.
Therefore, as they approach this sacrifice, he encloses it on all sides with a stone-fortress, for collyrium is indeed stone.
It is from the Trikakud mountain.
Or, when Indra slew Vṛtra, that which was his eye became this mountain Trikakud; therefore, when there is a Trikakuda stone, he thereby bestows sight upon the eye.
That is why it is made of Trikakuda stone; if one should not find a Trikakuda stone, [one may use] even one from another mountain.
For the kinship of the ointment is indeed uniform.
3.1.3.[13] He anoints with a reed-shaft. The reed is indeed a thunderbolt, for the sake of driving away the Rakṣases. It has tufts; it is, as it were, rootless.

This Rakṣas, cut off on both sides, wanders through the intermediate space, just as this man, rootless and cut off on both sides, wanders through the intermediate space; therefore, that it has a tuft is for the sake of driving away the Rakṣases.
He first anoints the southern one.
In human practice one begins with the left hand; in the case of the gods, it is thus.
He anoints [the eye], saying: "Thou art the pupil of Vṛtra. For this is indeed the pupil of Vṛtra. "Thou art the giver of sight;
give me sight"—in this there is nothing obscure.

He anoints the southern [corner] once with a *yajus* formula, once silently; then the northern one he anoints once with a *yajus* formula and twice silently. Thus he makes that northern one possessed of the latter [characteristic]. 3.1.3. [17]

Now, as to why he anoints five times: the sacrifice is commensurate with the year, and there are five seasons in the year; he thus obtains it by means of five [anointments]. Therefore, he anoints five times. 3.1.3. [18]
Then he purifies him with a strainer of *darbha* grass.

Man is indeed impure when he speaks untruth; by that he is foul within. *Darbha* grass is pure; [the thought is: "Having become pure, let me undergo consecration (*dīkṣā*). For *darbha* grass is a means of purification.
"Initiation is purified by the *pavitra*"; therefore, he purifies him with a *darbha*-blade *pavitra*. It should indeed be one; for this [wind] blows as one alone.
Therefore, it should be one, in accordance with the form of that very [wind]. 3.1.3 [19–20]

Moreover, there may also be three. For this breath blows as one alone; yet it has entered within the person and is divided threefold as prāṇa, udāna, and vyāna. It follows the measure of this very [one], and therefore there may be three. 3.1.3. [21]

Moreover, there may even be seven; for there are these seven vital breaths in the head, therefore there should be seven. Or rather, there should be thrice-seven, which is twenty-one; this indeed is the perfect number. 3.1.3. [22]

He purifies it seven times with each [verse]. With "May the Lord of Thought purify me," he says, "May Prajāpati, who is indeed the Lord of Thought, purify me. With "May the Lord of Speech purify me," he says, "Prajāpati is indeed the Lord of Speech."
"May Prajāpati purify me"—this is what he says. "May the god Savitṛ purify me": he whom the god Savitṛ purifies is indeed well-purified;
therefore he says, "May the god Savitṛ purify me. "With a flawless strainer": that which blows here is indeed the flawless strainer;
by this he means it. "With the rays of Sūrya": the rays of Sūrya are indeed the purifiers.
"Therefore he says, 'With the rays of the sun.
[He says,] 'Of thee, O Lord of the Purifier';
for he is indeed the Lord of the Purifier. [He says,] 'Of thee, purified by the purifier'; for he is indeed purified by the purifier."

"Whatever desire I may have, may I fulfill that; may I reach the conclusion of the sacrifice"—this is what he says by this. Then he causes [the sacrificer] to recite the commencement of the blessings:
"O gods, we seek from you desirable wealth as the sacrifice proceeds; O gods..."
"We invoke the blessings of those worthy of sacrifice"—thus the officiating priests (ṛtvij) offer blessings for him that are truly his own.
3.1.3. [25] Then he bends his fingers: "Svāhā! To the sacrifice from the mind!"—two [times]; "Svāhā! From the wide atmosphere!"—two [times]; "Svāhā!"—[one time].

"To Heaven and Earth," he says; [with this], two [handfuls]; "Svāhā! From the wind I take hold," with these words he closes his fists. Indeed, one does not take hold of the sacrifice as if it were directly perceptible, as one would a staff or a garment; for the gods are beyond the senses, and the sacrifice is beyond the senses. 3.1.3. [26]

When he says, "Svāhā! The sacrifice from the mind," he undertakes it from the mind; when he says, "Svāhā! From the wide atmosphere," he undertakes it from the atmosphere; when he says, "Svāhā! From heaven and earth," he undertakes it from these two, heaven and earth, upon which all this rests; when he says, "Svāhā! I undertake from the wind," the wind indeed—
The sacrifice is indeed this [fire]; thus he begins the sacrifice visibly.
Now, when he says "svāhā!
svāhā!", the utterance "svāhā" is the sacrifice; he thereby places the sacrifice within himself right here.
He restrains his speech; for speech is indeed the sacrifice—it is the sacrifice itself that he thus places within himself. 3.1.3.
[28] Then he causes him to enter the hall.
He goes behind the Āhavanīya fire and in front of the Gārhapatya fire; this is his [path].

This is his path of movement for the sake of the Soma-pressing. Now, as this is his path of movement for the sake of the Soma-pressing—Agni is indeed the womb of the sacrifice, and the consecrated one is the embryo; for between the womb and the embryo the embryo moves.
Since he moves here and there, and turns hither and thither, therefore these embryos move and turn hither and thither. Therefore, this is his [path].
"Be attentive for the sake of the pressing. 3.1.4.
[1] Indeed, all the sacrificial formulas (*yajus*) of the consecration (*dīkṣā*) are *audgrabhaṇa* (lifting-up) formulas;
for he indeed lifts himself up by means of them.

When one who is consecrated (*dīkṣita*) ascends from this world toward the world of the gods, he supports himself by means of these very *yajus* formulas; therefore they say, "All the *yajus* formulas of the consecration are support-formulas" (*audgrabhaṇa*). Yet they call them specifically "the intermediate support-formulas," for they are indeed oblations (*āhuti*), and the sacrifice is an oblation. The *yajus* formula is muttered in a low voice (*parokṣa*), whereas this [other part] is...
The sacrifice is manifest when there is an oblation; by means of this sacrifice, he seizes the world of the gods from this world.
Then, as for those three [oblations] which he offers with the *sruva*-ladle, they call them the "studied *yajus*-verses" (*ādhītayajūṃṣi*) for the sake of completeness.

Then that which is offered as the fourth, and that which he offers with the *sruva*-ladle as the fifth—this indeed is the *audgrabhaṇa* offering in its manifest form; for he offers it with an *anuṣṭubh* verse. The *anuṣṭubh* is speech, and speech is the sacrifice. By means of the sacrifice, the gods [attained their supremacy]. 3.1.4. [3] By means of the sacrifice, the gods...

They won this victory which is theirs; they said, "How can this [world] of ours be made unassailable by men? Having sucked the essence of the sacrifice—just as honey-makers would suck out the honey—they drained the sacrifice, obstructed it with the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), and vanished. Then...
Because they chose it by means of this, therefore it is called the *yūpa*. Now, this was handed down by tradition among the seers (*ṛṣi*):
they collected the sacrifice; just as this sacrifice was thus collected, so indeed—
He prepares the sacrifice when he offers these oblations.
He offers five of them;
for the sacrifice is commensurate with the year, and there are five seasons in the year.
One obtains it by means of five; therefore, one offers five oblations.
Now, therefore, concerning the oblation itself:
"To Ākūti, to Prayuj, to Agni, svāhā!"—for at the outset, one forms the intention, "May I sacrifice."
Thus, whatever part of this sacrifice [is missing], that very thing he gathers together here and makes it his own:
"To Medhā, to Manas, to Agni, svāhā!
For it is by means of *medhā* (insight) and *manas* (mind) that one intends, "May I sacrifice. Therefore, whatever is here...
Having thus gathered these [materials] for the sacrifice, he places them within himself.
"To consecration, to austerity, to Agni, svāhā!"—this is merely spoken after the fact; it is not actually offered as an oblation.
"To Sarasvatī, to Pūṣan, to Agni, svāhā!

Sarasvatī is indeed speech, and the sacrifice is speech; Pūṣan is indeed cattle, for Pūṣan is nourishment, and nourishment is cattle; cattle are the sacrifice—therefore, whatever part of the sacrifice is here...
Having gathered that very [sacrificial essence], he makes it for himself.
Regarding this, they say: "These oblations are offered as if they were non-existent; they are without support, not directed toward the gods, and in them there is neither Indra, nor Soma, nor Agni."

"To Ākūti, to Prayuj, to Agni, svāhā!"—for Agni is indeed manifestly established; whatever one offers in the fire, by that very act these offerings become manifest and thereby established. Therefore, in all [oblations], one says, "To Agni, svāhā."
He offers; therefore, these are called the *ādhītayajus* formulas:
"To Ākūti, to Prayuj, to Agni, svāhā! For at the very beginning, one forms a mental intention (*ākūti*) within oneself, thinking, "May I sacrifice"; it is from that very self [that he acts].
That which he applies and that which he extends—these two deities, *ākūti* (intention) and *prayukti* (application), are established within his self.
"To *medhā* (insight), to *manas* (mind), to *agni* (fire), svāhā!"—for it is by means of insight and mind that one intends, "May I sacrifice"; these two belong to him.
The two deities, Medhā and Manas, are placed within the self. (3.1.4.14) [He offers with:
"Svāhā to Sarasvatī, to Pūṣan, to Agni!
Sarasvatī is indeed speech, and the sacrifice is speech.
This deity is deposited within his own self; speech is indeed Pūṣan, and Pūṣan is nourishment, for nourishment is cattle, and cattle are the sacrifice.
Thus, these cattle are deposited within his own self. Because these deities are deposited within his own self, they are called the *ādhīta-yajūṃṣi*. 3.1.4. [15]
Then he offers the fourth oblation with:
"O divine waters, vast, bringing welfare to all; O Heaven and Earth, and wide Atmosphere!
Let us worship Bṛhaspati with an oblation, Svāhā! This [verse] is indeed closer to the sacrifice, for it mentions the waters, and [the waters] are indeed [the essence].

"O Heaven and Earth, the sacrifice! O wide atmosphere!"—for thus he proclaims the worlds. "To Bṛhaspati let us pay homage with an oblation, Svāhā!"—Bṛhaspati is indeed the Brahman, and the sacrifice is the Brahman; by this [formula], this [offering] becomes closer to the sacrifice. Now, as for that which he offers with the ladle as the fifth [offering]:
That indeed is the manifest sacrifice, for he offers it with the *anuṣṭubh* verse; speech is the *anuṣṭubh*, and speech is the sacrifice.
Now, as for the clarified butter that remains in the *dhruvā* ladle...

He brings that [clarified butter] into the *juhū* ladle; three times he takes [butter] from the melting-pot into the *juhū* with the *sruva* spoon. That which he takes for the third time, he fills the *sruva* with it. 3.1.4. [18] He offers the oblation: "May every mortal choose the friendship of the god who leads; everyone seeks wealth; [may we obtain] glory..."
"Choose for our prosperity, Svāhā! (3.1.4.19).
This [verse] thus becomes a *paṅkti* by means of its deities: "Of every god... is for the Viśvedevas; "of the leader... is for Savitṛ; "the mortal... [is for Agni].
"May he choose" is for Mitra; "may he choose glory" is for Bṛhaspati—for Bṛhaspati is indeed glory; "may he prosper" is for Pūṣan.
This [verse] thus becomes a *paṅkti* by means of its deities.

The sacrifice is fivefold, the animal is fivefold, and there are five seasons in the year; he attains this very [fivefold nature] by means of this [verse], in that the *pañkti* consists of the deities.
He offers it with an *anuṣṭubh* verse.

Speech is the *anuṣṭubh*, and speech is the sacrifice; thus he directly attains the sacrifice. Regarding this they say: "One should offer this one alone for whatever desire [one may have], for by this very [offering] one attains that desire. If one were to offer it as a single [oblation], one should offer it full; for the full is indeed everything.
By means of this [offering], he obtains all this; and when he fills the *sruva* spoon, he thereby fills the *sruk* ladle, and he offers it when it is full.
This is merely stated figuratively, for indeed all [the oblations] are offered. 3.1.4.
[23] He offers it with an *anuṣṭubh* verse.

This very Anuṣṭubh consists of thirty-one syllables: ten fingers of the hands, ten toes of the feet, ten vital breaths, and the self as the thirty-first, in which these vital breaths are established. Such indeed is the person (puruṣa); the sacrifice is the person; the sacrifice is commensurate with the person. As great as the sacrifice is—
Whatever measure belongs to this [Anuṣṭubh], that much he thereby obtains when he offers with the thirty-one-syllabled Anuṣṭubh.
To the south of the Āhavanīya fire, he spreads out two black antelope skins with their necks pointing eastward.
He consecrates him over these two;
if there are two, that is the form of these two worlds, and thus he consecrates him over these two worlds. They have their ends joined together. 3.2.1 [2]
For these two worlds, as it were, have their ends joined;
behind them are the *tardma* (the opening) and the *samudra* (the ocean). Having thus made these two worlds a pair, he consecrates him upon them.
But if there is only one [opening],...

This is the form of these worlds; he thus consecrates him with respect to these worlds. Those which are white are the form of heaven; those which are black are the form of this [earth]. Or alternatively, those which are black are the form of heaven and those which are white are the form of this [earth]; and those which are brownish-yellow are the form of the intermediate region.
Thus he consecrates him over these worlds.
3.2.1.[4] He should then throw the *antaka* brick behind;
having thus paired these very worlds, he places him over them.
He initiates him.

3.2.1.[5] Then, behind the black antelope skin, he sits down to the west, facing east, with his knees bent. At the very place where the junction of the white and black hairs occurs, touching it thus, he mutters: "You two are the artistic forms (*śilpa*) of Ṛc and Sāman. For indeed...

"That craft is a fitting counterpart; you two are the counterparts of the Ṛg-verses and the Sāman-chants"—this is what he thereby says. "I take hold of you two. He who undergoes initiation becomes, as it were, an embryo; he enters into the meters.
Therefore he becomes like one with his fingers bent inward; for embryos are indeed like those with their fingers bent inward.

When he says, "I take hold of you two," he thereby means, "I enter into you two. When he says, "Protect me until the conclusion of this sacrifice," he thereby means, "Guard me until the completion of this sacrifice."
Then he mounts [the chariot] with his right knee, saying:
"Thou art protection; grant me protection. This is indeed the skin of a black antelope;
that is his human protection, while among the gods it is divine; therefore he says, "Thou art protection; grant me protection," and adds, "Homage be to thee!"

"Do not harm me!"—for he who mounts the sacrifice mounts something superior; the sacrifice is indeed the black antelope skin. Thus he makes a plea to that very sacrifice, and so the sacrifice does not harm him. Therefore he says: "Homage be to you;
do not harm me. 3.2.1. [9]
He should indeed sit at the very back, as it were.

For if he were to sit right in the middle at the beginning, and someone were to pull him away from there head-first, he would either vomit or fall down; it would surely happen exactly thus. Therefore, [he should sit] at the back.
He should sit facing the east. 3.2.1.[10] Then he puts on the girdle.
Indeed, the Aṅgirases found weakness in those who were consecrated.
They did not allow any food other than the vow-food; they perceived this as strength and as completion.

They placed that strength, which is completion, in the middle of their own selves, and by means of it, they reached completion. In the same way, this [sacrificer] now places that strength, which is completion, in the middle of his own self, and by means of it, he reaches completion. 3.2.1. [11]
It is indeed made of hemp;
for hemp is soft, so they say. When Prajāpati was born as an embryo from this sacrifice, that which was his innermost membrane became the hemp; therefore, hemp emits a pungent odor.

That which was his membrane became the garment of the consecrated; for the amnion is indeed internal to the membrane, therefore this [garment] is worn between the [other] garments. Just as Prajāpati was born from there after becoming an embryo from this very sacrifice, even so is he born from there after becoming an embryo from this very sacrifice. 3.2.1. [12]
It indeed consists of three parts;
for food is threefold, since cattle are food. The father is one part, the mother is the second, and that which is born is the third;
therefore it consists of three parts. 3.2.1 [13]
It is woven with a cord of muñja grass;
for the reed is a thunderbolt, and this serves to ward off the evil eye.
It is released in the manner of letting go of a tuft of hair; if it were released hitherward (prasalavi), it would be like other human ropes; if it were released awayward (apasalavi).
It belongs to the Pitṛs as its deity; therefore, it becomes a creation of the *stukā* (hair-tuft).
3.2.1.[14] He moves it aside with the formula:
"Thou art strength, belonging to Aṅgiras. For the Aṅgirases saw this strength; [he says], "O soft as wool, [place] strength in me."

"Place [it]"—in this there is nothing hidden. 3.2.1.[15] Then he conceals the fringe [of his garment] with the formula, "Thou art the fringe of Soma"; for previously, this belongs to one who is not initiated.
The fringe (nīvi) is present; now, this belongs to the consecrated Soma, therefore he says, "Thou art the fringe of Soma.
Then he covers himself;
for he who undergoes consecration becomes an embryo, and embryos are indeed covered by the amnion.
Therefore, he covers [the fire] as with a placenta.
He covers it, saying: "Thou art the protection of Viṣṇu; thou art the protection of the sacrificer. For he who is here becomes both of these.
Both Viṣṇu and the sacrificer undergo consecration. On the day he undergoes consecration, he becomes Viṣṇu; when he sacrifices, he becomes the sacrificer.
Therefore he says: "Thou art the protection of Viṣṇu, the protection of the sacrificer.
Then he ties the black antelope horn to his garment.

Both the gods and the asuras, the offspring of Prajāpati, came to the inheritance of their father Prajāpati. The gods took hold of the mind, while the asuras took hold of speech; thus the gods took hold of the sacrifice, and the asuras took hold of speech.
The gods took hold of yonder [heaven], while the asuras took hold of this [earth]. 3.2.1. [19]

Those gods said to the sacrifice, "This speech is indeed a woman; address her, and she will surely call out to you. Or rather, he himself considered: "This speech is indeed a woman; let me address her, and she will surely call out to me."
He invited her; she, however, showed resentment toward him from afar even at the very beginning.
Therefore, when a woman is invited by a man, she shows resentment from afar even at the very beginning. He said, "She has indeed shown resentment toward me from afar.
They said, "O Venerable One, invite her again; she will surely call you. He invited her again. She—
He spoke to her as if with his lips pressed together; therefore, when a woman is addressed by a man, she speaks as if with her lips pressed together.
He said, "She has indeed spoken to me as if with her lips pressed together.
They said, "Venerable sir, please address her further; she will surely call you. He addressed her, and she—

He did not call him; therefore, even today, a woman calls a man. He was the last to be called. He said, "They have indeed called me. Then the gods reflected: "This speech is indeed a woman; let us not leave her here alone. 3.2.1 [22]

"Go to him while he is standing," he said; "and when she has not yet arrived, report back to me. She then went to him while he was standing there. Therefore, even today, a woman goes to a man while he is standing after his consecration (*saṃskṛta*). When she had returned to them, he reported: "She has indeed come. 3.2.1 [23]

The gods withheld that [speech] from the Asuras; having taken it for themselves and enclosed it within Agni, they offered it as a complete oblation (*sarvahuta*), for the oblation is the food of the gods.

That very *anuṣṭubh* verse which they offered—that is how the gods then made it their own. Those Asuras, deprived of speech, saying "O wretches! O wretches! (*he 'lavas, he 'lavas*), were utterly defeated. 3.2.1 [24]
In this regard, they also uttered this saying:
"That barbarian (mlecha) is to be shunned; therefore, a Brāhmaṇa should not speak like a barbarian.
For that speech belongs to the Asuras; indeed, he takes away the speech of his hateful rivals, and they, being deprived of their speech, perish."
He who knows this thus—this very sacrifice thought of speech: "May I have union with her; may I become one with her. He had union with her.
Indra indeed reflected:
"A great monster will surely be born from here, from the union of the sacrifice and speech; let it not overcome me. Thereupon, Indra himself became an embryo within that union.
He entered. After he had been born for a year, he reflected:
"Powerful indeed is this womb that bore me."

"May no great divine monster be born after me, and may it not overcome me," he thought. Having reflected upon that, he enclosed it with a surrounding wall and built it up. He placed it upon the head of the sacrifice, for the sacrifice is Kṛṣṇa.

That which was the sacrifice is this black antelope skin; that which was the womb is this black antelope horn. And because Indra wrapped himself around it and lay upon it, therefore it is as if wrapped. Just as Indra was born from there, having become an embryo from this union, even so is he born from there, having become an embryo from this union. 3.2.1 [29]
Or he binds it as if turned face upwards;

for the womb bears the embryo as if turned upwards. Then he touches the forehead repeatedly above the right eyebrow, saying, "Thou wast the womb of Indra," for this is indeed the womb of Indra, or from that [place].
Entering her, he enters; or rather, being born from her, he is born. Therefore they say, "Thou art the womb of Indra.
Then he scrapes [the ground], saying, "Make the crops well-ripened. He thereby generates the sacrifice, for when there is a good harvest...
When it is sufficient for sacrifice, and when it is difficult to endure, then it is not even sufficient for oneself; thus he generates that very sacrifice. 3.2.1. [31] Now, he is not yet consecrated.
One might scratch with a piece of wood or with a fingernail; for he who undergoes initiation (*dīkṣate*) becomes an embryo.
If one were to scratch an embryo with a piece of wood or a fingernail, it would fall away and die; therefore, the initiated one would become afflicted with scabies (*pāmana*).
Or, following the initiated one, the seminal fluids [would be affected]; therefore, the seminal fluids would be produced as scabby. Therefore, one should not do so.

Indeed, it does not harm the seed; this black antelope horn is its own womb, and thus it does not harm him. Therefore, one who is consecrated should scratch himself only with the black antelope horn and with nothing else than the black antelope horn. 3.2.1 [32]
Then he hands him a staff.
The staff is indeed a thunderbolt, for the sake of warding off evil spirits.
It is made of Udumbara wood.
The udumbara is indeed food and strength; it is for the attainment of strength and the eating of food that it is made of udumbara wood.
It is made to the height of the mouth.
"Such indeed is its strength: as much strength as there is, so great it becomes when it is level with the mouth.
He raises it up.
"O Lord of the Forest, rise up; standing erect, protect me from evil until the conclusion of this sacrifice"—by saying this, he means "standing erect, guard me until the completion of this sacrifice.
At this point, some indeed bend down their fingers and restrain their speech, thinking, "From now on, there is nothing at all that we shall mutter."

Some say that one should not do it in that way; for just as if one were to pursue someone running away from him and fail to catch him, so indeed does he fail to obtain the sacrifice. Therefore, one should bend the fingers right there and request the speech right there. 3.2.1. [37]
Now, when one who is consecrated utters a Ṛg-verse, a Yajus-formula, or a Sāman-chant,
he thereby takes hold of the sacrifice firmly, indeed most firmly.

Therefore, he should restrain his fingers right there, or he should restrain his speech right there. Now, as to why he restrains his speech: the sacrifice is indeed speech; thus he places the sacrifice within himself. And as to why he is one who restrains his speech...

Therefore, when he speaks, this sacrifice, once released, turns away. In that case, one should mutter either a verse or a sacrificial formula addressed to Viṣṇu; for Viṣṇu is the sacrifice, and thus one takes hold of the sacrifice again. This is the expiation for it. 3.2.1.
[39] Now, some say:
"This Brahmin is initiated, this Brahmin is initiated"—by saying this, he announces him, who is already announced, to the gods, saying: "This one of great power has reached the sacrifice;
he has become one of you; protect him! He says this three times, for the sacrifice is threefold.
Regarding the sacrifice (yajña) 3.2.1 [40]:
Now, as for why he says "the Brāhmaṇa"—his prior birth was, as it were, non-existent; for thus it is said.
Rākṣasas pursue a woman; furthermore, it is said that Rākṣasas alone deposit the seed [in her].

Yet, truly, he is born who is born from the Brahman and who is born from the sacrifice. Therefore, one should call even a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya a "Brāhmaṇa," for he is born from the Brahman and born from the sacrifice. Therefore they say: "One should not kill a performer of the Soma-sacrifice, for he is a sinner."
"Indeed, she is one who has performed the pressing. 3.2.2.1 He restrains his speech.
Restraining his speech, he remains seated until sunset; that is why he restrains his speech. 3.2.2.2

By means of sacrifice, the gods indeed won this victory which is theirs; they said, "How can this [victory] of ours be made unassailable by men? Having extracted the essence of the sacrifice, as bees [extract] honey, they...
Having milked out the sacrifice and having obstructed it with the sacrificial post (yūpa), they disappeared;
and because they obstructed it with this, it is called the "yūpa.
This, indeed, was heard by the seers (ṛṣis) as a traditional report.
They brought together the sacrifice; just as this sacrifice was brought together, so indeed does he who undergoes initiation bring together the sacrifice. Speech, indeed, is the sacrifice.
At sunset, he releases that speech.

Prajāpati is indeed the year, and Prajāpati is the sacrifice. The year consists of day and night, for these two, revolving around it, bring it about. He was consecrated on the day; he reached the night.
Having thus obtained the sacrifice in its entirety—whatever its extent and whatever its measure—he releases his speech. 3.2.2. [5]

Now, some release their speech upon seeing a star, saying, "At this point, [the sun] has set according to the rule. One should not do so; for what would happen if there were clouds? Therefore, one should release speech at the very moment one considers the sun to have set according to the rule. 3.2.2. [6]
Because of this, some release their speech, saying, "Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ! We cause the sacrifice to swell; we join the sacrifice together.
One should not do so; for he neither causes the sacrifice to swell nor does he join it together.
He who releases his speech with this [formula], 3.2.2.[7] should release his speech with this very one:
"Perform the vow! Perform the vow! Agni is the Brahman; Agni is the sacrifice."

"The tree worthy of sacrifice"—for this indeed becomes his sacrifice here; it is the oblation just as the *agnihotra* was of old. Thus, having gathered the sacrifice by means of the sacrifice, he establishes the sacrifice upon the sacrifice; he extends the sacrifice by means of the sacrifice, for his vow remains continuous until the pressing day. He says [the formula] three times, for the *trivṛt* is threefold.
The Sacrifice (Yajña) 3.2.2. [8]:
Now, having turned toward the fire, he releases his speech.
He indeed neither causes the sacrifice to swell nor does he restore it, who [does not do so] from this point.
Or he releases speech by means of another; when he speaks first, he utters the truth of speech:
"Agni is Brahman"—for Agni indeed is Brahman; "Agni is the sacrifice"—for Agni indeed is the sacrifice; "the tree worthy of sacrifice."

"Thus, the trees are indeed worthy of sacrifice; for if there were no trees, humans would not be able to sacrifice. Therefore he says, 'The tree is worthy of sacrifice. Then they cook the sacrificial food (vrata) for him.
He who undergoes consecration approaches the gods; he becomes one of the deities.
The sacrificial oblation of the gods must indeed be cooked, not uncooked; therefore they cook it. This very person consumes it as his fast-food (vrata), but he does not offer it in the fire.
That is why this very person consumes it as his fast-food, but does not offer it in the fire. 3.2.2. [11]

By means of the sacrifice, the gods indeed won this victory which is theirs; they said, "How can this [victory] of ours be made unassailable by men? Having extracted the essence of the sacrifice, as bees [extract] honey, they...
Having milked out the sacrifice and having obscured it with the sacrificial post (yūpa), they vanished; and because they obscured it with this [post], therefore it is called the *yūpa*.
This, indeed, was heard by the seers (*ṛṣi*) as a traditional report.

They brought together the sacrifice just as this sacrifice was brought together; for he who undergoes initiation (dīkṣate) is indeed the sacrifice here, since it is he who extends it and he who generates it. Thus, whatever of the sacrifice has been drained away here and whatever has been milked out, that very thing he causes to swell again by means of this very vow (vrata).
One does not offer an oblation in the fire, nor should one cause it to swell; for if one were to offer an oblation in the fire, one would think that one is indeed offering while not offering.
3.2.2. [13] These, indeed, are the vital breaths (*prāṇa*):
born of the mind, yoked by the mind, possessing skill and resolve; speech is the fire, and the out-breath and in-breath are the two ladles.

Mitra and Varuṇa are the eye, Āditya is the ear, and the Viśve Devas are these [plants]. Thus, it is indeed into these deities that his offering becomes offered. 3.2.2. [14] Now, some, at the first fast-day, sow both rice and barley, thinking, "By means of both juices, whatever there is here..."

Saying, "Whatever has been drained from the sacrifice, whatever has been milked out—that we shall replenish," if the cow that yields the *vrata* milk should not yield, he may perform the *vrata* for whomever he desires from this point on; for thus both rice and barley remain in contact with him. However, he should not do it in that way, for he does not thereby replenish the sacrifice.

He does not join together [the two grains]; for he who sows both rice and barley, it is for this reason that one should sow only one or the other. Indeed, these two—rice and barley—are his sacrificial oblation (*havis*). Since these two constitute his *havis*, they remain in contact with it. However, if the cow yielding the fast-milk (*vratadughā*) should not yield, he may perform the fast-rite with whatever he desires from that point onward. 3.2.2. [15]

Now, some people, at the first vow, throw in all kinds of herbs and all kinds of fragrant substances, thinking, "If affliction should befall the consecrated one, he may treat it with whatever he desires; let him treat it as if by means of the vow.
But one should not do so; for they are performing a human act at the sacrifice, and that is indeed a failure of the sacrifice.

Thinking, "I shall perform that which is human and not unsuccessful at the sacrifice," if affliction should befall the consecrated one, he should treat it with whatever means he desires, for completion alone is meritorious.
Then he hands over the vow-food to him.

Having passed the human time—namely, evening-milked [milk] in the latter part of the night and morning-milked [milk] in the afternoon—he distinguishes it by means of the *vyākṛti* formula; for he thus distinguishes both the divine and the human. 3.2.2. Then, about to give him the vow-food (*vrata*), he makes him touch water.

"We meditate upon the divine intellect, the most gracious, for our aid—the bestower of splendor, the bearer of sacrifice; may it provide us with good paths. For previously he cleansed himself for human hunger, but now for the sake of the divine intellect; therefore he says, "We meditate upon the divine intellect."
"May she be very gracious for our aid, bestowing splendor and carrying the sacrifice; may she be for us a good ford and a source of power.
With this [verse], whenever he is about to undertake any vow whatsoever, he should touch water; with this alone he should touch it.
Then he undertakes the vow.
"Those gods who are born of the mind, yoked by the mind, possessing skill and wisdom—may they protect us;
may they guard us; to them, svāhā! Thus, this becomes for him like an oblation offered with the *vaṣaṭ* call. Then, having observed the vow, he touches his navel.
"O Waters, become refreshing when drunk;

be very gracious within our bellies. May those divine, immortal waters, which increase the *ṛta*, be sweet for us—free from consumption, free from disease, and free from sin. Indeed, he who undergoes consecration (*dīkṣā*) approaches the gods; he becomes one of the deities.

The oblation for the gods must indeed not be over-sprinkled; otherwise, the one who gives the vow (the *vrata-prada*) acts falsely by sprinkling over the vow and thereby violates the vow. This [formula] is the expiation for that: thus it does not become a false act for him, nor does he violate the vow. Therefore he says: "O waters, may you, when drunk, be refreshing."

"May they, who are very gracious within our bellies, may those goddesses—free from disease, free from sickness, and sinless—enjoy us, they who are immortal and increase the cosmic order (*ṛta*). Having observed whatever vow he has undertaken, he should touch his navel with this [formula]. For who knows whether the one who bestows the vow might pour out the vow? 3.2.2. [20]
Then, where he is about to urinate, he strikes a clod of earth or something else with the black antelope horn, saying:
"This is your sacrificial body. For this earth is indeed the goddess Devayajanī; she must not be defiled by the consecrated one. Of her—

Having grasped this very sacrificial body, he then urinates upon his non-sacrificial body with the formula, "I release the waters, not offspring. For both of these come from here: water and seed. He thus releases only the water, not the offspring, with the words, "Releasing from distress, consecrated by Svāhā! For they indeed release themselves from distress—that which was pent up within the belly.
"Therefore, [he says], 'O you who release from distress, svāhā! Enter the earth. Having thus become oblations, he says this: "Enter the earth, being pacified. 3.2.2. [21]
Then he places a clod of earth [on the footprint].
This earth arises from the earth; she is indeed the goddess Earth, the place of sacrifice for the gods.
She must not be defiled by one who is consecrated (*dīkṣita*). Therefore, having lifted up her sacrificial body, he [places the clod] so as to remove what is non-sacrificial.
He sprinkles his body; he thereby bestows upon it that very body of his which is fit for sacrifice. Therefore he says, "Be united with the earth. Then, having entrusted himself to Agni, he sleeps.
He who undergoes consecration (*dīkṣā*) approaches the gods; he becomes one of the deities.

Now, the gods do not sleep, yet sleep has not been secured for him. Agni is the Lord of Vows (*vratapati*) among the gods; having entrusted himself to him, he sleeps. "O Agni, may you be well awake; we [shall be] well..."

"May we be refreshed," O Agni—"you be awake while we sleep"—this is what he says. "Protect us, being vigilant"—this is what he says, meaning "guard us without negligence. "Make us wakeful again"—this is what he says, meaning "act so that after sleeping from here, we may wake up safely. 3.2.2. [23]
Then, at the place where one has slept and is about to rise again, he causes him to recite: "May my mind return; may my life-span return;
may my breath return; may my self return; may my sight return; may my hearing return to me. All [of this].

Verily, these [senses] depart from one who sleeps; indeed, it is the vital breath (*prāṇa*) alone that does not. Having slept with them, one reunites with them again. Therefore he says: "Mind has returned to me, life has returned to me; breath has returned to me, the self has returned to me; sight has returned to me, hearing has returned to me; may Agni Vaiśvānara, the undeceivable protector of the body, protect us."

"From misfortune, from blame"—this means that whatever wrong deed has been done here either in sleep or by [waking] thought, "from all that may Agni protect us," this is what he says. Therefore he says: "May Vaiśvānara, the undeceivable, the protector of bodies, Agni, protect us from misfortune, from blame. 3.2.2. [24]
Now, when one who is consecrated speaks what is unrighteous or becomes angry, he performs a falsehood and violates his vow;
for the consecrated man must indeed be free from anger. Agni is the lord of vows among the gods; it is to him that he thus resorts.

"O Agni, you are the guardian of vows, a god among mortals; you are to be praised at the sacrifices"—this is indeed the expiation for that [transgression]. Thus, this act of his does not become wrongly performed, nor does he violate his vow. Therefore he says:
"O Agni, you are the guardian of vows, a god among mortals; you are to be praised at the sacrifices. 3.2.2. [25]
Now, when they bring [gifts] to one who has been consecrated (*dīkṣita*), he causes him to recite:
"O Soma, grant this; bring more! For indeed, that which they bring to the consecrated one is offered to him as Soma. When he says, "O Soma, grant this," he means "grant it to us."
"Is this much Soma?"—this is what he says; "Bring more!"—this is what he means by saying, "Bring us more.
"May the divine Savitṛ, the giver of wealth, give us wealth"—thus, impelled by Savitṛ, this [Soma] becomes available for him to give.
Prior to sunset, he speaks.

He says, "Initiate, restrain your speech," and he releases that speech after sunset, before sunrise; he says, "Initiate, restrain your speech," and he releases that speech at sunrise. This is for the sake of continuity; thus he connects the day with the night and the night with the day. 3.2.2. [27]
One should not follow after him as he moves elsewhere;

one should not rise before him as he sleeps. For if one were to follow after him as he moves elsewhere, one would exclude him from the night; and if one were to rise before him as he sleeps, one would exclude him from the day.

Because it is contained within that [rite], there is no expiation for this; one must simply guard against it. One should not descend into water before the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*), nor should rain fall upon him. For it is improper that he should descend into water or that rain should fall upon him before the *avabhṛtha*. Furthermore, he speaks speech that is distorted or indistinct, but never ordinary human speech.
Now, as for why he speaks with a faltering voice and not in ordinary human speech:
by means of the sacrifice, the gods won this victory which is theirs; they said, "How shall this [victory] be ours? 3.2.2. [28]

Thinking, "Let it be unassailable by men," they sucked out the essence of the sacrifice—just as honey-makers would suck out honey—and having drained the sacrifice and blocked it with the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), they vanished.
And because they blocked it with this [post], therefore it is called the *yūpa*. 3.2.2. [29]
Or rather, this was heard by the seers:

they gathered together the sacrifice; just as that sacrifice was gathered together, so indeed does he who undergoes initiation gather the sacrifice. Speech is the sacrifice; therefore, whatever of the sacrifice has been lost here—

That which has been milked, he causes that very thing to swell again by speaking speech that is faltering; for were he to speak human speech that is fluent, he would not cause it to swell. Therefore, he speaks speech that is faltering, not human speech that is fluent. 3.2.2. [30]
He indeed consecrates himself;

for he consecrates himself for speech, for he consecrates himself for the sacrifice, for the sacrifice is speech. "Consecrated" (dīkṣita) is truly a name for that which is consecrated for speech. 3.2.3.1.
He offers a pap of cooked rice to Āditya as the introductory oblation.

For when the gods were performing the sacrifice on this earth, they excluded her from the sacrifice; she then caused their sacrifice to become confused, thinking, "How is it that the sacrifice [is performed] without me?"
"Let them not exclude me from the sacrifice by thinning it out," he thought; but they did not recognize that sacrifice.
They said, "Since we have indeed forgotten the sacrifice in this very [sacrifice], how is it that it has not increased for us, and how is it that we do not recognize it?"
They said, "While performing the sacrifice upon this very [earth], we have excluded her from the sacrifice; it is she who has confounded our sacrifice. Let us resort to her. 3.2.3.
[4] They said, "Since we have forgotten the sacrifice in you alone, how was it confounded for us? How did it not [confound us]?"
"We understand," they said.
She replied: "Weaving the sacrifice within me alone, you have excluded me from the sacrifice. Therefore, it was I who caused your sacrifice to be confounded.
Now, provide a portion for me; then you shall see the sacrifice, and then you shall understand it."

"So be it," the gods said. "The *prāyaṇīya* (opening oblation) shall be yours alone, and the *udayanīya* (concluding oblation) shall be yours. Therefore, this very Āditya becomes the *prāyaṇīya*, and Āditya becomes the *udayanīya*; for this earth is indeed Aditi. Then they beheld the sacrifice and performed it. 3.2.3 [7]

When he offers the *caru* for Aditi as the introductory oblation (*prāyaṇīya*), it is for the very purpose of beholding the sacrifice; thinking, "Having beheld the sacrifice, I shall purchase [the Soma] and extend it," he therefore offers the *caru* for Aditi as the introductory oblation. That [oblation], once poured out...
The sacrificial oblation was present, but the deity had not yet been sacrificed to.
Then Pathyā Svasti became pleasing to them; they sacrificed to her, for Pathyā is indeed Speech.
"May there be well-being; speech is the sacrifice. Seeing that sacrifice, they performed it.
Then Agni became dear to them.
They sacrificed with him; whatever part of the sacrifice belonged to Agni, they saw that. Whatever indeed... [3.2.3.9]

That part of the sacrifice which was dry and related to Agni, they perceived and performed it. Then Soma became pleasing to them; they sacrificed with it, and whatever part of the sacrifice was related to Soma, that they perceived. Or rather... 3.2.3. [10]
That which was moist in the sacrifice was the essence of Soma; they saw it and spread it out.
Then Savitṛ shone forth to them;
they sacrificed to him, for Savitṛ is indeed cattle, and cattle are [the means].

They saw that sacrifice; they performed it. Then, for whichever deity the oblation had been set aside, they sacrificed to her. These, indeed, are the five deities to whom he sacrifices. That sacrifice which was bewildered—verily, it was fivefold.
The seasons were bewildered; they recognized them by means of these five deities. The seasons were bewildered; they recognized them by means of these very same five deities.
The five directions were bewildered;
they discerned them by means of these very five deities: the northern direction alone.
3.2.3.[15] The northern direction alone.

They discerned [the way] by means of the path and well-being; therefore, here speech speaks more loudly from the north, among the Kurus and Pañcālas, for this speech is so called by its very origin, since they discerned the northern direction by means of it, and the northern direction belongs to it.
[They recognized] the eastern direction alone.

They discerned it by means of Agni; therefore, having taken up Agni from behind toward the east, they worship him, for by him they discerned the eastern direction, and the eastern direction belongs to him. 3.2.3. [17]
[They] discerned the southern direction by means of Soma; therefore, they carry the purchased Soma toward the south.
Therefore they say, "Soma has the Pitṛs as its deity," for by means of it they discerned the southern direction, and the south belongs to him.
The western direction: they recognized the western direction through Savitṛ. He who shines yonder is indeed Savitṛ; therefore, this [is so].
They went toward the west, for by means of this [fire], they recognized the western direction; for the western direction belongs to it.
They recognized the upward direction by means of Aditi; for Aditi is indeed this earth, and therefore upon her the plants grow upward.
The trees grow upright, for by this direction they recognized the upward; for this direction is indeed upward. 3.2.3.[20] The guest-offering (*ātithya*) is indeed the head of the sacrifice;
the introductory and concluding offerings (*prāyaṇīya* and *udayanīya*) are the arms; for the arms are on both sides of the head.
Therefore, you have these two oblations as hospitality from him: the Prāyaṇīya and the Udayanīya.

Regarding this they say: "Whatever is performed at the Prāyaṇīya should be performed at the Udayanīya; whatever serves as the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) for the Prāyaṇīya, that same serves as the sacrificial grass for the Udayanīya. Having removed it, he sets aside that vessel.

Having wiped the stirring-spoon, which has become somewhat emaciated, he sets it down. Those who are the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) of the introductory sacrifice (*prāyaṇīya*) are the same as those who are the officiating priests of the concluding sacrifice (*udayanīya*). In that this same [procedure] is performed in the sacrifice, by that the two arms are similar;
by that they are of the same form. 3.2.3. [22]

One should not do it in that way. One may indeed throw this sacrificial grass (barhis) into the fire; having washed the stirring-spoon (mekṣaṇa), one should set down the vessel (sthālī). Those who are the officiating priests (ṛtvij) of the Prāyaṇīya sacrifice are the same who are the officiating priests of the Udayanīya sacrifice.
If they were distinct, they would indeed be different; but because he sacrifices to the same deities and the oblations are the same, his two arms are thus similar and thus of the same form.
He sacrifices to five deities at the introductory offering (prāyaṇīya).

There are five [oblations] at the *udayanīya* sacrifice; therefore, there are five fingers here on this side, and it concludes with the *śamyu*-formula. They do not perform the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings. For the arms are the forepart of one's own body;
thus he prepares the forepart of the sacrifice. Therefore, it concludes with the *śamyu*-formula, and they do not perform the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings.
They perform the *saṃyājana* offerings. 3.2.4.
[1] Soma was indeed in heaven.
Now the gods were here on earth; those gods desired, "May Soma come to us; once he has arrived, [we shall use him]."

"Let us sacrifice! they said, and they created these two illusions, Suparṇī and Kadrū; this is explained in the Brāhmaṇa concerning the *dhiṣṇya* hearths in the section on Suparṇī and Kadrū, how that came to be.
Then Gāyatrī flew away toward them, carrying the Soma.
As she was bringing it, the Gandharva Viśvāvasu stole it away.
The gods realized, "Soma has indeed slipped away to the other side; that is why he does not come to us; the Gandharvas have surely stolen him. 3.2.4. [3]

They said, "The Gandharvas are indeed lustful for women; let us send Vāc (Speech) to them, and she shall come back to us together with Soma. They sent Vāc to them, and she came back to them together with Soma. Having followed after them, those Gandharvas said:

"Soma is yours, but speech is ours," they said. "So be it," the gods replied. "If he has come here, do not let him escape; let us call her away. They called her away. 3.2.4. [5] For her, the Gandharvas...
"We know this—we know this," they said, "that we shall proclaim the Vedas alone.
Then the gods, having fashioned a lute, sat down playing it and singing, saying, "We shall sing thus;
we shall delight you. That [lute] turned toward the gods; indeed, that which turned toward them was in vain.

She turned away from those who were praising and reciting toward dance and song; therefore even now women are considered to have "vain intentions," for speech thus turned away toward them, and other women follow after her. Consequently, it is toward him alone who dances or sings that these [women] are most intensely attracted.
Now, both of these were among the gods:

Soma and Speech. In that he purchases Soma, it is so that he may sacrifice with what has arrived; for he sacrifices with Soma that has not arrived who sacrifices with [Soma] that has not been purchased. 3.2.4. [8]
Then, whatever clarified butter remains in the *dhruvā* vessel, he portions it out four times into the *juhū* ladle;
having tied a piece of gold with a blade of sacrificial grass (*barhis*) and placed it therein, he offers it, thinking, "May I offer with the entire quantity of milk," for they share a common origin.
"Indeed, both milk and gold have Agni as their seed.
He places the gold down with the words, "This is thy bright body, O Śukra; this is thy luster. For gold is indeed luster.
"Go to her for union, go to Bhrāja. When he says, "Go to her for union," he means "Be united with her";
when he says, "Go to Bhrāja," Soma indeed is Bhrāja, so he means "Go to Soma. 3.2.4.
[10] Just as the gods did then...
They sent forth Soma; and in this very same way, he now sends her forth for the purchase of Soma.
For the cow used to buy Soma is, in its essential nature, Speech; he gratifies her with this oblation so that, being gratified, she may purchase the Soma.
3.2.4. He offers it, saying: "Thou art swift" (*jūrasi*). Now, "thou art swift" is indeed one of her names. "Held by the mind" (*dhṛtā manasā*); for by the mind...

"This speech is held by the mind; for the mind indeed precedes speech [when one says], 'Speak thus; do not speak that. For if the mind were not present, speech would indeed speak incoherently. Therefore he says, 'Held by the mind. 3.2.4. "Pleasant to Viṣṇu."

"Approved for Soma," he thereby says; "whomsoever we shall worship," he says; "at the impulse of thee, whose impulse is true," he says, "be thou of true impulse for us"; "bring Soma hither for us," he thereby says; "may I attain the support of my body, Svāhā!"—verily, he who reaches the conclusion of the sacrifice attains the support of his body, [he who reaches] the conclusion of the sacrifice.
"Come hither," he thereby says.
Then he takes out the gold;
he thus makes the gold among men. As for why it is with gold—
He should offer it away; for he would thus be extracting gold from among men, and that gold would not be found among men. He then draws it out.

Having offered the entire quantity of milk with the formula, "Thou art bright; thou art shining; thou art immortal; thou belongest to the All-gods," he says this very thing when he says, "Thou art bright," for it is indeed bright; "thou art shining," for it is indeed shining; "thou art immortal," for it is indeed immortal; "thou belongest to the All-gods," for it indeed belongs to the All-gods. Having released [the vessel],...
He throws a blade of grass onto the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) and ties a piece of gold with a cord.
Then, having taken another four spoonfuls of clarified butter, he says, "Yajamāna, hold on! and they uncover the hall.

At the gate, on the right side, she stands as the Soma-purchase cow (*somakrayaṇī*). He has thus sent her forth while she is already dispatched; for the Soma-purchase cow is, by its very nature, Speech. By means of this oblation, he has sent her forth with the thought, "With her being gratified, I shall purchase the Soma. 3.2.4. [16]
Then, having gone out, he consecrates [the horse] with:
"Thou art consciousness (cit), thou art mind (manas). For this speech follows after the mind or the thought (citta).
With [the words], "Thou art intelligence (dhī), thou art skillful (dakṣiṇā)," for by means of this very intelligence, human beings desire to live on through what has been recited, as it were.
As if with spontaneous verses, as if with *gāthās*, he therefore says, "Thou art wise," [and] "Thou art the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*)," for she is indeed the sacrificial fee;

"Thou art a Kṣatriya, thou art worthy of sacrifice," for she is indeed a Kṣatriya and she is indeed worthy of sacrifice; "Thou art Aditi, double-headed. In that he speaks of what is common as being reversed—that which is subsequent he places before, and that which is prior [he places after]—[it is thus].
The next [verse] is "by that one with two heads"; therefore he says, "Thou art Aditi with two heads.
"May she be well-disposed toward us from the front and well-disposed toward us from behind. 3.2.4. [17]
"Be well-disposed toward us; come hither for our Soma"—this is what he says by this.
"Be well-disposed toward us; come back with our Soma"—this is what he says by this. Therefore he says: "Be well-disposed toward us, both forward and backward. 3.2.4. [18]
"May Mitra bind you by the foot," he says.

For this rope belongs to Varuṇa; if it were bound with a rope, it would belong to Varuṇa; if it were not bound at all, it would be as if it had slipped away. Therefore, that which belongs to Mitra is free from Varuṇa.
Just as it happens for one who is bound by a rope, so it is with this [verse] when he says, "May Mitra bind you by the foot.
Regarding the words, "May Pūṣan protect the paths":
Pūṣan is indeed this earth; and he whose protector on the path is this [earth], for him—
"No stumbling occurs at all; therefore he says, 'May Pūṣan protect the paths.
When he says, "For Indra, the overseer," he thereby says, "May he be one who has a good overseer. Thus [he says] after [the verse].

"May the mother permit, may the father, may the brother from the same womb, and may the friend from the same herd permit. By this he means to say: "Permitted by them according to that birth of yours, go to press the Soma. "Go, O Goddess, to the God," he says; for she is a goddess and goes to a god, namely to the Soma; therefore he says, "Go, O Goddess, to the God. "The Soma for Indra," he says; for Indra indeed—
The deity of the sacrifice is therefore addressed as "Soma for Indra. With the words, "May Rudra turn you back," he says this so that there may be no destruction; for cattle do not pass beyond Rudra.
With the words, "Come back again, O friend of Soma," he says this: "Come back to us safely with Soma. 3.2.4. [21]
Just as the gods then sent her forth to Soma and she came back to them together with Soma, even so does he now send her forth to Soma and she comes back to him together with Soma. 3.2.4. [22]
Just as of old the gods called her away from the Gandharvas and she returned to the gods,
even so does the sacrificer now call her away and she returns to the sacrificer.
They step beyond it toward the north, for the north is the direction of men;
this is indeed the direction of the sacrificer, therefore they step beyond it toward the north.
He steps along seven paces.
He thus wins her; therefore he strides after her seven steps. For when the meters were born from Speech, the *śakvarī* consisting of seven feet was their most excellent.
It is that very *śakvarī* which he thereby wins, turning it away from the beyond toward this side; therefore he strides after her seven steps. 3.3.1 [2]
He indeed follows along by means of the very form of speech:
"Thou art a Vasu; thou art Aditi; thou art Ādityā; thou art Rudrā; thou art Candrā.
For she is indeed a Vasu, she is indeed Aditi, she is indeed Ādityā, she is indeed Rudrā, she is indeed Candrā. "May Bṛhaspati place thee in happiness..."
"May he find rest"—Bṛhaspati is indeed the Brahman; "may Bṛhaspati turn you back with what is good," this is what he thereby says.
"May Rudra with the Vasus lead you back"—this he says for the sake of non-destruction, for cattle do not go beyond Rudra.
3.3.1. [3] Then they sit down around the seventh footprint.

Having placed gold in her footprint, he offers it; for indeed, no oblation is offered in that which is not fire. Gold is indeed the seed of Agni; thus this oblation of his becomes one offered in that which possesses fire.
Ghee is indeed a thunderbolt; by means of this thunderbolt, the ghee, he overcomes her, and having overcome her, he makes her his own. 3.3.1. [4]
He offers with [the formula]: "Aditi has heated thee on her head. Aditi is indeed this earth, for he offers on her head.
"On the earth's place of sacrifice"—for he offers on the earth's place of sacrifice.
"Thou art the footprint of Iḍā, rich in ghee, svāhā!"—Iḍā is indeed the cow, for he offers at the cow's footprint. "Rich in ghee, svāhā! he says.
For this becomes as if offered with clarified butter.

3.3.1.[5] Then, taking up the wooden sword (*sphya*), he traces around [the altar]. The wooden sword is indeed a thunderbolt; it is thus by means of the thunderbolt that he traces around it three times.
He draws around it; thus, by means of the threefold thunderbolt, he encloses it on all sides so that [the enemy] may not pass beyond.
He draws around it, saying, "Rejoice in us!"—this indeed means, "Rejoice in the sacrificer! Then, having scraped up the soil, he takes the footprint.
He pours [the grain] into the pot with the words, "Thy kinship is with us"; by this he means to say, "Thy kinship is with the sacrificer. Then he pours water down [into the pit].
For wherever they injure it while digging, they strike it dead.
Water is peace; with that water, by means of peace, he pacifies it, and with that water, he unites it. Therefore, he pours water upon it.
Then he hands over the footprint to the sacrificer [with the words], "In thee, riches. Riches indeed are cattle; thus, "In thee, cattle."
Thus he says this; when the sacrificer accepts [the gift], saying "May wealth be mine," "wealth" indeed refers to cattle, so he thereby says, "May cattle be in me.
Then the Adhvaryu touches himself.
"May we not be separated from the increase of wealth"— thus the Adhvaryu does not exclude himself from the cattle.
Then they carry away the footprint of the wife.
The house is indeed the support for the wife;
thus he establishes her in that very support, in the house. Therefore, they carry away the footprint of the wife. 3.3.1. [11]
The Neṣṭṛ makes her recite:
"Hither wealth... Then he causes her to look at the Soma-purchase cow; for Soma is indeed a male and the wife is a female, and here the Soma-purchase cow becomes Soma—this is a productive union.
Therefore, he causes her to look at the Soma-purchase cow.
He causes her to look, saying: "I have looked with the divine intellect, with the far-seeing Dakṣiṇā; do not diminish my life."
"May I not forget you; may I, O Goddess, find a hero in your sight"—this is the very blessing he invokes.
A hero is indeed a son; thus he says, "May I find a son in your sight. 3.3.1 [13] Now, she who is brown with reddish-brown eyes...
That is the cow for purchasing the Soma. Wherever Indra and Viṣṇu divided a thousand [cows] into three parts, one remained over; they brought that one forth by dividing it into three.
Therefore, even now, if anyone were to divide a thousand into three parts, one would remain over. 3.3.1. [14]

She who is brown with reddish-brown eyes is the one for purchasing Soma; she who is ruddy is the "Vr̥tra-slayer," which the King here brings forth after winning a battle. And she who is ruddy with white eyes is sacred to the Fathers—the one whom they bring here for the Fathers.
They strike [the cow].
3.3.1.[15] That which is brown with reddish-brown eyes—
that should be the *somakrayaṇī* (the cow for purchasing Soma), provided that one does not find a brown one with reddish-brown eyes.
If one cannot find a reddish-brown cow, it should be a reddish one that destroys enemies; for by killing a reddish cow, one might as well lead toward the hope of obtaining a white-eyed one.
It should be a cow that has not been impregnated.
This Soma-purchase cow is indeed speech as its source. This speech is not exhausted; it is unexhausted when it is unbarren. Therefore, she should be unbarren.

She should be one that is not mutilated—neither hornless, nor with deformed horns, nor one-eyed, nor earless, nor marked with a defect, nor seven-hoofed; for she is uniform, and this speech is indeed uniform. 3.3.2.1.
Having poured out the portion, he washes his hands.
As to why he washes his hands: ghee is a thunderbolt and Soma is seed;
[he does this] thinking, "Lest I injure the seed, Soma, with the thunderbolt, ghee. Therefore, he washes his hands. 3.3.2. [2]
Then he ties gold to it.
This world is indeed twofold; there is no third: truth and falsehood.
The gods are truth, and human beings are falsehood. Gold is indeed the seed of Agni; with truth I shall touch the stalks.
"By means of truth, may I drive away Soma," [he thinks]; therefore, indeed, he binds gold to her. Then he issues the command:
"Bring the Soma-cloth! Bring the Soma-wrapper! Bring the turban! He...

Whatever is beautiful should be the Soma-wrapper; for this is his garment, and his garment is indeed beautiful. He who serves him with something beautiful truly shines. Now, as for those who say, "Whatever it may be," since whatever it happens to be [is acceptable], therefore, whatever is beautiful should be the Soma-wrapper, and whatever it may be.
[He should use] the Soma-wrapping cloth (somaparyāṇahana). 3.3.2.
[4] If he should find a turban (uṣṇīṣa), it should be a turban;
if he does not find a turban, [he should use] the Soma-wrapping cloth itself.
The Adhvaryu or the sacrificer cuts off the uṣṇīṣa-vessel by two or three finger-breadths;
whoever it may be takes the *somopanaha* (the cloth for wrapping the Soma) and the *somaparyāṇahana* (the cloth for binding the Soma).
Then they search for the King [Soma] in front of him.
