Then a water-pot is placed nearby; a Brāhmaṇa sits beside it, and they approach it facing eastward.
As they are coming, he causes them to recite: 3.3.2. [6] "As they are coming... (he causes them to recite).
"Say this for me to Soma: 'This is your Gāyatra portion'; say this for me to Soma: 'This is your Triṣṭubh portion'; say this for me to Soma: 'This is your Jagatī portion';
say this for me to Soma: 'Go to the sovereignty over the names of the meters. For indeed, when he is being purchased, he is purchased as one [of these].
"They slay him indeed when they press him;
therefore he says this: 'I purchase you for the sovereignty of the meters, for the imperial sway of the meters, not for slaughter.
Then, having gone forward, he sits down facing the east. 3.3.2. [7]
He touches it, saying, "Thou art ours," for when he has arrived, this [cup] becomes as if his own; therefore he says, "Thou art ours.
He says, "The *śukra* is to be drawn from thee," for he is about to draw the *śukra* cup from it. He says, "May they sift thee, being themselves sifted."
He says this for the sake of completeness.

3.3.2.[8] Here, some people, having picked up a blade of grass or a piece of wood, throw it away; but one should not do so. Soma is indeed the *kṣatra* (the ruling power), and other plants are the *viś* (the common folk). The *viś* is the food of the *kṣatriya*. It is as if, after swallowing something, one were to spit it out and discard it.
He should thus throw it away; then he should touch it again with the formula, "May they find you, searching for you. Thus, those who are his searchers find him.
3.3.2. [9] Then the garment: he spreads out a double or a quadruple fold, either with the fringe toward the east or with the fringe toward the north, over which he places the king.
He measures. Because he measures the King (Soma), therefore there is a measure among men, and whatever other measure exists as well.
He measures with the Sāvitrī verse.
Savitṛ is indeed the impeller of the gods; thus, for him, this [act] is indeed impelled by Savitṛ.
It serves for purchase (3.3.2.11).
He measures with an *aticandas* [verse].
This *aticandas* indeed contains all the meters; thus, for him, this [purchase] is performed by means of all [the meters].
It is measured by means of meters; therefore, he measures it with the *aticandas* meter.
He measures: "I praise that god Savitṛ, who is within the two bowls, whose wisdom is that of a seer, whose impulse is true, the bestower of jewels—the beloved, the sage of thought."
Whose lofty intelligence has shone forth for the sake of impulsion—the golden-handed one of good wisdom has measured out the light with his form.
(3.3.2)[14] With this [verse]; with all [of them];
with these four; with these three; with this.

With two [verses], with this one, with this one, with this one—[that is,] with three; with this one, with this one, with this one—[that is,] with four; with all [of them] together, he pours [the grain] from his joined palms into the mortar.
He measures it out while moving both upwards and downwards.

When he measures out both upwards and downwards, he thereby makes these fingers distinct from one another; therefore they are born separate. But if he were to measure with all [the fingers] together, they would indeed be born as if stuck together; therefore he measures out both upwards and downwards. 3.3.2. [16]

Or rather, when he measures out the *udāc* and the *nyāc*, he thereby makes these [fingers] possessed of diverse powers; therefore these have diverse powers, and for this reason he measures out the *udāc* and the *nyāc*. 3.3.2. [17]
Moreover, when he measures out the *udāca* and the *nyāca*, he thereby yokes both the *virāj* that is turned away and the one that is turned toward [us].
Turned away, it carries the sacrifice to the gods; turned toward [us], it protects human beings. Therefore, indeed, there is the *udāca* and the *nyāca*.
He measures [the Soma]. Now, as to why he measures ten times:
the Virāj consists of ten syllables, and Soma is of the nature of the Virāj; therefore, he measures ten times.
He measures [it]. Then, having drawn together the ends of the Soma-wrapper, he ties it with a turban, saying: "For the sake of offspring, thee!"
For he purchases this [sacrifice] from the subjects; thus, he now makes for it that very part which here [in the body] is as if pressed between the head and the shoulders.
Then, in the middle, he leaves a space with his finger.
"Let the subjects breathe after you," he says.
For by having yoked him together, as it were, he has made him, as it were, breathless; thus, from that very center, he releases his breath for him.
Then, as he breathes, the subjects breathe after him. Therefore he says, "Let the subjects breathe after you. He—
"He gives it to the seller of Soma; now, therefore, follows the very act of bargaining.
He indeed bargains with the King (Soma).
Because he bargains with the King, therefore all this [world] is once for all a commodity for sale. He says:

"O Soma-seller, is your King Soma for sale? "He is for sale," says the Soma-seller. "Then I shall buy him from you," [says the Adhvaryu]. "Buy him," says the Soma-seller. "I shall buy him from you for a sixteenth part (kalā)," [says the Adhvaryu]. "King Soma is surely worth more than that," says the Soma-seller.
"King Soma is indeed worth more than that; however, the greatness of the cow is great," says the Adhvaryu. 3.3.3. [2]
The fresh milk of the cow; from that, boiled milk; from that, curdled milk; from that, whey; from that, the thickening agent;
from that, fresh butter; from that, clarified butter; from that, the solid curds (*āmikṣā*); from that, the whey (*vājina*). 3.3.3. [3]
"I will buy [Soma] from you for a hoof," he said.

"King Soma is indeed worth more than that," replied the Soma-seller. "King Soma is indeed worth more than that," said the Adhvaryu, "but great indeed is the greatness of the cow. He [the Adhvaryu] takes these same ten [cows].

Having enumerated the various forms of effort (*vīrya*), he says: "I buy from you for a foot, for half [of you], for a cow. The seller of Soma says: "King Soma has been bought," and then, "Declare the birds!
He replies: "The moon is your garment; a goat is yours; a milch-cow is yours; a pair of cattle is yours; three other [cattle] are yours. Thus he speaks.
Because they bargain for it beforehand and complete the transaction afterwards, therefore this entire thing is bargained for beforehand and completed afterwards.
Now, while the Adhvaryu alone proclaims the powers of the cow, the Soma-seller does not proclaim those of the Soma;
for Soma is indeed exalted, since Soma is a god. Therefore, the Adhvaryu magnifies the cow, and for her—
"Beholding the manly powers, let him buy," he says; therefore, it is the *adhvaryu* alone who enumerates the manly powers of the cow, not the Soma-seller.
Then, as for why he barters five times:

The sacrifice is indeed commensurate with the year, and there are five seasons in the year; he attains it by means of five [stages], therefore he bargains five times. Then he makes him recite over the gold.

"I buy thee, the bright, with the bright," for he buys this bright one with the bright, namely Soma with gold; "the radiant, with the radiant," for he buys this radiant one with the radiant, namely Soma with gold;
"the immortal, with the immortal," for he buys this immortal one with the immortal, namely Soma with gold. 3.3.3. [7]

Then he shakes the Soma-seller, saying, "In thy cart is the cow"; by this he means, "In thy [possession], O sacrificer, is the cow. Having brought it toward the sacrificer, he sets it down, saying, "In us be thy bright ones. He then says: "O Soma-seller, do thou look on; we shall look on thee. The seller of Soma places his vigor in himself; he takes away only the body. Therefore, it is from the seller of Soma that [the buyer] receives it.
3.3.3.[8] Then, while facing westward toward a goat, he makes him recite:
"Thou art the body of austerity. For this [goat] is indeed the body of Prajāpati, born of austerity.
Since she was born from that which is unborn, he says, "Thou art the body of austerity. She is the color of Prajāpati;

in that she brings forth three times in the course of a year, she is the color of Prajāpati. "Thou art purchased with the supreme animal," for in that she brings forth three times in the course of a year, she is the supreme animal. [May she grant] a thousandfold prosperity.
"I may prosper"—this is the very blessing he invokes here. A thousand is indeed abundance; "May I attain abundance," this is what he says.
He gives the goat with this [verse], and with this he takes the king (Soma). This goat is indeed named *ājā*; it is by means of her that he [attains] the king.
For he drives him toward it from behind; this they call "driving" (ājati) in an indirect sense (*parokṣa*). 3.3.3. [10] Then he takes up the King (Soma):
"As a friend, come to us, O bestower of good friends"—by this he says, "Auspicious and peaceful, come to us. He...
Having pushed aside the garment on the sacrificer’s right thigh, he places [the Soma] down with the words, "Enter Indra’s right thigh.
For the sacrificer here indeed becomes Indra; therefore he says, "Enter Indra’s right thigh.
With the words, "Eager, the eager," he means "the beloved, the beloved. With the words, "Gentle, the gentle," he means "the auspicious."
"He says 'Auspicious'—that is what he says. [3.3.3.11] Then he points out the Somakrayaṇas:
"Svāna, Bhrāja, Aṅghāri, Bambhāri, Hasta, Suhasta, Kṛśānu—these!"
"O Soma-purchasers, guard these [cows] of yours; let no one deceive you. These are indeed the portions of the *dhiṣṇya* hearths;
these are the names of the *dhiṣṇyas*, and he thus points them out to them by their very names.
Then, at this point, he uncovers [his head].

He who undergoes consecration (*dīkṣate*) becomes, as it were, an embryo; embryos are indeed covered, as by the caul and the placenta. Him they have now brought forth here; therefore he uncovers himself. He indeed becomes an embryo here; therefore he is covered, for an embryo is, as it were, covered by the caul and the placenta. 3.3.3 [13]
Then he causes him to recite: "O Agni, protect me from evil conduct; do not abandon me, but grant me a share in good conduct. While he is seated, this [Agni] approaches him;
when he has arrived, he rises up. That makes it false; he violates his vow. For him, this [is the expiation].
"Thus indeed is his expiation; this act of his does not become false, nor does he fail in his vow. Therefore he says:
'O Agni, protect me from evil conduct; grant me a share in good conduct.
Then, taking up the King (Soma), he stands up.

"By our life-span, by our own life-span, we have risen up after the immortals. For he who rises after the purchased Soma rises after the immortal; therefore he says, "By our life-span, by our own life-span, we have risen up after the immortals. Then, taking the King (Soma), he approaches the ascent.
"We have set out upon the path that leads to well-being, free from danger,
by which one avoids all enemies and finds wealth. (3.3.3.16) Indeed,
the gods, while performing the sacrifice...
They were terrified by the attachment of the *asuras* and *rakṣases*;

they beheld this *yajus* as a means of well-being (*svastyayana*). By means of this *yajus*, having struck away the destructive *nāṣṭras* and *rakṣases*, they attained well-being in the safety and freedom from destruction provided by this *yajus*. In the same way, this [sacrificer] now, by means of this *yajus*, [strikes away] the destructive...
Having struck down the *rakṣases* by means of this *yajus*, he attains well-being in a state free from fear, free from harm, and free from wind; therefore he says:
"We have reached the path that leads to well-being and is free from danger, by which one avoids all enemies and finds wealth.
They carry it away, saying "That indeed! They transport it by means of a cart; they thus magnify it. Therefore, they carry the seed on the head and bring it back by means of a cart. 3.3.3. [18]
Now, as to why he purchases [the Soma] at the edge of the waters:

the waters are indeed essence; thus he purchases it together with its essence. And as to why there is gold: he purchases it together with its brilliance. And as to why there is a garment: he purchases it together with its skin. And then...

In that it is a goat, he thereby purchases it with penance; and in that it is a milch-cow, he thereby purchases it with the *soma*-mixture (*āśira*); and in that there are two of them as a pair, he thereby purchases it with a pair. He should indeed purchase it with ten [cows], not with fewer than ten; for the *virāj* consists of ten syllables, and Soma is of the nature of the *virāj*; therefore, he should purchase it with ten.
One should purchase [the soma] with ten [cows]. 3.3.4.1.
He spreads a black antelope skin in the nest, saying:
"Thou art the skin of Aditi"—that is indeed the same as before.
A kinsman makes him mount it, saying, "Mount the seat of Aditi. This earth, indeed, is Aditi; she is this foundation.
Thus he establishes him upon this very foundation. Therefore he says, "Mount the seat of Aditi.
Then, having approached it in this manner, he causes him to recite:
"The bull has propped up the sky and the mid-air," he says.

Indeed, the gods, while performing the sacrifice, were afraid of an attack from the Asuras and Rakṣasas; they made him (Agni) greater than even a weapon by saying, "The bull has propped up the sky and the mid-air. 3.3.4. [3]
"He measured out the breadth of the earth"—by this he wins over these worlds; for there is neither slayer nor killer of him by whom these worlds have been won.
Therefore he says, "He measured out the breadth of the earth. 3.3.4. [4]

"He has sat down as sovereign over all beings"—thereby he makes all this world secure for himself; for there is no slayer and no killer of him by whom all this has been made secure. Therefore he says, "He has sat down as sovereign over all beings. 3.3.4. [5]

"All these are the ordinances of Varuṇa"—by this he makes all this that exists whatsoever conform to his will, so that there is no one who stands against him; therefore he says, "All these are the ordinances of Varuṇa.
Then he wraps it around with the Soma-wrapper.

"Lest the destructive Rākṣasas seize it"—for this [sacrificial cake] becomes an embryo, and embryos are, as it were, concealed; this [cake] when wrapped is, as it were, concealed. The gods are, as it were, concealed from men, and this [cake] when wrapped is, as it were, concealed; therefore he wraps it. 3.3.4. [7]
He girds it on [with the verse]:
"In the forests he has stretched out the intermediate space. For in the forests this intermediate space is indeed stretched out, among the tops of the trees.
"Speed in the horses, milk in the cows"—speed is indeed vigor; the stallions are males.

"He places this vigor in males; milk in the cows"—for indeed, this milk is placed within the cows. "Varuṇa [placed] wisdom in hearts, Agni among the people"—for this wisdom, swift as thought, has entered into the hearts; "Agni among the people"—for he is indeed among the people, among the subjects. "He placed Sūrya in heaven, Soma on the rock"—for yonder Sūrya is indeed placed in heaven.
"Thou hast placed Soma upon the mountains," he says, for Soma is indeed on the mountains; therefore he says, "Thou hast placed Sūrya in heaven and Soma upon the mountains.
Now, if there are two black antelope skins, he fastens one of them [to the pole]; this is the practice regarding the fastening.
If there is only one [antelope skin], having cut off its neck, he fastens it back on;
[with the verse]: "The eye of Sūrya, the pupil of Agni's eye, ascend thou, shining with the wise Etasas, wherewith thou goest.
He thus places Sūrya in front; Sūrya in front [drives away] the destructive spirits (*nāṣṭrā*).
Driving away the *rakṣas* demons, he approaches; then they carry [the fire] around with a state of fearlessness and freedom from evil.
When the two boards have been raised and the *udgītha* chanted, the *subrahmaṇya* priest stands between them and urges [the horse] forward.
This [chariot] becomes superior through its ascent; for who indeed is worthy of ascending it? Therefore, standing between [the two poles], he drives.
He drives with a branch of the *palāśa* tree.
When Gāyatrī flew toward Soma, her foot was cut off as she was bringing him away.
Having rushed forward, she cut off a leaf—either of Gāyatrī or of King Soma. Having fallen, it became a *parṇa* (leaf);
therefore it is called *parṇa*. [He thinks: "Whatever of Soma is deposited here, let that also be present here."
Therefore, he drives [the oxen] away with a Palāśa branch (3.3.4).
Then they drive two oxen forward;
if both of them should be black, or if one of them is black, then—
"One should know: 'This year Parjanya will rain; it will be a year of abundant showers'—this is the knowledge. 3.3.4. [12] Then he yokes them with:
"O two oxen, you who are bearers of the yoke! For they are indeed oxen, and they are indeed bearers of the yoke.
"May you two be joined as non-slaughterers," he says; for "non-slaughterers" means "unharmed.

"As those who do not slay heroes," he says; that is, "as those who do no evil. "As impellers of the sacred word (*brahman*)," he says; for they are indeed impellers of the sacred word. "Go in safety to the house of the sacrificer," he says, so that no destructive spirits or demons (*rakṣas*) may [assail] them on the way.
For they would thus cause injury; this is what he says. 3.3.4.
[13] Then, having walked around by the rear and reached the support-beam, he says: "Recite for the purchased Soma!"—for Soma.
"Being carried around," [he says], as the wind may desire in whichever direction. Then he makes [the sacrificer] recite:
"Thou art auspicious for me; move forward, O Lord of the World! For this [wind] indeed becomes auspicious for him.
Therefore, he does not honor anyone else; even kings who are his equals come to him, and he salutes the king first, for he is indeed auspicious (*bhadra*);
therefore he says, "Thou art auspicious unto me. With the words, "Descend, O Lord of the World," for he is indeed the lord of the worlds;
with "Over all abodes," the "all abodes" are the limbs, and thus he addresses the very limbs.

"May those who lie in ambush not find you; may those who waylay you not find you; may the malevolent wolves not find you"—by saying this, he means that they should not find him on the way, just as the destructive spirits (*nāṣṭrā*) and demons (*rakṣāṃsi*) would not find him.
"Having become a hawk, fly away! [3.3.4.15] he says.
He causes it to fly away as soon as it has become a bird; for verily, the *nāṣṭra* demons do not follow after that which is fierce. This is indeed the swiftest and strongest among birds;
he thus causes it to fly away as soon as it has become that [bird]. When he says, "Having become a hawk, fly away," [he effects this]. 3.3.4. [16]
Then they carry the body itself away, saying, "Go to the house of the sacrificer; there it shall be prepared for us. There is nothing here that is obscure. 3.3.4. [17]

Then he calls the Subrahmaṇyā. Just as one would say to those for whom he intends to cook on a certain day, "On such-and-such a day I shall cook for you," even so does he announce the sacrifice to the gods, saying: "Subrahmaṇyo! Subrahmaṇyo! three times.
For Brahman indeed causes the gods to move forward; he says it three times, for the sacrifice is threefold.
"O Indra, come!"—Indra is indeed the deity of the sacrifice; therefore he says, "O Indra, come! O Lord of Bay Horses, come!"
"O Medhātithi! O bull of Vṛṣaṇaśva! O Menā! O Gaurāvaskandin! You have begotten [a son] for Ahalyā!"—by these very words, which are his own modes of address, he thereby seeks to delight him.
"O Kauśika! O Brāhmaṇa! O you who call yourself Gautama! [he says].
This has always been known by Āruṇi;

"O Gautama, as you say. If he should so desire, he may speak thus; but if he should not so desire, he need not pay heed to it. "On which day is the Soma-pressing? [He replies: "On such-and-such a day is the pressing. 3.3.4. [20]
"O gods and Brahmins, come! He said this to both the gods and the Brahmins, for there is need here of both—of both the gods and the Brahmins. 3.3.4 [21]
Then the Pratiprasthātṛ stands before the hall with the animal victim for Agni and Soma;
for Agni and Soma place him within their jaws who undergoes initiation, since that initiatory offering belongs to Agni and Viṣṇu.
He who is Viṣṇu is indeed Soma; he who consecrates himself becomes that very oblation.
Thus they place him between their jaws, and by means of the victim, he ransoms himself.
Now, some indeed bring a firebrand from the Āhavanīya fire, saying, "This is Agni, this is Soma; together with these two..."
Saying, "We shall extract it from the two good ones," they do not, however, act in that manner; for wherever these two are, there they are always together.
That [fire-altar], indeed, becomes of two forms.

For it belongs to two deities; they say that because of the inequality of the two deities, it should be a black-spotted antelope, for this is its most perfect form; if one should not find a black-spotted antelope, then it may also be a red-spotted one. 3.3.4. [24]
While he recites over it:
"Homage to the eye of Mitra and Varuṇa; pay worship to that great god, the truth!
To the far-seeing, god-born banner, to Sūrya, the son of Heaven, speak forth!"—he thereby pays homage to him.
"By this, he indeed creates a bond of friendship.
3.3.4 [25]. Then the Adhvaryu releases the mounting-block;
with the formula, "Thou art the support of Varuṇa," he props it up with the support-pole, [saying] "The loosener of Varuṇa's pillar."

"Ye are firm," with these words he draws up the two wedge-blocks. When he says, "Ye are the releasers of Varuṇa's bolt," it is because the Soma, once purchased, now belongs to Varuṇa. Then four men take up the king’s throne.
Two men take [the sacrificial fee] for this human king,
but four take it for him who rules over all at once.
It is made of udumbara wood.
The udumbara tree is indeed food and strength; it is for the attainment of strength and the eating of food that the post is made of udumbara wood.
It reaches up to the navel.
In this place food is established, and Soma is food; therefore, it reaches up to the navel.
In this very place is the receptacle of semen, and Soma is semen; therefore, it reaches up to the heart.
He touches it.

With the words, "Thou art the seat of Varuṇa in the abode of Truth," he then spreads the black antelope skin with the words, "Thou art the seat of Varuṇa in the abode of Truth. Then he places him [the Soma] upon it with the words, "Sit thou on the seat of Varuṇa in the abode of Truth. As for why he says, "Sit thou on the seat of Varuṇa in the abode of Truth," it is because at this moment he (Soma) becomes related to Varuṇa. 3.3.4. [30]
Then he causes him to enter the hall;
while causing him to enter, he makes him recite: "May those abodes of yours which they worship with oblation—may you encompass all those at this sacrifice."
"May you, O Soma, who increase the field, who bring across, who are rich in heroes, and who do not slay heroes, enter our dwellings.

For "duryāḥ" means dwellings; he thereby says, "May you, who are auspicious, peaceful, and free from evil-doing, enter our dwellings. Regarding this, some here pour out a vessel of water, thinking, "Just as one brings water for a king who has arrived, so is this."

Regarding this, they say: "One should not do it in that way, for they perform what is human at the sacrifice; and whatever is human in the sacrifice is a failure of the sacrifice. Thinking, 'Lest I should cause a failure in the sacrifice,' one should therefore not pour water down.
The guest-offering (*ātithya*) is indeed the head of the sacrifice, while the introductory (*prāyaṇīya*) and concluding (*udayanīya*) offerings are its two arms.
The arms are indeed on both sides of the head; therefore, these two oblations, the Prāyaṇīya and the Udayanīya, are on both sides of the Ātithya.
Now, as to why it is called the Ātithya.
This purchased Soma indeed comes as a guest to this [sacrificer].
Therefore, just as one might cook a large bull or a large goat for a king or a Brahmin—that being a human oblation for the gods—so does he perform this hospitality for him. 3.4.1. [3]
Regarding this they say: "One should take it after passing by on the left. For when they do not show respect to an Arhat who has arrived, he indeed becomes angry there;
thus he is properly honored.
Alternatively, one of the two may be liberated [from the debt].

If one [of the two] were not yet liberated, then he should take [the vessel]; for since the other was liberated, he has arrived [as a guest], and since the other was not liberated, he has been honored. One should not do it in that way; rather, having first set [the victim] free and then led it forward, he should take [the vessel]. For such indeed is the conduct of the gods. 3.4.1.[5] That is how it should be.

It follows the nature of human beings; therefore, as long as he has not released [the horse] among men, they do not bring water for him nor do they pay him honor, for he is not yet arrived. But when he releases it, then they bring water for him and pay him honor, for then he has truly arrived. Therefore, one should let him loose and lead him forward.
He should take [the water].
He should take it as if in a hurry; thus he becomes honored. His wife then takes hold of him from behind.

The sacrificer indeed follows along while it is being carried around; then here the wife also follows along from both sides as a couple. For when a worthy person arrives, all the members of the household move about there as if they were his dependents; in this way, he becomes honored. 3.4.1 [7]

Or rather, he should take it with another *yajus* than that, or with the same one used for other oblations; for when this [Soma] is being purchased, he is purchased as a single portion for the sovereignty of the meters, for the imperial rule of the meters. For him—
Just as the subordinate kings, who are not kings themselves but perform the duties of a king, stand in attendance around a king, so too do the *caṇḍas* stand in attendance around him on all sides.
This is not indeed plausible.

If one were to take [the draught] only with the formula "To the metres," then those who cook for an Arhat would be excluded from participation on both sides—namely, the non-kings among the king-makers, such as the Sūtas and Grāmaṇīs; therefore, wherever one takes [the draught] for this [deity], there alone one should include the metres in the distribution. 3.4.1. [9]
He takes it up with the formula: "Thou art the body of Agni; for Viṣṇu, thee! Indeed, Agni is the Gāyatrī; thus he causes the Gāyatrī to participate.
With "Thou art the body of Soma; for Viṣṇu, thee!"—Soma is indeed the Kṣatra, and the Kṣatra...
He thus causes the *triṣṭubh* to participate in that *triṣṭubh*:
"Thou art the guest-offering for the guest; for Viṣṇu, thee! This is his special portion (*uddhāra*), just as there is a special portion for the most excellent; even so is this his.
"Except for the meters" (3.4.1.12):
"For the Śyena, the bearer of Soma; for Viṣṇu, thee!"—thereby he causes the Gāyatrī to participate. Since that Gāyatrī is the Śyena...

Having become a falcon, he brought the Soma from heaven; therefore that falcon is the bearer of Soma. By means of that very power, he thus causes her to share in a second portion. "For Agni, the giver of the increase of wealth; for Viṣṇu, thee! [he says].
Cattle indeed are the increase of wealth, and cattle are the *jagatī*;
thus he causes the *jagatī* to participate in that.
Now, as to why he draws [the cup] five times:

The sacrifice is indeed commensurate with the year, and there are five seasons in the year; he attains it by means of five [drawings]. Therefore, he draws five times. And as to why he draws [saying], "For Viṣṇu thee! For Viṣṇu thee!", it is because he draws for Viṣṇu—whosoever draws for the sacrifice, he draws for Viṣṇu. 3.4.1. [15]
There is a cake on nine potsherds.
The guest-offering (ātithya) is indeed the head of the sacrifice. The Gāyatrī consists of nine syllables:
there are eight syllables which he recites, and the *praṇava* is the ninth. The Gāyatrī is the fore-part of the sacrifice; this [cake] is in the fore-part.
Therefore, for this sacrifice, there is a cake on nine potsherds (puroḍāśa).
The enclosing sticks (paridhi) are made of *kārṣmarya* wood.
Indeed, the gods [prepared] this [wood] among the trees as a slayer of demons (*rākṣoghna*).
They saw that the *kārṣmarya* tree was indeed the head of the sacrifice; [they used it] so that the destructive *rakṣas* demons would not injure the head of the sacrifice.
Therefore, the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) are made of *kārṣmarya* wood.
The *prastara* grass-bundle is made of *aśvavāla* grass.
The sacrifice indeed departed from the gods; it became a horse and turned away.

The gods, pursuing it, seized its tail-hairs and plucked them out. Having plucked them out, they threw them down together, and from that these plants arose—namely, the *aśvavāla* grasses. The guest-offering (*ātithya*) is indeed the head of the sacrifice, and the tail-hairs are its hind part.
In this way, he encloses the sacrifice on both sides when the *prastara* is made of *aśvavāla* grass.

The two separating blades (*vidhṛtī*) are made of *ikṣu* grass, so that the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) and the *prastara* do not become entangled. Then, having purified the clarified butter, all [the substances] indeed—
He takes four portions of clarified butter, for there are no after-offerings (anuyājas) here.
Having placed the oblations, he churns the fire;
for the guest-offering is indeed the head of the sacrifice; they thus produce it.

This which they churn is indeed [the production] of him; for one being born is born first from the head, and so he thus generates the sacrifice first from the head. Agni is indeed all the deities, for in Agni they offer to all the deities; the Guest-offering (ātithya) is the head of the sacrifice, and thus he endows the sacrifice with all the deities from the very head.
Therefore, he churns the fire (3.4.1.20). He takes a splinter for the churning, [reciting]:
"Thou art the birthplace of Agni," for it is here that Agni is born.
Therefore he says, "Thou art the birthplace of Agni. (3.4.1.21) Then he places two young *darbha* blades [upon it], saying, "Ye two are stallions.
Just as these two [testicles] are born together with a woman, so indeed are these two. (3.4.1.22)

Then he places the lower churning-stick (adharāraṇi) with the formula, "Thou art Urvaśī. Then he touches the upper churning-stick (uttarāraṇi), which is used for melting the clarified butter, with the formula, "Thou art Āyu," and he places it [upon the lower stick] with the formula, "Thou art Purūravas. For Urvaśī was a nymph (apsaras) and Purūravas was her husband. Then...
That which was born from that union was *āyus* (life-force). In this very same way, he generates the sacrifice from this union.
Then he says: "Recite for Agni as he is being churned! 3.4.1.
[23] He churns.
"With the Gāyatrī metre I churn you; with the Triṣṭubh metre I churn you;
with the Jagatī metre I churn you"—with these metres he indeed churns him.
He recites the metres for the one being churned; he thus causes the metres to follow the sacrifice, just as the rays [follow] that sun.
"Recite for the one born," he says when [the fire] is born; "for the one being cast forward," as he casts it forward. He casts it forward [with the words]:
"May you two be of one mind for us, of one thought, free from blemish; do not harm the sacrifice."
"O Jātavedas, be auspicious today to the lord of the sacrifice," he says; he thus utters this peace for them so that they may not harm one another.
Then, having taken up clarified butter with the *sruva* spoon...

He makes an oblation into the fire with the verse: "Fire moves within fire, having entered it; the son of the seers, the protector against curses—may he, being gracious, sacrifice for us here with a good sacrifice, never neglecting the oblation for the gods, svāhā! For they have indeed generated this [fire] for the sake of the oblation.
He sent him forth with this oblation; therefore he offers in this manner.
That [offering] ends with the *iḍā*;
they do not perform the after-offerings (*anuyāja*s). The guest-offering (*ātithya*) is indeed the head of the sacrifice, and the head is the forepart.

He thus prepares the forepart of the sacrifice. If he were to perform the after-offerings (*anuyāja*), it would be as if, having carried [the head] around from the top, one were to set the feet back on; therefore, it ends with the *iḍā*, and they do not perform the after-offerings. By means of the Guest-offering (*ātithya*), the gods, having sacrificed, [attained their goal].
When they had attained that state of equilibrium, they dispersed in four directions, unable to endure one another’s splendor:
Agni with the Vasus, Soma with the Rudras, Varuṇa with the Ādityas, and Indra with the Maruts;
Bṛhaspati with the Viśvedevas—so say some—but those who are these [others] are indeed the Viśvedevas.

They fled in four directions; as they were fleeing, the Asuras and Rakṣases pursued them from behind. They realized: "We have indeed become worse off; the Asuras and Rakṣases have pursued us from behind. We are surely falling into the power of our enemies. Come, let us agree among ourselves and stand for the glory of one. So they [stood] for the glory of Indra.
They stood still; therefore they say, "Indra is all the deities; Indra is the best of the gods.
Therefore, indeed, his own people should not act with hostility toward one another.
Whosoever among them becomes as it were more distant, he falls away from them. They...
They do what is pleasing to their enemies and fall victim to those enemies; therefore, one should not be distressed.
For he who, knowing this, is not distressed, does what is displeasing to his enemies and does not fall victim to them; therefore, one should not be distressed.
They said: "Come, let us act in such a way that this [world] shall belong to us alone, from time immemorial, and be our undecaying possession."

Those gods gathered together their beloved bodies and dear abodes. They said, "By this [means] he shall be distinct from us; by this he shall be dispersed—whoever among us should transgress this. "Of whom shall he be the witness? they asked.
"Of Tanūnapāt Śākvara," they replied. Now, this very Tanūnapāt Śākvara is the witness of living beings.
These two, prāṇa and udāna, have entered it. Therefore they say:
"The gods do not know the mind of a human being," for one forms intentions with the mind.

That [mind] enters into the vital breath (*prāṇa*); the vital breath enters into the wind (*vāta*); the wind reports it to the gods, just as the mind of a person [reports]. 3.4.2. [7] Therefore, this has been declared by the Seer (*ṛṣi*):
"One wills with the mind; that enters into the wind; the wind [reports it] to the gods."

"He tells [the truth], O man, as to what your mind is," thus [it is said]. 3.4.2. Those gods gathered together their beloved bodies and dear abodes; they said, "By this may he be separated from us, by this may he go astray—he who would transgress this of ours. Even now, the gods do not transgress that; for who indeed...?
For were they to transgress this, they would indeed speak untruth. The gods observe one single vow: truth alone.

Therefore, their victory is invincible and their glory is such; likewise, for him who, knowing this, speaks the truth, his victory becomes invincible and his glory is such. This, then, is the *tānūnaptra* by way of its origin. 3.4.2. [9]

Those gods gathered together their beloved bodies and dear abodes; then these [sacrificers], taking portions of the clarified butter, gather together their beloved bodies and dear abodes. Therefore, one should not descend together with everyone, thinking, "Lest my beloved bodies and dear abodes descend together with theirs. By which...

He should descend together [with him] and should not act treacherously toward him; for they say this: "One must not act treacherously toward one who performs the *anūnaptra* rite. 3.4.2. [10] Now, therefore, he draws [the cup], saying: "I draw thee for the one who flies hither, for the one who flies around. Verily, he who blows here is indeed this [wind]. And...
"He falls and he flies around," for it is from him that he draws [the draught]; therefore he says, "I draw thee for the Lord of Falling, for the Lord of Flying Around.
"For Tanūnapāt, for Śākvara," for he who blows here is indeed Tanūnapāt, the Śākvara; it is from him that he draws [the draught].
Therefore he says, "To Tanūnapāt, the powerful one" (3.4.2.12), [and] "to the most mighty of the powerful.
He indeed is the most mighty of the powerful; for it is for him that he draws [the libation]; therefore he says, "of the powerful."
"Ojiṣṭhāya" (3.4.2.13).
Now, therefore, they indeed touch [the victim] together.
For the gods gathered this [victim] more fully, thinking, "In this way, may he be ours."
"Lest he, being in yonder world, should pass us by"—thinking thus, they come together to this same point, saying, "In this way, lest he, being in yonder world, should pass us by.
3.4.2. [14] They touch one another.

"Unassailable, unassailable is the vigor of the gods"—for the gods were indeed unassailable, being together and speaking with one accord, holding fast with one accord; "the vigor of the gods"—these are indeed the bodies dear to the gods, their beloved abodes; "beyond reproach, protectors against reproach, beyond the reach of reproach."

"For all the gods have crossed over every curse; 'May I straightway attain truth,' he says—this means, 'May I speak the truth; may I not transgress my mind. 'Place me in well-being,' he says—for in well-being the gods placed themselves when they spoke the truth and performed what was true; therefore he says, 'Place me in well-being. 3.4.2. [15]
Now, those beloved bodies and dear abodes which the gods had gathered together, they deposited them all in Indra.
This one who shines yonder is indeed Indra; for in the beginning, he did not shine forth as he does now.

This other [sun] is indeed black; it was thus, and by that very power it burns. Therefore, if many should undergo initiation, they should hand over the fast-food (vrata) after pouring it out for the householder alone, for he becomes their vessel for Indra. But if one should undergo initiation accompanied by sacrificial gifts (dakṣiṇā), they should pour out the fast-food for the sacrificer himself.
For they say this: "Indra is indeed the sacrificer.
Now, those beloved bodies and dear abodes which the gods had formerly set aside together—that was [the portion] set aside together.
He struck it; that became the *sāman*. Therefore they say, "The *sāman* is truth; the *sāman* is born of the gods.
Now, after the gods had performed the *ātithyeṣṭi*, discord (*samad*) overcame them.
They stilled that discord by means of the *tānūnaptra* rites. This is its...
They sought an atonement for one another's sin; they did not speak of it until after the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*).
They prepared a second consecration (*dīkṣā*), and they perceived this intermediate consecration.
They then had their skin girt with fire itself.
Austerity indeed is Agni, and austerity is the consecration; they underwent that intermediate consecration. Because they underwent that intermediate consecration, it is called the *avāntaradīkṣā*.
They drew their fingers closer together and drew their girdle closer together; thus they tightened it while it was already fastened.
In the same way, whatever unrighteous act he has performed or unrighteous word he has spoken prior to this,
he thereby effects an expiation for that very thing. He then causes his skin to be turned inside out by means of fire alone.

Austerity indeed is Agni, and austerity is the consecration (*dīkṣā*). Thus he enters an intermediate consecration; he makes his fingers closer together, and he makes his girdle (*mekhalā*) closer together. This very girdle, which was already wound around, he now winds around once more. By that means, the gods attained progeny. 3.4.3. [4]
They burned their skin with fire;
for fire is the maker and progenitor of the couple, and thus they attained offspring. They drew their fingers closer together and drew their girdle closer together.
They took that offspring into themselves; and in the same way, this [sacrificer] now approaches that very offspring.
He envelops himself with a skin by means of fire alone;
for fire is indeed the maker of the pair, the progenitor.
He obtains offspring for that [person]; he weaves the fingers more closely together and weaves the girdle more closely together; thus he makes offspring his own. 3.4.3.
[6] Of those gods who were consecrated, whoever neglected the kindling of the fires or the private recitation of the Veda, him indeed—
"By means of one another's form, they seek to slay one another—the Asuras and Rakṣasas.
They would approach me while speaking evil, saying, 'Thus indeed you have intended to harm me,' or 'You have sought to slay me.
For Agni alone spoke thus to another, and no other spoke thus to Agni. 3.4.3 [7]

They said, "O Agni, did they speak thus to you? He replied, "I have spoken neither to another, nor has another spoken to me. They understood: "He is indeed the one among us who most effectively drives away the *rakṣas* demons. Let us assume his very form; by that we shall escape the *rakṣas*, and by that we shall attain the heavenly world. Thus, they became Agni himself.

By assuming the form of Agni, they were released from the Rakṣases and thereby attained the heavenly world. In the same way, this sacrificer now assumes the very form of Agni; by that he is released from the Rakṣases and thereby attains the heavenly world.
Indeed, by placing the fuel-stick upon the fire, he enters the intermediate consecration. 3.4.3. [9]
He places a fuel-stick upon the fire with the words:

"O Agni, guardian of vows, in thee [is] the guardian of vows. For Agni is the lord of vows among the gods; therefore he says, "O Agni, guardian of vows, in thee [is] the guardian of vows. "That body of thine which is this, let it be in me; that of mine [which is this], let it be in thee."
"This body of mine is that very one in you; O Lord of Vows, let our vows be united"—with these words, he wraps his skin around himself with fire.
"May the Lord of Consecration approve my consecration; may the Lord of Penance approve my penance"—with these words, he enters the intermediate consecration.
He closes his fingers more tightly and draws the girdle tighter; thus, what was already wrapped around him is now wrapped even more firmly. 3.4.3. [10]
Then they attend upon him from here with the *madantī* waters.
Agni is indeed heat, and the *madantī* waters are heat; therefore, they attend upon him with the *madantī* waters. 3.4.3.[11]

Then, having touched the *madantī* waters, they cause the King (Soma) to swell. Now, as to why they cause the King to swell after touching the *madantī* waters: ghee is indeed a thunderbolt (*vajra*), and Soma is seed; [they do this] lest the seed, Soma, be struck by the thunderbolt, the ghee.
"Let us not injure it. Therefore, having touched the *madantī* water, they cause the King (Soma) to swell.

Regarding this, they say: "Since this swelling is performed as hospitality for Soma, they should first cause him to swell, then perform the intermediate consecration (*avāntaradīkṣā*), and then the *tānūnaptra* rites. But one should not do it in that way; for [this is] the sacrifice's...

Thus, either they performed this rite for them here, or he first brought about their complete pacification, then the intermediate consecration (*avāntaradīkṣā*), and then the nourishment (*āpyāyana*). As for why they perform the nourishment: 3.4.3. [13] As for that which they nourish—
Soma is indeed a god, for Soma is in heaven. Soma was indeed Vṛtra;
that which is the mountains and the stones is his body, and from that this herb called *uśānā* is born—so said Śvetaketu Auddālaki. Having brought that [herb] here, they press it. That...

"They make Soma by means of the consecration (dīkṣā), the Upasad rites, the Tānūnaptra oaths, and the swelling (āpyāyana) [of the Soma]," so they say; and in the very same way, he now makes this [earth] into Soma by means of the consecration, the Upasad rites, the Tānūnaptra oaths, and the swelling.
"It is honey from the bees," they say.
The sacrifice is indeed the honey of the *sāragha* bees; and these officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) are themselves the *sāragha* honey-makers.
Just as honey-makers would cause honey to swell, even so do they cause this sacrifice to swell. 3.4.3. [15]

By means of sacrifice, indeed, the gods won this victory which is theirs; they said, "How can this [world] of ours be made unassailable by men? Having extracted the essence of the sacrifice, just as honey-makers [extract] honey, they...
Having milked out the sacrifice and having obscured it with the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), they vanished; and because they obscured it with this, therefore it is called the *yūpa*.
This, indeed, was heard by the seers (*ṛṣi*) as a traditional report.

They brought together the sacrifice; just as this sacrifice was brought together, so indeed does he who undergoes consecration bring together the sacrifice. Speech is the sacrifice; thus, whatever of the sacrifice has been drained away here, whatever has been milked out, that he now replenishes again. 3.4.3 [17]
Having become six, they indeed cause [the breaths] to swell;
for there are six seasons, and having become the seasons, they thus cause them to swell. 3.4.3. [18] They cause them to swell.
"O divine Soma, may ray after ray of thine swell," he says;

thus he causes each ray of his to swell. "For Indra, the finder of single wealth," he says; for Indra is indeed the deity of the sacrifice, therefore he says, "for Indra. "The finder of single wealth"—formerly, he used to bestow upon each of the gods a hundred [cows] one by one.
"Thus this sunbeam, the sole wealth, swells; or ten by ten, may Indra swell for you, and may you swell for Indra.
Indra is indeed the deity of the sacrifice; thus he causes that very deity of the sacrifice to swell.
"May you swell for Indra"—by this he bestows this swelling upon him. "Swell us, your friends, with gain."
"O wise one!"—by this he expresses whatever he intends to win; "O winner!"—by this he expresses that which he recites; "O giver!"—by this he expresses that [which he desires].

"May I obtain thy blessing, O divine Soma, may it be true"—of these there is indeed one blessing for both the officiating priests and the sacrificer: "May we reach the conclusion of the sacrifice. By saying this, he means: "May I reach the conclusion of the sacrifice. 3.4.3. [19]
Then they conceal [the remnants] on the *prastara* grass-bundle.
The sacrifice indeed proceeds from the north;
now, having moved along toward the south, they cause it to swell. Agni is the sacrifice; thus they place the sacrifice behind them.
They make that [act] false; they are cut off from the gods. The *prastara* is indeed the sacrifice; thus they take up the sacrifice again.
This is its expiation (*prāyaścitti*). Thus, this act of theirs does not become false, nor are they cut off from the gods.
Therefore, they make amends over the *prastara*. 3.4.3. [20]

Regarding this they say: "Should they conceal [the coals] when they are smeared, or when they are not smeared? They should indeed conceal them when they are not smeared, for there is no throwing [of coals] into the fire for those that have been smeared.
Thus they conceal them.
"I desire riches for the impulse and for fortune; truth for those who speak the truth"—by this he means "truth for those who speak the truth.
"Homage to Heaven and Earth!"—by this they offer their submission to these two, Heaven and Earth, upon whom all this rests. 3.4.3 [22]
Then, having snatched up the *prastara* grass-bundle, he says, "O Āgnīdhra, come with the gladdening waters. "With the gladdening ones," the Āgnīdhra replies.

"Come with them," [the Adhvaryu says], and he carries it over the fire again and again. As for why he does not throw it into the fire: it is because from this point onward, the subsequent days [proceed] by means of this.
When he is about to proceed, he then carries the fire upwards; that very act constitutes its portion already offered.
He hands it to the Āgnīdhra, and the Āgnīdhra places it down. 3.4.4.
The Upasads are indeed the neck of the sacrifice, and the Pravargya is the head.
Therefore, if there is a *pravargya* ceremony, having performed the *pravargya*, they then proceed with the *upasads*; that serves to restore the necks.
Now, those which are the invitatory verses (*anuvākyā*) in the forenoon—

Those [verses] that are the invitatory verses (*yājyā*) in the afternoon become the offering verses (*anuvākyā*); thus he interlocks them. Therefore, these joints of the neck are interlocked, and these are the bones. 3.4.4.
The gods and the asuras, indeed...
Both the gods and the asuras, being offspring of Prajāpati, contended with one another.
Then the asuras constructed fortresses in these worlds: one made of iron in this world, one of silver in the intermediate space, and one of gold in heaven.
The gods, however, desired to take them down.
They sat near with these *upasads*; because they sat near (*upāsīdan*), they are called *upasads*.
They shattered the fortresses in front and conquered these worlds; therefore, they say, "One conquers a fortress by means of the *upasad*.
For when they sit near [in worship], by that they conquer this human fortress. 3.4.4. [5]
By means of these very *upasad* rites, the gods shattered the fortresses and conquered these worlds; in the same way,
no one at all can now build a fortress against him in this world.
It is these very worlds that he thus pierces; he conquers these worlds. Therefore, he performs the Upasad rites.
These [Upasads] indeed have clarified butter as their oblation. Clarified butter is a thunderbolt; by means of this thunderbolt, namely clarified butter, the gods [struck down] the fortresses.

He split these worlds and conquered them; in the very same way, this [sacrificer], by means of this *vajra*—the clarified butter (*ājya*)—splits these worlds and conquers these worlds. Therefore, they consist of the oblation of clarified butter. He takes eight portions into the *juhū* ladle.
Regarding the fourfold taking in the *upabhṛt*—they say otherwise: one should take four times in the *juhū* and eight times in the *upabhṛt*.
However, he indeed takes eight times in the *juhū*.
He places that thunderbolt in the *upabhṛt* ladle with a downward pressure;
by means of that thunderbolt with its downward pressure, he splits these worlds and conquers these worlds.
Agni and Soma are indeed the two yoked companions among the gods.
Together with those two, he takes [the butter] for Viṣṇu alone;

he offers only one of the two libations—that which he offers with the *sruva*-ladle—or, having offered the second libation, he does so thinking, "May I conquer through conquest"; therefore, he offers only one of the two libations.
[He offers] with the *sruva* ladle.
Then, having called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he does not choose a *hotṛ*.
He simply says, "Sit down, O *hotṛ*," and the *hotṛ* sits down on the *hotṛ*-seat.
Having sat down, he gives the impulse; being impelled, the Adhvaryu takes up the two offering-spoons.
He says, "Recite for Agni," while stepping across.
Having called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he says, "Sacrifice to Agni," and offers the oblation when the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered.
Then he says, "Recite the invitatory prayer for Soma. Having called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he says, "Offer the oblation to Soma," and at the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*, he makes the offering.
Now, as for the clarified butter that remains in the *upabhṛt* ladle...

While bringing it together, he says, "Recite the invitatory verse for Viṣṇu"; having called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he says, "Offer the oblation to Viṣṇu," and when the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered, he makes the offering.
As for why he offers while standing in the same place:
It does not proceed as if it were moving about with the thought, "I shall conquer by means of conquest";
rather, when he sacrifices to these deities, he thereby prepares the thunderbolt: Agni as the point, Soma as the barb, and Viṣṇu as the head.
The year is indeed the thunderbolt.
Agni is the day, Soma is the night; and that which is between them is Viṣṇu. Thus he makes the revolving year. 3.4.4. [16]
The year is the thunderbolt.
By means of this year as a thunderbolt, the gods indeed shattered the fortresses and conquered these worlds; and in the same way, he [the sacrificer] now, by means of this year—
With the thunderbolt he splits these worlds; he conquers these worlds. Therefore, he sacrifices to these deities.
He should indeed perform three *upasads*;
for there are three seasons in the year; this is the form of the year itself.
He performs this for a year; he thereby prepares it. He proceeds twice with one [offering] and twice with another. These amount to six.
There are indeed six seasons in the year; thus, the form of the year itself is produced.
Thus he prepares the year itself.
If, however, he should perform twelve *upasads*,
there are indeed twelve months in a year.
This is indeed the form of the year that is being fashioned; he thus prepares the year itself. He proceeds twice with one [offering] and twice with another;
these amount to twenty-four.

There are indeed twenty-four half-months in a year; thus, this form of the year is created, and it is the year itself that he thereby consecrates. 3.4.4. [21] As for the fact that he performs [the rites] in the evening and in the morning:
For it is thus that he attains success: when he performs the ritual in the forenoon, he conquers;
then, when he performs it in the afternoon, it is as if he has already conquered. And when he offers the oblation—this [world] is indeed a fortress;
having conquered it, they enter their own [home], which is truly theirs. 3.4.4. [22]

When he proceeds, he fights; when he concludes, he conquers; and when he offers the oblation, he enters his own [self] which is already present. He offers with the verse: "O Agni, that [flame] of yours which lies in iron... whereby he becomes one who shall proceed twice on a single day. 3.4.4. [23]
"The most excellent body, dwelling in the depths, has warded off the fierce word;
it has warded off the dazzling word, svāhā!"—for such was its form, for it was made of iron.
Then he offers the oblation.

With [the verse]: "O Agni, that body of thine which lies in the dust, most excellent, dwelling in the abyss, with it thou didst ward off fierce speech, with it thou didst ward off dazzling speech—Svāhā! for such was its form; it was indeed silver. 3.4.4. [25]
Then he offers an oblation with [the verse]:

"O Agni, that body of thine which lies in gold, most excellent, which has warded off harsh speech, which has warded off dazzling speech—svāhā! For such indeed is its form. This is for one who is about to proceed with the rite of the second day.
For she was indeed a doe; therefore, if one should perform the twelve *upasads*, he should proceed with one [cow] for four days and with another for four days.
Now, therefore, regarding the vows and the *upasads* themselves.

Some of these Upasad days are *paraurvī*, others are *parohvī*. Those for which he milks one cow on the first day, then two, then three—those are *paraurvī*. And those for which he milks three cows on the first day, then two, then one—those are *parohvī*. Indeed, those that are *parohvī* are the same as the *paraurvī*.
"Higher and wider, higher and more distant.
(3.4.4.27) By means of austerity, indeed, they conquer the world. Therefore, this austerity of his becomes higher and higher, further and further, more extensive. Higher and higher.

He who, knowing this, approaches the Upasad days with the *parāhūti* formula conquers a better world and indeed becomes more prosperous in this world; therefore, one should approach the Upasad days with the *parāhūti* formula alone. However, if one should approach with twelve Upasad days, one should have [the cow] milked for three days during the first four-day period, two days during the second four-day period, and one day during the third four-day period. 3.5.1.1. 3.5.1.[1]
Now, from that very central pillar which stands at the eastern end and is the tallest, he strides forward three steps and drives in a peg; that is the *antaḥpāta*. 3.5.1. [2]
Therefore, from the middle gnomon, he strides fifteen steps to the south and drives in a gnomon there; that is the southern hip. 3.5.1[3]
Therefore, from the middle peg, he strides fifteen steps toward the north and drives in a peg; that is the northern hip. 3.5.1.[4] From that middle peg...
He strides thirty-six steps toward the east and drives a peg there; that is the eastern end. From that middle peg... 3.5.1. [5] ...from that middle peg.
He strides twelve steps to the south and drives in a peg; that is the southern shoulder. From that middle peg... [3.5.1.6] ...to the south.
He strides twelve steps toward the north and drives in a peg;
that is the northern shoulder. This is the measure of the altar. Now, as for why it is thirty steps behind.

The Virāj indeed consists of thirty syllables; by means of the Virāj, the gods established themselves in this world. In the same way, this [sacrificer] now establishes himself in this world by means of the Virāj. Furthermore, there may also be thirty-three.
The Virāj indeed consists of thirty-three syllables; by means of the Virāj, he becomes firmly established in this world. Now, as for why the eastern side is thirty-six steps long.

The *bṛhatī* consists of thirty-six syllables; by means of the *bṛhatī*, the gods indeed attained the heavenly world. In the same way, this sacrificer now attains the heavenly world by means of the *bṛhatī* alone; thus, his *āhavanīya* fire becomes celestial. 3.5.1. [10]
Now, as for the fact that there are twenty-four strides in front:
the Gāyatrī indeed consists of twenty-four syllables, and the Gāyatrī is the fore-part of the sacrifice; this [altar] belongs to the fore-part of the sacrifice, therefore it has twenty-four strides.
This measure of the altar is in front.
Now, as for the fact that it is wider behind:
they praise a woman by saying she is "wider behind" and "broad-hipped."
Moreover, because it is wider at the back, he thereby makes the organ of procreation wider at the back;
therefore, from this wider organ of procreation at the back, these creatures are born.
3.5.1. [12] This high altar (uttaravedi) is indeed the nose of the sacrifice.
Now, because he scatters it on the northern part of the altar,
therefore it is called the *uttaravedi* (northern altar). Indeed, in the beginning, there were two kinds of creatures here.
The Ādityas and the Aṅgirasas were there; then the Aṅgirasas first prepared the sacrifice.
Having prepared the sacrifice, they said to Agni, "Announce this to the Ādityas tomorrow at our Soma-pressing: 'Sacrifice for us with this sacrifice. 3.5.1 [14]
Those Ādityas said:
"Devise a plan so that the Aṅgirasas shall officiate at our sacrifice, and we shall not [officiate] for the Aṅgirasas.
They said: "There is no way out from the sacrifice other than by means of the sacrifice itself; let us remain within the Soma-pressing. Thus they spoke.

They gathered the sacrifice together; having prepared the sacrifice, they said: "O Agni, you have indeed announced to us that the Soma-pressing is tomorrow; now we announce to you that the Soma-pressing is this very day, as well as to the Aṅgirases. You shall be our Hotṛ. 3.5.1. [16]
They sent another one.
And those Aṅgirasas, having sent that Aṅgirasa, became as if angry with Agni upon his return, saying, "How is it that you, acting as our messenger, did not heed us? 3.5.1.[17]

He said: "They chose me while I was blameless; since I was chosen by those who were blameworthy, I was unable to withdraw. Therefore, one who has been chosen by the blameless should not withdraw. With this [rite], the Aṅgirasas caused the Ādityas to perform the Sadyaḥkrī sacrifice;
that is the Sadyaḥkrī. 3.5.1. [18]
They brought speech as the sacrificial gift (*dakṣiṇā*) for them.

They did not accept it, saying, "We shall lose [the sacrifice] if we accept it. Thus, that part of the ritual action of the sacrifice which was intended for the *dakṣiṇā* was not released. 3.5.1. [19]
Then they brought the sun as the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) for them.
They accepted it; therefore, indeed, they say, "We are the Aṅgirases, we are the officiating priests, we are worthy of the sacrificial fee; even this [sun] which is here has been accepted by us."

Because it heats, therefore the horse is the sacrificial fee for the Sadyahkriya sacrifice; it is white. 3.5.1.[20] A gold disk is placed before it; thus its form is made to correspond to that which shines yonder, if [one offers] the horse.

If one could not find a white [bull], even a tawny one would serve as white; a golden plate is placed before it, for that is the form of him who shines yonder, which is thereby being made. 3.5.1. [21] Speech became angry with them.

"By which kinsman is he superior, that he has accepted him and not me? she said, and she departed from them. Having become a lioness, she wandered between the two sides—the gods and the asuras—as they were engaged in battle, seizing [the prey]. The gods called out to her, and the asuras called out to her.
Agni alone was the messenger of the gods; Saharakṣas was the messenger of the Asuras and Rakṣases.
She, intending to turn toward the gods, said:
"If I were to turn toward them, what would be mine from that? [She went] even before [the others].
"Your oblation shall reach Agni," he said; then she spoke to the gods, "Whatever blessing you shall invoke through me, all that shall be fulfilled for you. Thus she turned back toward the gods.
Now, while the fire is being maintained...
He sprinkles the high altar (uttaravedi) with ghee. Because the gods said of her then, "The oblation shall reach you before Agni," therefore this oblation now reaches her before Agni;
for she is Speech by her very nature. And as to why he scatters [earth] on the high altar, it is for the completeness of the sacrifice, for the sacrifice is indeed Speech.
For this is speech. He measures it with a yoke and a pin:
with the yoke where they carry [the fire], and with the pin from where they carry it.
With a yoke-pin they indeed yoke the draft-animal; since she (the earth) formerly moved about having become a lioness and was thus unappeased, he now yokes her in this sacrifice.
Therefore, one should not accept a gift from which the sacrificial fee has been withdrawn.
Becoming a lioness, she destroys him;

he should not fail to do so, for becoming a lioness, she indeed destroys him. He should not give her to another, for he would thereby perform the sacrifice elsewhere than in himself. Therefore, if there should be even one who is like a kinsman yet as if wicked, to him he should give her.

Whatever he gives, that he does not diminish for him even after becoming a lioness; what he gives to a kinsman, that he does not do for anyone other than himself. This is the firm foundation for the cessation of the sacrificial gift. 3.5.1. [26] Now he takes up the wooden pin and the wooden sword.
Now, from that peg which is in the eastern half and the northern half, he strides three steps toward the west and traces around the *cātvāla* pit; this is the measure of the *cātvāla*.
There is no fixed measure here other than where one should personally deem it right in one's mind; one should trace around the *cātvāla* in front of the rubbish-heap (*utkara*). 3.5.1. [27]
From the edge of the altar, he places a yoke-pin pointing northward; he then draws a line around it, saying, "Thou art my path for heat.
By this, he says this very thing: "In her, one goes forth heated. 3.5.1.[28]
Then, to the east, he places a wooden pin (śamyā) pointing northward; he traces around it, saying, "May there be a path for me to find my way.
By this, he says: "In this very [earth], having found it, one moves. 3.5.1. [29]
Then, while it is being measured out, he places a wooden pin (śamyā) toward the east; he draws a line around it with the words, "Protect me from distress" (avatān mā nāthitāt).
By this, he says this very thing: "Wherever there is distress, protect me from that. 3.5.1 [30]

Then, on the north side, he places a wooden pin (śamyā) pointing eastward; he draws a line around it with the words, "Protect me from distress. By this, he says to this very earth: "Where there is distress, protect me from that. 3.5.1 [31]
Then he carries [the fires].
Wherever he carries them, there he sits down beside the Āgnīdhra fire-altar. He indeed carries them while uttering the names of the fires themselves;
for those very fires which the gods chose at the beginning for the office of Hotṛ fled away, and they are these very ones.
Crawling over this earth, he says, "Two of these [worlds] are beyond it. By that very means he carries them away.
He strikes [the earth], saying: "Agni has found the sky by name; O Agni Aṅgiras, come hither with the name of Āyu!
In that he has run forward (prādhanvat), he bestows life (āyu); he impels it, saying, "He who is upon this earth. He who is upon this...
Having taken it with the words, "Thou art on the earth," he deposits it with the words, "With that name of thine which is unassailable and worthy of sacrifice, with that I place thee.

By this he means: "With that name of thine which is unassailable by the *rakṣases* and worthy of sacrifice, with that I place thee. He carries it for the fourth time with the words, "Thee for the enjoyment of the gods"; by this he means: "I carry thee, who art dear to the gods. That [he does so] indeed...
From the four-cornered *catvāla* pit he carries [the earth]; for there are four quarters; thus he carries it from all these quarters. 3.5.1.
[33] Then he spreads it out with the formula: "Thou art a lioness, overcoming rivals; be prepared for the gods! For she is indeed that lioness over there.

Having become a lioness, she moved about; it is for this reason that he says to her: "Thou art a lioness," meaning "thou art the overcomer of rivals. By saying, "May we through thee make our rivals more wretched," he means exactly this. "Be prepared for the gods!"—for the high altar (uttaravedi) is indeed a woman; it is her he thus prepares for the gods. 3.5.1. [34]
He makes it a yoke’s length on all sides, or ten steps for each of the sacrificer;
for the Virāj consists of ten syllables, the Virāj is speech, and the sacrifice is speech. He makes it like a navel in the middle while sitting in the same place.
"I shall sprinkle it," [he says].
(3.5.1.35) He sprinkles it with water.
Because she, having become a lioness there, moved about unappeased, and water is appeasement, he sprinkles it with water.
The woman is indeed the high altar (*uttaravedi*); he thus impels her toward the gods. Therefore, he sprinkles it with water.
He sprinkles it, saying:
"Thou art a lioness, overcoming rivals; be purified for the gods! Then...
He strews sand; indeed, sand is an ornament, for sand shines as it were. Sand is indeed the ash of Agni Vaiśvānara; he is about to place Agni upon this [earth], and thus Agni does not injure her.
Therefore he strews sand. He strews it, saying: "Thou art a lioness, overcoming rivals."
"Be pure for the gods!"—with these words he covers it, and she remains with it for that night. 3.5.2.
They place fuel on the fire;
they prepare the supporting ladles (upayamanī), set the clarified butter over the heat, and [prepare] the dipping-spoon (sruva) and the offering-ladle (sruk).

Having wiped [the ladle] and purified the clarified butter, he takes five portions when the fuel has become well-kindled. Then they lift up the fuel; they take up the supporting ladles; then he says, "To Agni..."
"Recite for me as I strike! Follow with the single wooden sword (ekasphya)!

Thus commanded, the Pratiprasthātṛ follows with the single wooden sword from that middle footstep which is at the rear part of the altar (vedi). Whatever portion there has been cut off from the Gārhapatya fire by the intervening space of the altar, [he thus joins it].
He continues that very same [sequence].
3.5.2.[3] Now, some carry it out beyond the northern altar; but one should not do so. Instead, he should carry it out along this middle joint. They come and arrive at the northern altar. 3.5.2.[4]
The Adhvaryu takes up the sprinkling waters.
Standing facing north, he first sprinkles from the front, saying:
"May Indra’s shout protect you from the east with the Vasus; may Indra’s shout [protect] you with the Vasus."
"May he protect you from the front," this is what he says.
Then he sprinkles [the water] behind:
"May Pracetas protect you from behind with the Rudras; may Pracetas with the Rudras [protect you]."
"May he protect you from behind"—this is what he thereby says.
Then he sprinkles [the earth] on the south, saying:
"May Manojavā, together with the Fathers, protect you from the south. "Manojavā"—[he means] may he...
"May the Fathers protect you from the south"—this is what he thereby says.
Then he sprinkles from the north:
"May Viśvakarman, together with the Ādityas, protect you from the north. Thus [he says]. Viśvakarman...
"May the Ādityas protect thee from the north"— this is what he thereby says.
Then, as for the sprinkling waters that remain,
of those two front corners, it is the southern one [to which they belong].

With the formula, "This heated water I cast out from the sacrifice," he pours it outside the altar. Whatever heat she displayed when she became a lioness and moved about unappeased—that very heat he now casts out from her, away from the sacrifice.

If he does not intend to practice sorcery, he should do this; but if he intends to practice sorcery, he should point it out, saying, "This heated water I cast out against so-and-so," and he should strike him with that [formula].
He pierces with grief; grieving indeed, he goes to that world. 3.5.2.
[9] Now, when the fire has been maintained, he sprinkles the *uttaravedi* altar. Just as the gods did there—

They said, "The first oblation shall reach you from Agni. Thus, this very first oblation reaches her from Agni. And because she said to the gods, "Whatever blessing you shall invoke through me, all that shall be fulfilled for you," it is with this [formula] that the priests now invoke a blessing for the sacrificer; all that [blessing] comes to him.
It prospers. 3.5.2.[10] Now, by performing this one thing, he performs two:
namely, when he sprinkles the *uttaravedi*, and then that which belongs to them...

In the middle, it is like a navel; of its two eastern corners, he pours the oblation into the southern one with the mantra: "Thou art a lioness, svāhā! Then, into the northern of the two western corners, [he pours it] with: "Thou art a lioness, winning the Ādityas."
With "Svāhā! he offers on the southern of the two western [hearths]. On the northern of the two eastern [hearths], he says: "Thou art a lioness, winning Brahman, winning Kṣatra; Svāhā!
For in the *yajus* formulas, there is indeed much benediction (*āśis*); thus he prays for both Brahman and Kṣatra, both types of power.
Then, on the northern of the two eastern [hearths].

"Thou art a lioness, bringing good offspring, winning abundance of wealth, Svāhā!"—by saying "bringing good offspring," he prays for progeny; by saying "winning abundance of wealth," since abundance of wealth is indeed plenitude, he thereby prays for plenitude. Then he pours the libation in the middle.

"O Siṃhya, bring the gods for the sacrificer, svāhā!"—thus he causes the gods to be brought for the sacrificer. Then he lifts up the offering-spoon, saying, "For the beings, thee!"—the beings are indeed offspring;
thus he says, "For offspring, thee! 3.5.2. [14]

Then he lays down the enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*). With the formula, "Thou art firm; do thou steady the earth," he lays down the middle one. With "Thou art dwelling in the firm; do thou steady the atmosphere," he lays down the southern one. With "Thou art dwelling in the unshakable; [do thou steady] the sky," [he lays down the northern one].

With the word "dṛṃha" (be firm), he scatters the secondary materials over the fire with the formula, "Thou art the soil. As for why there are these secondary materials, it is for the sake of the completeness of Agni.
Indeed, his body is made of *pītudāru* wood.
In that the enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*) are made of *praitudāru* wood,
he thereby provides him with a body and makes him complete;
for his marrow (*māṃsa*) is indeed *gulgulu*.
In that there is bdellium, he thereby provides this [victim] with flesh;
he makes it complete.
And its fragrant reed-grass is indeed its fragrance.
Now, as for the fact that there is fragrant grass (*sugandhitejana*):
by means of its fragrance, he thus provides this [horse] with prosperity and makes it complete.
Then, as for the fact that there is a stallion's tuft (*vṛṣṇe stukā*).

For Agni indeed dwelt for one night between the two horns of a bull. Therefore, whatever part of Agni was hidden there, that should also be present here; thus, it is made from the hair of a bull. Consequently, one should tear out and bring a tuft of hair from the part of the head closest to the top; however, if one cannot find such, one may take any [hair] at all.
And he should bring that which serves as the enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*), for the sake of protection; for the upper enclosing-sticks come toward him from a distance. 3.5.3.
3.5.3.[1] The sacrifice is indeed man.
The sacrifice is a person, because the person extends it; for while it is being extended, it is fashioned to be exactly as large as a person. Therefore, the sacrifice is a person.
His head, indeed, is the oblation-holder (*havirdhāna*).
Furthermore, it belongs to Viṣṇu by deity; for the Soma that is in it is indeed the oblation (havis) of the gods, and therefore it is called Havirdhāna.
The Āhavanīya fire is its mouth.
When he offers in the Āhavanīya fire, it is as if he were pouring [an offering] into his mouth.
His *stūpa* is the sacrificial post (*yūpa*);
his two arms are the Āgnīdhrīya and Mārjālīya hearths.
His belly indeed is the *sadas*;

therefore they consume [the sacrificial food] in the *sadas*, for whatever one eats here, all that is established in the belly. And because all the gods (*viśve devāḥ*) sat down (*asīdan*) in it, it is called the *sadas*. They...
Thus, these Brahmins of various lineages sit around him.
Now, as for these two fires behind [him], these are his two feet; for he, while being extended, is as large as this very [altar].
The person is prescribed as being of that same measure; therefore, the sacrifice is the person.
The *havirdhāna* shed has doors on both sides, and the *sadas* hall has doors on both sides; therefore, this person [is likewise].
Having smoothed the ground all around, he stands by the two Havirdhāna carts as they are being cleansed.
3.5.3. [8] They turn them around:
the southern one by the south, the northern one by the north; whichever is larger, that is the southern one.
It may be so when those two are equal in size.
If they do not find a *cadi*, they place it over [the other], provided it is commensurate with the *cadi*.
They fasten the wall against it, they enclose the forehead-beam with two upright posts, and they place the roof-covering behind;
or rather, they make the wall equal in height to the roof-covering. 3.5.3. [10] Then, having entered again—

Having taken four portions of clarified butter, he offers the oblation to Savitṛ for impulsion. For Savitṛ is the impeller of the gods; [he thinks], "Impelled by Savitṛ, we shall extend the sacrifice. Therefore, he offers the oblation to Savitṛ. 3.5.3. [11] He offers it with the verse: "They harness the mind, and they harness the thoughts. For it is with both mind and speech that they extend the sacrifice. He...

When he says, "They harness the mind," he thereby harnesses the mind; and when he says, "And they harness the thoughts," he thereby harnesses speech—for by means of this [speech], thought after thought, men desire to perform [the sacrifice], as if with what has been recited, as if with spontaneous utterances, as if with songs.
With these two harnessed, they extend the sacrifice. 3.5.3. [12]

"Of the great, wise sage, O sages"—those Brahmins who have heard [the Vedas] and are learned in sacred lore are indeed the "sages"; it is to them that he says this with the words "of the great, wise sage. The sacrifice, indeed, is the great, wise sage.
"Great and wise, he indeed speaks this very sacrifice: 'He alone, the knower of the way, ordains the priestly offices,' for they indeed ordain the priestly offices while extending the sacrifice.
'Great is the praise of the god Savitṛ; Svāhā!'—this he offers as belonging to Savitṛ for the sake of impulsion. 3.5.3 [13]
Then, having taken another fourfold portion of clarified butter,
he goes out; they cause the wife to go out by the southern door, and he, having placed gold upon the southern track of the southern *havirdhāna* cart, [proceeds].

He offers [the oblation] with the mantra: "Viṣṇu strode through this; in three places he planted his step; his footstep is gathered in the dust, svāhā! He pours the residue into the hand of the wife; she anoints the corner of her eye to ward off affliction.
With the words, "O you two who hear the gods, proclaim it among the gods," he hands over the *sruk* ladle and the butter-melting vessel to the *pratiprasthātṛ*; they then carry them around.
Both [the Adhvaryu and the Pratiprasthātṛ] take four portions of clarified butter and, behind the two fires,
the Pratiprasthātṛ [stands] at the southern [corner] of the northern Havirdhāna cart.

Having placed gold upon the track, he offers with the mantra: "O you two who are rich in cattle and rich in milch-kine, be full of good pasture for Manu; you have propped apart these two worlds, O Viṣṇu; you have supported the earth on all sides with your rays, Svāhā!
He pours the residue from the *saṃsrava* vessel into the hand of the wife; she anoints her eye with it, [reciting] "O you two who hear the gods."
"Proclaim this among the gods!"—this is why he offers in this manner. 3.5.3.
[15] The gods, while performing the sacrifice, were afraid of an attack from the Asuras and Rakṣases; for the thunderbolt was indeed...
With this very thunderbolt of clarified butter, they struck down the destructive spirits and Rakṣases from the south; thus they could not follow their path.

In the same way, he now strikes down the destructive spirits and Rakṣases from the south with this thunderbolt of clarified butter, so that they cannot follow his path. As for why he offers with two verses addressed to Viṣṇu, it is because [the path] belongs to Viṣṇu.
The Havirdhāna [Shed] 3.5.3.[16]:
Now, as to why he anoints the eye of the wife with the heat [of the sun];
this is indeed an act of procreation, for when it concerns a woman...
And when the man suffers [with desire], then semen is emitted; from that, offspring is produced. It unites with what is distant, for semen is indeed emitted toward what is distant.
