Then he says, "Recite for the two *havirdhāna* carts as they are being moved forward. 3.5.3.
[17] Then he makes [the sacrificer] recite.
"Go forward, fashioning the sacrifice"—the sacrifice is indeed the *adhvara*;
thus he says, "Go forward, fashioning the sacrifice. "Lead the sacrifice upward; do not falter"—he thereby says, "Lead this sacrifice upward to the world of the gods; do not falter."
Therefore, he prays for safety for this [horse]: they should set it in motion as if lifting it up together, so that it may not neigh;
for this speech of the horse is indeed demonic (*asuryā*), lest demonic speech should speak here.
If the two should neigh, he should recite this: *3.5.3.[18]*.
"Speak for your own stall, O Goddess; do not speak away our life, do not speak away our progeny"—this is the atonement for that.
Regarding this, they say: one should step three strides westward from the high altar (uttaravedi) and establish the two oblation-carts (havirdhāna) there. That...
"The measure of the two Havirdhāna carts"—there is no such fixed measure here; wherever he himself thinks in his mind, he should place them neither too close nor too far.
He then addresses them with these mantras.
"Rejoice here on the summit of the earth," he says, for this indeed becomes the summit of the earth;
for his *āhavanīya* fire is in heaven. He places it in the center, for that is the form of security (*kṣema*).
Then the Adhvaryu goes around by the north.

He supports the southern *havirdhāna* cart with [the verse]: "I shall now proclaim the heroic deeds of Viṣṇu, who measured out the earthly regions; who propped up the highest dwelling place, striding out in three steps, the wide-strider. With "For Viṣṇu," he drives in the wedge on the other side, and then further.
[At the place] for humans 3.5.3.[22].
Then the Pratiprasthātṛ props up the northern *havirdhāna* cart with [the verse]: "O Viṣṇu, whether from heaven or from earth..."
"O Viṣṇu, from the great, wide mid-air, fill both your hands with wealth; bestow it from the right and from the left.

For Viṣṇu, thee! With these words he drives in the wedge on this side. And as they proceed with the sacrificial formulas addressed to Viṣṇu in human practice, so it is here, for the Soma-cart (havirdhāna) belongs to Viṣṇu. 3.5.3. [23]
Then, having touched the middle roof-beam, he causes [the sacrificer] to recite:
"Viṣṇu is praised for that heroic deed; like a terrifying beast, roaming and dwelling in the mountains, in whose three wide strides all beings abide."
"Viśve" (all) refers to this very skull-plate of his which is on top; for the other skull-plates lie beneath it, as it were. Therefore he says, "They lie above.
Then, having touched the forehead-bone, he makes [the sacrificer] recite.

"Thou art the forehead of Viṣṇu," he says; for this indeed is its forehead. Then, having touched the two *ucchrāyyā* bricks, he makes [the sacrificer] recite: "Ye are the corners of Viṣṇu's mouth"; for these indeed are its two corners of the mouth. And as for this wooden plank (*caṣāl*) which is behind, this indeed is its skull-bone which is behind. 3.5.3. [25]
Then he sews it with a cord made of *laspūjanī* grass, saying, "Thou art Viṣṇu’s seam.
Then he makes a knot, saying, "Thou art Viṣṇu’s firm one," so that it may not fall apart. He seeks it for the primary rite; thus indeed...
A seizing spirit finds neither the Adhvaryu nor the sacrificer; he touches it when it is completed, saying, "Thou art Vaiṣṇava," for the Soma-cart is indeed dedicated to Viṣṇu. 3.5.4.
[1] For two reasons the sounding-holes are dug out.

The *havirdhāna* (sacrificial cart) is indeed the head of the sacrifice; those four hollows which are here—these two pairs, these two [on each side]—it is these very ones that he thereby makes. Therefore, he digs out the *uparavas*.

The gods and the asuras, both of them offspring of Prajāpati, contended with one another. Then the asuras buried magic spells (*kṛtyā*) and secret charms (*valaga*) in these worlds, thinking, "In this way we shall overcome the gods. 3.5.4. [3]
The gods indeed desired to win that over;
they dug up the *kṛtyā* and the *valaga* with these [verses].
For when one digs up a *kṛtyā*, it becomes powerless and futile; in the same way, this [sacrificer] does so now regarding whatever [evil] is here.
A certain hostile rival digs up *kṛtyā* and *valaga* spells; it is these very things that he now digs out. Therefore, he digs the *uparava* pits.
He digs them beneath the front part (*prauga*) of the southern *havirdhāna* cart.
He then takes up the spade.

"On the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, I take thee; thou art a woman"—this is the common bond of this sacrificial formula (*yajuḥ*). For this [spear] is indeed a woman; therefore he says, "Thou art a woman. 3.5.4. [5]
He traces around them, leaving a space of a span, with the formula:
"Here I cut off the necks of the Rakṣases. The spade is indeed a thunderbolt;
by means of the thunderbolt, he thus cuts off the necks of the destructive Rakṣases. 3.5.4. [6]

Now, regarding these two former [altars]: he should first trace around the southern one of those two, then the northern one of the latter two, then the southern one of the other two, and finally the northern one of the first two. 3.5.4. [7]
Moreover, they say otherwise:

one should first draw the northern line of the two western [enclosures], then the southern line of the two eastern ones, then the southern line of the two western ones, and then the northern line of the two eastern ones; or else, one may indeed do them in regular order.
One should indeed trace this one last; he who is the northernmost of the two preceding ones should trace it. 3.5.4.
[8] He digs them in the very order they were traced, starting from the front, with the mantra:
"Thou art great, O great roar."

Thus he praises them; indeed, he magnifies them when he says, "Thou art great, O great roar! He says, "Utter the great speech for Indra. Indra is the deity of the sacrifice, and the *havirdhāna* (sacrificial cart) belongs to Viṣṇu; thus he makes it belong to Indra.
Therefore he says, "Utter the great speech for Indra. 3.5.4. [9]
"Slayer of Rakṣases, destroyer of spells... For these two are dug for the destruction of the spells of the Rakṣases.
"Belonging to Viṣṇu," for the speech in the two Havirdhāna sheds belongs to Viṣṇu. 3.5.4 [10]
He throws them up exactly as they were dug:
"I throw up this worm (valaga) which a stranger or a kinsman has buried for me. Either a stranger or a kinsman buries a magical charm (kṛtyā) as a worm.
With this, he digs those very [worms] out:
"Here I dig up that worm which a kinsman or a non-kinsman has buried for me. A kinsman...

Whether it be an equal or an unequaled person who buries a *kṛtyā* or secret spells (*valaga*), he thereby digs them up. "Here I dig up that secret spell which my kinsman or my non-kinsman has buried for me. 3.5.4. [12]
Whether it be a relative or a non-relative who buries a *kṛtyā* or sorcery-spells, he now digs them up with this [verse]:
"Here I dig up that spell which a kinsman or a stranger has buried for me. Whether it be a kinsman or...

Or, one who is not born [into the lineage] digs up the *kṛtyā* and the *valagas*; he thereby digs them up. Saying, "I cast away the *kṛtyā*," he finally throws them out; thus he casts away the *kṛtyā*. He should dig those [holes] to the depth of an arm.
This [altar] is indeed within; by means of the end (anta), he thus confuses the ritual action (kṛtyā). They join them crosswise;
if one cannot do so crosswise, one may even join them straight. Therefore, these vital breaths (prāṇas) are joined further apart.
He touches them exactly as they were dug.
"You are self-ruling, the slayer of rivals; you are all-ruling, the slayer of the arrogant;
you are people-ruling, the slayer of demons; you are universal-ruling, the slayer of enemies"—this is indeed a blessing for this rite;
he thereby invokes a blessing. 3.5.4 [16]
Then the Adhvaryu and the sacrificer touch [the altar] together;
the Adhvaryu stands on the southern side of the front two [stones], and the sacrificer on the northern side of the rear two. The Adhvaryu asks: "O sacrificer, what is here?"
"May it be auspicious for us both," says the Adhvaryu in a low voice.
Then, the Adhvaryu stands to the south of the two rear [stones], and the sacrificer stands to the north of the two front [stones]. The Adhvaryu asks: "O Adhvaryu..."

"What is here?"—"Blessing," he says; "That is mine," says the sacrificer. When they thus touch one another, they thereby make their vital breaths (prāṇas) companions; therefore these vital breaths are in close union with one another. Then, when asked, "What is blessing? he replies; he speaks what is auspicious through human speech. Therefore, when asked, he says, "Blessing."
Having brought them back, he sprinkles them; for this is the single bond of the sprinkling: he thereby makes them pure.
He sprinkles them with the formula, "O slayers of Rakṣas, O destroyers of secret spells," for these are indeed slayers of Rakṣas and destroyers of secret spells.
"I sprinkle those belonging to Viṣṇu," he says, for these indeed belong to Viṣṇu.
Then, whatever sprinkling water remains, he pours it into the pits; thus, those waters which are here in the vital breaths—those he pours in.
Thus he places this; therefore these waters are in these vital breaths.
He pours them out with the words:
"I pour you out, the Rakṣas-slayers, the spell-destroyers, belonging to Viṣṇu. Then [he places] the sacrificial grass.

He spreads [the grass] with its tips pointing eastward and its tips pointing northward; he thereby places those very hairs that are in the vital breaths (prāṇa), and therefore these hairs are on these vital breaths. He spreads it thus.
"Driving away the Rakṣases, driving away the Valagas, I strew you, belonging to Viṣṇu," he says;
then he covers the sacrificial grass over [the altar] as it were his own body; for these are indeed his hair.
Then he places the two pressing-boards upon it.

"O you two, slayers of demons, destroyers of secret spells, belonging to Viṣṇu, I set you down"—these two are indeed his jaws; then he pours [earth] around them with the words, "O you two, slayers of demons, destroyers of secret spells, belonging to Viṣṇu, I pour you around"—he thus makes these firm and renders them looseless. 3.5.4. [23]
Then the pressing-slat is trimmed;
it is entirely red, for this is indeed its tongue. As to why it is entirely red: this tongue is, as it were, red. He places it down with the formula, "Thou art Vaiṣṇava."
For this belongs to Viṣṇu. 3.5.4.
[24] Now he brings down the pressing-stones.
The stones are indeed his teeth; thus, when they press with the stones, it is as if...
One should chew with the teeth; thus he places them down with the formula, "Ye belong to Viṣṇu," for these indeed belong to Viṣṇu. This is the head of the sacrifice that has been restored. 3.6.1.1.
The Sadas is his belly.

Therefore they consume [the food] in the *sadas*; for whatever one eats here, all that is established within the belly. And because all the gods (*viśve devāḥ*) sat down (*asīdan*) in it, it is called the *sadas*.
It is these very Brāhmaṇas of various lineages who sit down in it; they belong to Indra by their deity. 3.6.1. [2]
In the middle of that [sadas], he erects a post of *udumbara* wood.
The *udumbara* is indeed food and strength; the *sadas* is his belly.
By placing it in the middle, he bestows the consumption of food upon him from the very center. Therefore, he erects the *udumbara* post in the middle. 3.6.1[3]

Now, from that middle peg which is at the rear part of the altar, he strides six steps eastward; he strides a seventh step to the south for the sake of perfection. There he traces around the pit. 3.6.1.4.
He takes up the hoe with the formula:

"At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, I take thee; thou art a woman. The significance of this sacrificial formula (yajus) is the same [as that of the preceding one]; for she (the hoe) is indeed a woman.
Because it has been dug out, he says, "Thou art not a woman" (3.6.1.5).
Then he draws a line around the pit, saying, "Here do I cut off the necks of the Rakṣases"; for [the spade] is indeed a thunderbolt.
With the spade, which is like a thunderbolt, he thus cuts off the necks of the destructive Rākṣasas. Then he digs;
having measured out the mound toward the east together with the sacrificer, he throws up the heap of earth. He [then] measures out the Audumbarī post.
He soaks it; he places it in front facing the east; he places sacrificial grass (*barhis*) of this same measure upon it. 3.6.1. [7] Now, the sprinkling waters contain barley grains.
Water, indeed, is the essence of plants; therefore, plants that are eaten alone do not satisfy. Plants, moreover, are the essence of water; therefore, water that is drunk alone does not satisfy.
Only when both have become mixed together do they satisfy, for then they are full of essence.
"They become sprinkling waters with [the verses] containing the word *saras*," [it is said]. 3.6.1.
[8] Now, the gods and the asuras, both of them offspring of Prajāpati, contended. Then, from the gods, all...
Thus did the plants go away; indeed, the barley alone did not go away from them. Then the gods desired to win them back.

By means of these [verses], they seized all the plants belonging to their rivals—because they seized them (ayuvata), therefore they are called *yava*. 3.6.1 [9]. It was there that the gods desired to win them back. By means of these [verses], they seized all the plants belonging to their rivals—because they seized them (ayuvata).
Therefore, [the name] "barley" (*yava*).

3.6.1.[10] They said: "Come now, let us place that which is the essence of all plants into the barley. So they placed that which was the essence of all plants into the barley; therefore, where other plants [wither],...

"When they are parched, these [plants] wither; but when they rejoice, they truly flourish. For in this way they infused sap into them, and so does he now join all the plants of his rivals with these [barley grains]. Therefore, the sprinkling waters contain barley. 3.6.1. He scatters the barley grains.

"You are barley; ward off from us hatred, ward off enemies"—in this there is nothing hidden, as it were. Then he sprinkles [the grain]; for the essence of sprinkling is one: he thereby makes it pure. 3.6.1. He sprinkles: "You are the world; you are the light; you are the heaven. "To the sky thee! To the atmosphere thee! To the earth thee!"—verily, by this he causes these very worlds to partake of strength and sap;
he bestows strength and sap upon these worlds. 3.6.1.
[13] Now, as for the sprinkling waters that remain over:
He pours them into the pit with the formula, "May the worlds, the seats of the fathers, be purified. For a dug well is sacred to the ancestors; he thus makes it pure for sacrifice.
Then [he spreads] the sacrificial grass.

He spreads [the grass] with its tips pointing eastward and northward, saying, "Thou art the seat of the Pitṛs. For that part of it which is dug in belongs to the Pitṛs as its deity; thus, just as it would be firmly fixed among the plants when dug in, so indeed does it become firmly fixed among these plants. 3.6.1. [15]
He raises it with the words:
"Support the sky above, fill the intermediate space, be firm upon the earth.
By this, he causes these very worlds to partake in vigor and sap; he bestows vigor and sap upon these worlds. 3.6.1. [16]

Then he measures it, saying, "May Dyutāna Māruta measure thee. He who blows here is indeed Dyutāna Māruta; thus he measures it with him. "May Mitra and Varuṇa [measure thee] by the firm law," for breath and out-breath are indeed Mitra and Varuṇa.
Mitra and Varuṇa thus fix it with the out-breath and the up-breath. Then he heaps [the earth] around it, saying:
"I heap you around, winner of the priesthood, winner of the nobility, winner of the increase of wealth. For [earth] is indeed manifold.

In the *yajus* formulas there is a prayer for blessing; he prays for both the spiritual power (*brahman*) and the ruling power (*kṣatra*), as well as for both types of vigor, saying, "Possessing abundance of wealth. Abundance of wealth is indeed plenitude; thus he prays for plenitude. 3.6.1. [18] Then he wipes around.

"Strengthen the Brahman! Strengthen the Kṣatra! Strengthen life! Strengthen offspring!"—this is indeed the blessing of this rite; he thereby invokes this very blessing. He makes the earth level all around the pit, for it is either on the surface of the ground or above the pit; thus it is done among the gods, and in that way it does not become a pit. 3.6.1. [19]
Then he pours water upon it.
For wherever they make it rough while digging, they strike it;
water is a means of pacification (*śānti*). Thus, with water as a means of pacification, he pacifies it; with water, he heals it. Therefore, he pours water upon it. 3.6.1.[20]
Then, having approached it in this manner, he causes [the sacrificer] to recite:
"Thou art firm; may this sacrificer be firm in this abode through offspring," or "through cattle. Whatever desire he may desire, that desire of his is fulfilled. 3.6.1.[21]
Then, having taken up clarified butter with the *sruva*-ladle, he offers it over the summit [of the fire] with the formula: "O Heaven and Earth, may you be filled with ghee!
Thereby he causes these two, heaven and earth, to partake of strength and sap; he bestows strength and sap upon them, so that they become possessed of sap.

These subjects live upon that which is to be lived upon. 3.6.1.[22] Then he lays down the roof-covering with the formula: "Thou art Indra’s roof-covering," for the sitting-hall belongs to Indra; and [he says], "for the sake of all people."
For Brahmins of all lineages sit within this [sadas]; therefore, he places two *ca-diṣī* bricks on both sides, three to the north and three beyond them;
these amount to nine. The sacrifice is indeed threefold (*trivṛt*), and the threefold consists of nine; therefore there are nine. 3.6.1.
[23] Thus, the *sadas* has its beam directed toward the north.

The Havirdhāna shed has its beams directed eastward; for this Havirdhāna belongs exclusively to the gods. Therefore, they do not eat nor do they consume anything there, for this belongs exclusively to the gods.
Should anyone eat or consume anything there, his head would surely fall off. Now, these...
When the Āgnīdhra shed and the Sadas are mixed together, therefore they eat from those two; therefore they consume [the remains], for these two are mixed.
The northern direction indeed belongs to humans; therefore the Sadas has its beams facing north.
"O lover of songs, may these songs encompass you on every side."
"May the prosperities follow the prosperous one; may the enjoyments be welcome.
Indra, indeed, is the one praised by songs (*girvān*); "songs" refers to the subjects (*viśaḥ*). Thus he makes this ruling power (*kṣatra*) prosper on all sides.
Therefore, this ruling power is made firm on both sides by the subjects. 3.6.1 [25]
Then he sews it with the *laspūjanī* needle, saying, "Thou art Indra’s seamstress.
Then he makes a knot, saying, "Thou art Indra’s firm [knot]," so that it may not fall apart; thus he seeks the performance of the ritual, and likewise for the Adhvaryu.
If a crocodile does not seize the sacrificer, he touches it when it is completed, saying, "Thou art Indra's," for the Sadas belongs to Indra.
Then, regarding the two Havirdhāna sheds: having looked at their rear half, he erects [the northern shed] to the north of the Āgnīdhra fire-shed.

Half of it should be within the altar and half outside the altar; or even more than half may be within the altar and less outside; or indeed the whole of it may be within the altar. When it is completed, he touches it with two [formulas]: "Thou art Vaiśvadeva. For that which all the gods [entered] into this on the previous day is indeed Vaiśvadeva.
They fast upon the *vasatīvarī* waters; by that, it belongs to the Viśvedevas. 3.6.1.
[27] The gods, while performing the sacrifice, were indeed afraid of an attack from the Asuras and Rakṣases.
The Asuras and Rakṣases placed themselves to their south; they drove them away from the *sadas* and conquered them.
They caused these hearths (*dhiṣṇya*) which are within the *sadas* to be moved out. Formerly, all of these used indeed to blaze.
Just as this Āhavanīya fire, just as the Gārhapatya fire,
and just as the Āgnīdhrīya fire— since they caused these fires to go out from that very place, they no longer burned there; they hemmed them in toward the Āgnīdhra shed,
and they overcame them even halfway to the Āgnīdhra shed, and then all the gods [recovered them].
They won immortality; therefore it is dedicated to the Viśvedevas. The gods then kindled them again, so that they might settle down;
therefore, at each pressing (*savana*), they [kindle them] again.
They rekindle [the fire]; therefore, he who is prosperous should act as the Āgnīdhra. Indeed, he who is well-known and learned in the Vedas is prosperous.

Therefore, they lead the sacrificial fee to the Āgnīdhra first, for from him all the gods won immortality. Therefore, if one should find weakness among those consecrated, let him say, "Lead this man to the office of the Āgnīdhra."
One should say that it is not afflicted and that it will not come to harm. Because the All-Gods (Viśve Devāḥ) won immortality from this [world], it is therefore called Vaiśvadeva.
His Dhiṣṇya hearths are indeed his brothers-in-law.
These are indeed the *samaṅkas*; those who are *samaṅkas* are these very ones, O Vijāmāna, for they are his own self. 3.6.2.
[2] Soma was indeed in heaven.
Now, those gods here were indeed gods; they desired, "May Soma come to us; having obtained him, we shall sacrifice with him.
They created these two illusions, Suparṇī and Kadrū: Vāc was Suparṇī and this [earth] was Kadrū. They caused a conflict between the two. 3.6.2. [3]
As they were being carried away, the two of them said, "Whichever of us sees further in the distance shall win our self. "So be it," she replied.
Then Kadrū said, "Look ahead! 3.6.2 [4]
Suparṇī said:
"On the far shore of this ocean, a white horse grazes at a post; that I see. "Do you see that very one? [Kadrū replied: "Yes, I do. Then Kadrū said: "Its tail is hanging down; that one over there—"
"The wind shakes it; I see that," [said Suparṇī].
As for what Suparṇī said—"On the further shore of this ocean"—the ocean is indeed the altar (vedi); she spoke thus of the altar, namely the horse.
"He serves at the white *sthāṇu*"; for the horse is indeed fire and the white sacrificial post is a *sthāṇu*. Now, as for what Kadrū said:
"A hair of his has become entangled; the wind shakes that off; that is what I see"—that was indeed the girth-rope.
Then Suparṇī said: [3.6.2] "That is indeed the girth-rope."
"Come, let us fly to find out which of us two wins," she said.
Kadrū replied, "You fly yourself; you shall indeed tell us which of us two wins. Then Suparṇī flew away.

It was exactly as Kadrū had said. When Suparṇī returned, he addressed her, saying, "Have you won, or have I? She replied, "I have. This is the explanation of the Suparṇī-Kadrū legend. Then Kadrū said:
"Verily, you have conquered yourself; that Soma is in heaven. Bring it down for the gods, and with it, ransom yourself from the gods.
"So be it," she said, and she created the meters. Gāyatrī brought the Soma from heaven. 3.6.2. [9]

He was indeed enclosed between two golden Kusha-grass mats. They, for their part, repeatedly aimed at him with razor-sharp edges; they were truly consecration and austerity. These Gandharvas were the guardians of Soma.

These two hearths despised these priestly offices. One of them plucked out a blade of *kuśa* grass and gave it to the gods; that became the consecration (*dīkṣā*), and by means of it the gods [prospered].
They were consecrated. 3.6.2.[11] Then he cut off a second blade of *kuśa* grass and gave it to the gods; by means of that, the gods performed austerity.
The Upasads are the means; for the Upasads are austerity.
With the Khadira wood he extracted the Soma;
therefore the Khadira is [used]; because he extracted it with this, therefore the sacrificial post is made of Khadira.

The wooden sword (sphya) was made of khadira wood; it carried him away in concealment, and thus the Acāvāka was excluded. Indra and Agni restored him for the procreation of offspring; therefore, the office of the Acāvāka belongs to Indra and Agni.

Therefore, those who have been initiated guard the king, thinking, "Lest someone should carry him off. For this reason, one should ensure he is well-guarded there; for if they carry him off while he is being guarded, he is indeed lost. 3.6.2. [15]

Therefore, students of sacred knowledge protect their teacher, thinking, "May he not carry off our houses, cattle, or food. For this reason, one should ensure that he is well-guarded there; for if they carry him off while he is being guarded, he is indeed deprived by that act—thus [says] Suparṇin.
He ransomed himself from the gods; therefore they say, "The sacrificer has won a world of merit.
Indeed, a man is born with a debt to death by his very birth; when he sacrifices, it is just as...
Just as Suparṇī ransomed herself from the gods, even so does he here ransom himself from death.
With that [soma], the gods performed the sacrifice. These Gandharvas, the guardians of Soma, followed after it. 3.6.2. [17] They...
Having approached him, they said, "Grant us a share in the sacrifice; do not exclude us from the sacrifice; let there be a portion for us in the sacrifice as well.
They replied, "What would accrue to us from that? [They said: "Just as we were its guardians in the other world, so shall we be its guardians here as well."
"We shall be your protectors," [they said].
"So be it," the gods replied. "They are indeed the purchasers of Soma. To them [he gave them].

This refers to the purchase of the Soma. Then they said to them, "At the third pressing, a libation of clarified butter shall reach you, but not one of Soma; for the drinking of Soma has been taken away from you, and therefore you do not deserve a libation of Soma. Thus, this libation of clarified butter reaches them at the third pressing alone, and not one of Soma, when he sprinkles the hearths with the fire-brands. 3.6.2. [20]

"Now, that which you shall offer in the fire, that will overcome you. When they offered it in the fire, it indeed overcame them. "And when they shall walk about right over you while carrying the Soma, that will overcome you. When they [walked] over them while carrying the Soma...

Carrying [the Soma], they move one above the other; thus he protects them. Therefore, the Adhvaryu should not pass between the Dhiṣṇya hearths, for the Adhvaryu carries the Soma. These [hearths] wait upon him with their mouths wide open; he might fall into their open mouths. Either Agni would burn him, or that god who rules over cattle would [burn him].
One should not look upon him [the fire]; therefore, if there should be a need in the Adhvaryu’s hall, one should pass along the north of the Āgnīdhrīya fire.
These two fires, indeed, are piled up for the protection of the Soma: the Āhavanīya in the east and the Mārjālīya in the south.
To the north of the Āgnīdhrīya fire, and to the west those that are in the Sadas; 3.6.2.
[22] they either scatter half of them or designate half of them; for these indeed have maintained this practice regarding the halves.
"Let them scatter the half-offerings and designate the world from which we have come— from heaven— and likewise let us recognize that world,
so that we shall not go astray. 3.6.2 [23] Now,
those [offerings] which they scatter—
Therefore, they become manifest in this world; and those whom they dedicate, they become manifest in that other world.
They indeed have two names.

They indeed established this: "We have not succeeded with these names by which they have carried away our Soma; let us make second names for ourselves. They made second names, and by them they succeeded with those whose Soma-drinking had been taken away, and then [performed] the sacrifice.
Therefore they have two names; for this reason, when a *brāhmaṇa* does not prosper, he should take a second name.
He who, knowing thus, takes a second name, truly prospers. 3.6.2.
[25] Now, as to why he offers in the fire:

In that he offers among the gods, therefore the gods exist; and in that they consume [the Soma] in the *sadas*, he thereby offers among men, and therefore men exist; and in that the *nārāśaṃsa* cups sit in the two *havirdhāna* sheds, he thereby offers among the fathers, and therefore the fathers exist. 3.6.2. [26]
Those offspring indeed who are not included in the sacrifice perish;

in this very way, he now causes these offspring that have not perished to participate in the sacrifice: after humans come the domestic animals, after the gods come the birds, and after [the gods] come the plants.

Whatever there is here, even down to the trees—all that is included in the sacrifice. Both these, gods and men, as well as the ancestors, drink together; this is their common drinking. Formerly they drank together while still visible, but nowadays they drink together while invisible. 3.6.3. [1]
He who undergoes consecration undergoes it for the sake of the whole; for he undergoes it for the sake of the sacrifice, and this whole world follows after that sacrifice.
Having prepared that sacrifice for which he undergoes consecration, he releases this whole world. 3.6.3. [2]
As for why he offers the Vaiśarjina oblations:

because he releases all this [that he has undertaken], they are called Vaiśarjina; therefore, whoever has completed his vow should take hold of him, but if he should go elsewhere, one need not heed it. Indeed, that which he offers is this very thing.
He releases everything. Furthermore, as to why he offers the Vaisarjina oblations: Viṣṇu is indeed the sacrifice; he strode this stride across this [earth] for the sake of the gods.

That which is this stride of his—this very [world] he strode with the first step, this intermediate space with the second, and the sky with the highest; indeed, Viṣṇu, the sacrifice, strides this very stride for him when he offers the oblation.
Therefore, he offers the Vaiśvadeva oblations. 3.6.3. [4]
In the afternoon,

having strewn the sacrificial altar (vedi) and having given half of the fast-food (ardhavrata), they enter [the hall]; they place the fuel (idhma) on the fire, prepare the supporting ladles (upayamanī), set the clarified butter (ājya) over the heat, and [prepare] the offering-spoons (sruk).

The sacrificer wipes his thighs and thereby makes himself a king. Then he scatters the footprint of the Soma-purchase cow behind the Gārhapatya fire; for one stands firm by means of a footprint, and it is for the sake of stability.
Regarding this, some divide [the earth] into four parts where they take out the Āhavanīya fire, using those as the supporting layers.
One-fourth of the axle [is the length], and they join it with one-fourth on these supporting bricks; one-fourth [is behind] the Gārhapatya fire, and one-fourth he scatters around. 3.6.3.
But one should not do it in that way.

He should strew [the grass] around together with it behind the *gārhapatya* fire; then, having purified the clarified butter, he takes four portions into the *juhū* ladle and five portions into the *upabhṛt* ladle for the speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*), saying: "Thou art light, of all forms;
the speckled butter belongs to the All-gods (*vaiśvadeva*). They hold the ladles when...
The fuel becomes aflame. 3.6.3.[7] Then he offers:
"O Soma, you are the one who grants wide protection from bodily injuries and from hostilities caused by others."
"Svāhā!"—by this very [utterance], he establishes himself upon this earth as his foundation; by this, he wins this world. Then, for the sake of attainment, he offers a second oblation.

"May the swift one, enjoying the clarified butter, partake of it; Svāhā!"—this, indeed, is what he said: "I am truly afraid of the Rākṣasas; so that the destructive Rākṣasas may not harm me on the way, lead me across by making me smaller than my enemy, even as small as a drop, for the swift one is indeed a drop."
Having made that very youngest one free from bondage, they led him away; only a small portion [remained], for the water was afraid of the Rakṣases.
Therefore, he offers a second oblation to the water. 3.6.3. [9] He lifts up the fuel.
They take up the *upayamanī* ladles. [The Adhvaryu says: "Recite for the fire as it is being carried forward;
or, 'Recite for Soma as he is being led forward'—but one should rather say, 'Recite for the fire as it is being carried forward. 3.6.3.[10] They take up the pressing-stones (*grāvan*).

The *droṇakalaśa* vessel, the *vāyavya* cups, the fuel, the enclosing sticks made of *kārṣmarya* wood, the *prastara* bundle of *aśvavāla* grass, the two *vidhṛti* separators made of *ikṣu* grass—that sacrificial grass is tied together;
the two omentum-spits, the two ropes, the two fire-drills, the lower fire-drill, and the two kindling-shavings—having taken all these, they go forward; this is the sacrifice standing upright.
Thus [ends] 3.6.3.[11]. When they are approaching, he causes them to recite:
"O Agni, lead us by a good path to wealth, O God who knows all ways."
"Drive away from us the crooked sin; we shall offer to you the most abundant word of homage.

By this, he places Agni in front; Agni goes in front, striking away the destructive spirits and demons. Then they carry [the fire] through a place that is safe and free from destruction. They come back and arrive at the Āgnīdhra shed.
He places it in the Āgnīdhra fire-shed. 3.6.3.[12] Once it has been placed, he offers an oblation:
"May this Agni make room for us; may he go before us, shattering our adversaries. This...
"May he win prizes in the winning of prizes; may he, exulting, conquer his enemies—Svāhā!
Thus, by this very means, he establishes himself upon that foundation in this intermediate space; by this, he secures this world. 3.6.3. [13] Then they set down the pressing-stones.
Having taken up the *droṇakalaśa* and the other vessels for the *vāyavya* cups, they come forward;
they set them down to the north of the *āhavanīya* fire. 3.6.3.
[14] The Adhvaryu takes up the *prokṣaṇī* sprinkling waters.

He sprinkles the fuel first, then the altar, and then they hand him the sacrificial grass (barhis); he places it down with its knot toward the east. Having sprinkled it, poured water over it, and untied the knot, the prastara-bunch made of *aśvavāla* grass is tied on; he takes it, and having taken it—
He spreads the sacrificial grass with a single layer, including the *prastara* bundle; having spread the sacrificial grass, he places the enclosing sticks made of *kārṣmarya* wood;
having placed the enclosing sticks, he lays two fuel-sticks upon the fire; having laid the two fuel-sticks, he then offers the oblation. 3.6.3. [15] Then he offers.
"O Viṣṇu, stride out widely; make wide room for our dwelling! O you whose source is ghee, drink the ghee;

further and further extend the lord of the sacrifice—Svāhā! By this [formula], he establishes himself upon this very world as a firm foundation; by this, he wins this world when he offers with this [verse]. 3.6.3. [16]
Or rather, as to why he offers with a verse addressed to Viṣṇu:

having made him smaller than this bond, they have led him across; for the drop is indeed the Apsus. Having reached that state of safety, he makes him that which he truly is—namely, the sacrifice itself.
For Viṣṇu is the sacrifice; therefore he offers with a verse addressed to Viṣṇu.
Then, having set down the offering-spoons and touched water, he causes the King (Soma) to enter. Now, as for why, having set down the spoons, he [touches] water...

Having touched water, he causes the King [Soma] to be set down. Ghee is indeed a thunderbolt and Soma is seed; [he does this] thinking, "Lest I should injure the seed, Soma, with the thunderbolt, ghee.
Therefore, having placed the offering-spoons and having touched water, he causes the King to be set down.
He spreads a black antelope skin in the interior of the southern *havirdhāna* cart.
Then he approaches it with the formula: "O God Savitṛ, this is your Soma; guard it, let them not harm you. Thus he entrusts it to the god Savitṛ for protection. 3.6.3 [19]
Then, having released [the vow], he worships with the formula:

"O divine Soma, as a god you have approached the gods; here I [approach] men together with the increase of wealth. Indeed, Agni and Soma place him between their jaws who undergoes consecration (*dīkṣate*).

For this consecration offering belongs to Agni and Viṣṇu. He who is Viṣṇu is Soma; indeed, he who undergoes consecration becomes the sacrificial food of the gods. Thus they place him between their jaws. He is visibly released from the food of Soma when he says: "O divine Soma, as a god you have approached the gods; here do I [approach them]."
"Men together with the increase of wealth"—the increase of wealth is indeed abundance; thus he says, "together with abundance.
3.6.3 [20]. Then he steps out, saying: "Svāhā! I am released from the noose of Varuṇa. For he was indeed within the noose of Varuṇa.
Whatever is not included within another [rite], that is its direct perception; one is released from Varuṇa’s noose when he says, "Svāhā!
May I be released from Varuṇa’s noose.
Then, having said "atha," he places a fuel-stick on the Āhavanīya fire.

"O Agni, guardian of vows, in thee is the guardian of vows"—for Agni is indeed the lord of vows among the gods; therefore he says, "O Agni, guardian of vows, in thee is the guardian of vows. "That body of thine which was in me, let that be in thee; that body of mine which was in thee, let that be in me; according to our respective natures, O Lord of Vows, let us follow our vows."

"The Lord of Consecration has consecrated me; the Lord of Penance has performed penance for me"—thus he is visibly released from Agni and sacrifices with his own true self. Therefore, people eat of him at this point, for he has become human;
therefore they take his name at this point, for he has become human. But why they do not eat of him before that is because he is like an oblation already offered.
Therefore, one should not eat in that manner; thus, one should not eat of what has been consecrated (*dīkṣita*). Then, in this case, he releases his fingers.
When about to cut the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), he offers an oblation with a verse addressed to Viṣṇu.
For the sacrificial post belongs to Viṣṇu; therefore, he offers with a verse addressed to Viṣṇu.
Furthermore, as to why he offers with a verse addressed to Viṣṇu:
Viṣṇu is indeed the sacrifice; it is by means of the sacrifice that he thus approaches the sacrificial post.
Therefore, he offers with a verse addressed to Viṣṇu. 3.6.4. [3]

If he offers with the *sruk* ladle, he offers after taking four spoonfuls of clarified butter; but if with the *sruva* spoon, he offers after dipping the *sruva* itself, [saying]: "O Viṣṇu, stride out widely; make wide room for our dwelling; [pour] the clarified butter."
"O you whose source is ghee, drink; further extend the lord of the sacrifice, Svāhā! (3.6.4).
He takes up whatever clarified butter remains;
the carpenter takes up whatever tool of the carpenter there is.
They come and choose whichever sacrificial post (*yūpa*) they please.
Having touched it in this manner, he mutters [the formula].
Or else, standing behind it facing east, he addresses it: "I have gone beyond others."

"I have gone beyond others; I do not go to others"—therefore he says, "I have gone beyond others, I have not approached others. "I have found you on this side of the further ones, and on the further side of the nearer ones. 3.6.4 [6]

"I have found you nearer than the farther ones," he says, for he cuts off those who are farther away from him; "farther than the nearer ones," he says, for he cuts off those who are nearer to him. Therefore he says: "I have found you nearer than the farther ones, farther than the nearer ones. (3.6.4)
"We take pleasure in you, O divine Vanaspati, for the sacrifice to the gods.
This is just as when one might take pleasure in someone from among many for the sake of a good deed; he, being well-disposed, [is chosen] for that task.
"It may well be so; indeed, he chooses this one from among many for a virtuous task, and with a gratified mind, he becomes fit for the felling.
"May the gods choose you for the sacrifice to the gods! [3.6.4.8]
That indeed is successful which the gods accept for a good deed;
therefore he says, "May the gods accept you for the sacrifice to the gods.
Then he touches it with the *sruva* spoon.
"For Viṣṇu, thee!"—for the sacrificial post belongs to Viṣṇu; Viṣṇu is indeed the sacrifice, for it is for the sake of the sacrifice that he fells it;
therefore he says, "For Viṣṇu, thee.
Then he places a young blade of darbha grass between [the axe and the post].

"O herb, protect!"—the axe is indeed a thunderbolt; thus this thunderbolt, the axe, does not harm him. Then he strikes with the axe, saying, "O svadhiti, do not harm him!"—the axe is indeed a thunderbolt; thus this thunderbolt, the axe, does not harm him. 3.6.4 [11]

The first chip that he cuts off, he takes up; or he should cut it so as not to strike against the axle-pin, for they indeed carry him by means of the mind; thus the chariot does not strike back at him. 3.6.4. [12]
He should cause it to fall facing east, for the east is the direction of the gods; or facing north, for the north is the direction of men;
or he may cause it to fall facing west, for he should indeed avoid the southern direction, as that is the direction of the ancestors.
Therefore, one should cause him to deviate from the southern direction. 3.6.4.[13] As he is moving forward, he addresses him with the mantra:
"Do not scratch the sky; do not harm the atmosphere; [do not harm] the earth."
He who fells the sacrificial post becomes a thunderbolt; from that thunderbolt as it falls, these worlds tremble.
He thus pacifies it for these very worlds, so that, being pacified, it does not harm these worlds. 3.6.4. [14]

When he says, "Do not scratch the sky," he means "Do not injure the heaven"; "do not injure the atmosphere"—in this there is nothing hidden; "be united with the earth" means "be in harmony with the earth. And when he says, "For this whetted axe has led you forth for great good fortune," it is because this axe is indeed leading him forth while being sharpened.
He leads [the horse] forward. 3.6.4.[15] Then he makes an offering upon the stump of the tree from which the branch was cut:
"Lest the destructive spirits and demons should rise up after this," for clarified butter is indeed a thunderbolt.

Thus, by means of that very thunderbolt, he drives away the destructive spirits and the Rākṣasas; so it is that the destructive spirits and the Rākṣasas do not rise up after him. Moreover, ghee is indeed seed; he thus places that seed in the trees. Therefore, from the cutting of the seed, the trees are produced in succession. 3.6.4. [16]
He offers the oblation: "From this, O divine Vanaspati, may you sprout with a hundred shoots; may we sprout with a thousand shoots.
There is nothing here that is obscure.
He then causes it to be trimmed.
It should be as long as he first cuts off;
it should be five *aratnis* in length.
The sacrifice is fivefold, the animal is fivefold, and there are five seasons in the year.

Therefore, one should have it trimmed to five cubits; or one should have it trimmed to six cubits, for there are six seasons in a year, and the year is the thunderbolt. The thunderbolt— 3.6.4.[19]—is [the sacrificial post].
Therefore, one should cut the sacrificial post to six cubits;
or one should cut it to eight cubits.
For the *gāyatrī* consists of eight syllables, and the *gāyatrī* is indeed the fore-part of the sacrifice.
This is the fore-part of the sacrifice; therefore, one should shave [the hair] to the extent of eight *aratnis*.
One should shave it to the extent of nine *aratnis*;
for the sacrifice is threefold (*trivṛt*), and the threefold is indeed ninefold; therefore, one should shave it to the extent of nine *aratnis*.
One should cut it to eleven aratnis in length.
For the triṣṭubh consists of eleven syllables, and the sacrificial post is a vajra; the triṣṭubh is a vajra, and the sacrificial post is a vajra.
Therefore, one should cut it to eleven aratnis in length. 3.6.4 [23]
One should cut it to twelve aratnis in length.
There are indeed twelve months in a year; the year is the thunderbolt, and the sacrificial post is the thunderbolt.
Therefore, one should cut it to twelve aratnis in length. 3.6.4.[24]
One should cut it to thirteen *aratni*s in length.
There are indeed thirteen months in a year; the year is the thunderbolt, and the sacrificial post is the thunderbolt.
Therefore, one should cut it to thirteen *aratni*s in length. 3.6.4.[25]
One should cut it to fifteen cubits.
For the thunderbolt is fifteenfold, and the sacrificial post is a thunderbolt; therefore, one should cut it to fifteen cubits. 3.6.4.[26]
The sacrificial post for the Vājapeya consists of seventeen cubits;

it should rather be of unlimited measure. For by this very unlimited thunderbolt, the gods conquered what is unlimited; and so does he, by means of this very unlimited thunderbolt, conquer what is unlimited.
Therefore, it should indeed be of unlimited size.
It is eight-cornered;
for the Gāyatrī consists of eight syllables, and the Gāyatrī is the eastern half of the sacrifice.
This is the front part of the sacrifice; therefore, it has eight corners. 3.7.1.
He takes up the spade with the formula:
"At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan..."

He takes it up with his two hands, saying, "Thou art no woman. This is the bond of that sacrificial formula (*yajuṣ*): for this spade is indeed a woman; therefore he says, "Thou art no woman. 3.7.1. [2] Then he traces around the pit.
"Here I cut off the necks of the Rakṣases," he says; for the spade is indeed a thunderbolt, and with that thunderbolt he thus cuts off the necks of the destructive Rakṣases. Then he digs.
He throws up the *utkara* mound facing east; behind it, he digs the hole for the sacrificial post;
at its front, he places the sacrificial post facing east; he places sacrificial grass of this same measure on top of it;
he likewise places a splinter of the sacrificial post on top; and he places the *caṣāla* (top-ring) in front and on the side. Then...
As many barley-grains as there are sprinkling-water vessels, such is their significance; this is the very same explanation [as before].
He scatters the barley-grains, saying:
"Thou art barley (yava); bar (yavaya) from us hatred, bar away enemies. There is nothing here that is obscure. Then...
One indeed sprinkles; this is the significance of the sprinkling: he thereby makes it pure. 3.7.1.
He sprinkles [the sacrificial post], saying:
"For heaven thee! For the atmosphere thee! For earth thee! The sacrificial post is indeed their thunderbolt.
"For the protection of the worlds; for the protection of these worlds, I sprinkle you"—this is what he thereby says. 3.7.1.
[6] Now, those sprinkling waters which remain, he pours them into the pit with the words: "May the worlds, the seat of the fathers, be purified."
Thus, this well is indeed dedicated to the ancestors (*pitṛ*); he thereby makes it pure. 3.7.1.

[7] Then he spreads sacrificial grass (*barhis*), both with the tips pointing eastward and with the tips pointing northward, saying, "Thou art the seat of the ancestors," for it is dedicated to the ancestors.

Or else this thought occurs to him: "Just as that which is dug in would be fixed among the plants, so too is he fixed among these plants. 3.7.1. [8] Then he throws a splinter of the sacrificial post (yūpa-śakala) [into the pit].

The outer splinter of the tree is indeed the vital energy (*tejas*) of trees; therefore, when they plane off the outer splinter, the trees wither, for that is their vital energy. When he throws the splinter of the sacrificial post (*yūpa-śakala*) [into the fire], he does so thinking, "May I set it up possessed of its vital energy. And why it must be this very one and no other is because this one alone has been consecrated by the *yajus* formula.
Therefore, he throws a chip of the sacrificial post (yūpa-śakala) [into the fire].
He throws it [with the formula]:
"Thou art the leader, easy of access for the Unnetṛs. For this [chip] is indeed cut off from the front of him.
Therefore he says, "Thou art the leader, easy of access for the Unnetṛs; know this: one shall stand over thee," for indeed one stands over him;
therefore he says, "Know this: one shall stand over thee. Then, having taken up clarified butter with the dipping-spoon (sruva)...

He makes an offering into the pit so that the destructive spirits and demons may not rise up from below; for ghee is indeed a thunderbolt, and thus by means of the thunderbolt he repels the destructive spirits and demons, so that the destructive spirits and demons do not rise up from below. Then, having gone around from the east, sitting facing the north—

He anoints the sacrificial post (yūpa). He says, "Recite for the post being anointed. He anoints it with the formula, "May the god Savitṛ anoint you with honey. Savitṛ is indeed the impeller of the gods; and this post is, by its very nature, the sacrificer. And all this that exists here is honey. Thus, he [anoints] it with this entire [world].
Savitr, the impeller, impels it for him; therefore he says, "May the divine Savitr anoint you with honey.
Then, having adjusted the top-ring on both sides, he fastens it.

With the words, "For the plants with good fruit," he indeed makes that which is in the middle of this [sacrificial post] like a gathered cluster of *pippala* fruit; for this *pippala* fruit is indeed fastened crosswise upon a tree.
Thus, he makes it exactly like this connection here, which is as if pressed inward.

Therefore, it is as if it is gathered in the middle. 3.7.1.[13] He anoints the one standing nearest the fire (agniṣṭhā). The sacrificer, indeed, is the one standing nearest the fire; the clarified butter is the essence.
He thus anoints the sacrificer with the very essence; therefore he anoints the post at the corner facing the fire until the end.
Then he touches the girding around on all sides. Then he says, "Recite for the one being raised!
And it is raised.
"With its top you have touched the sky; with its middle you have filled the atmosphere; with its base you have made firm the earth.
The sacrificial post is indeed a thunderbolt for the conquest of these worlds. By means of that thunderbolt, he wins these worlds; he excludes his rivals from these worlds. 3.7.1. [15]

Then he measures with this Triṣṭubh verse: "Those abodes of yours which we desire to go to, where the many-horned, tireless cows are—there indeed is that highest, far-striding step of Viṣṇu, which shines forth abundantly. With this verse, he measures.
The Triṣṭubh is a thunderbolt and the sacrificial post is a thunderbolt; therefore, he fixes it with a Triṣṭubh verse.
He fixes the post at the front corner (agniṣṭhā).
The sacrificer is indeed the front corner, and Agni is the sacrifice. It is he [the sacrificer].

If one were to cause the post standing nearest the fire (agniṣṭhā) of the fire-altar to waver, the sacrifice would waver and consequently the sacrificer would waver; therefore, he fixes the post standing nearest the fire immediately [after setting it], then he heaps earth around it, then he sprinkles it, and then he pours water upon it. 3.7.1. [17]
Then, having approached it in this manner, he causes [the sacrificer] to recite:

"Behold the deeds of Viṣṇu, from which he has made his vows manifest; Indra’s companion in battle. Indeed, he who has raised the sacrificial post has hurled the thunderbolt; [this is] the victory of Viṣṇu.
When he says, "Behold the deeds of Viṣṇu, from whence he beheld the sacred laws, the friend and companion of Indra," he truly means this:
Indra is indeed the deity of the sacrifice, and the sacrificial post belongs to Viṣṇu; he thus makes it possessed of Indra.
Therefore he says, "the friend and companion of Indra. 3.7.1. [18]
Then he gazes at the top-ring (*caṣāla*):

"The wise ever behold that highest step of Viṣṇu, like an eye stretched across the sky. For he who has raised up the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) has indeed hurled the thunderbolt; this is the victory of Viṣṇu.
By saying, "The wise ever behold that highest step of Viṣṇu, like an eye extended in the sky," he says, in effect, "Behold! 3.7.1 [19].
Then he girds [the post] around.
He girds it indeed for the sake of non-nakedness; therefore he girds it right here, for it is here that this garment comes to be.
He thereby bestows food upon him, for it is here that this food finds its support;
therefore he girds it right here. 3.7.1. [20]
He encircles it with a triple cord;
for food is threefold, and cattle are food. The father, the mother, and that which is born is the third;
therefore he encircles it with a triple cord. 3.7.1. [21]
He girds it with the formula:
"Thou art girt; may the divine subjects gird thee around; may wealth [gird] this sacrificer of men.
By saying, "may wealth [gird] this sacrificer," he invokes a blessing for the sacrificer.
"Of men," [so it is said]. 3.7.1.[22] Then he hides a chip of the sacrificial post with the formula, "Thou art the son of heaven. This offspring indeed belongs to him; therefore, if...

There should be a set of eleven sacrificial posts; one should tie each animal to its own post without confusion. For him, offspring are born that are not bewildered and remain obedient. But he who ties them in confusion, not each to its own post—for him offspring are born bewildered and do not remain obedient. Therefore, one should tie each to its own post without confusion. 3.7.1 [23]

This ascent to the heavenly world is made: the splinter from the sacrificial post [is connected] to this girdle, the splinter from the girdle to the splinter from the sacrificial post, and from the splinter from the sacrificial post to the top-ring; from the top-ring, he attains the heavenly world. 3.7.1. [24]
Now, as to why it is called *svaru*:
because it is cut off from this very [post], its own wound (*āru*) becomes its [wound];
therefore it is called *svaru*. 3.7.1. [25]

By that part of it which is dug in, he conquers the world of the fathers; then, by that part which is above the dug-in portion and up to the girdle, he conquers the world of men; then, by that part which is above the girdle and up to the top-ring, he conquers the world of the gods; and then...

"That which is two or three finger-breadths above the *caṣāla* is for the Sādhyas; by that he conquers their world. He who knows this indeed becomes one who shares the same world as the Sādhyas. 3.7.1.
[26] He fixes it in the eastern half.
The sacrificial post is indeed a thunderbolt, and the staff is a thunderbolt.
Having grasped the front part of the staff, he strikes; for this is the front part of the sacrifice. Therefore, he fixes it in the front part. 3.7.1. [27] By means of the sacrifice, the gods...

They won this victory which is theirs; they said, "How can this [world] of ours be made unassailable by men? Having sucked out the essence of the sacrifice—just as honey-makers might suck out the honey—they drained the sacrifice, blocked it with the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), and vanished. Then...
Because he grasped it with this [formula], therefore it is called the *yūpa*. Wisdom is indeed in front, and the speed of thought is in front; therefore, he fixes it in the eastern half.
It is eight-cornered.
The Gāyatrī indeed consists of eight syllables; the Gāyatrī is the fore-part of the sacrifice, and this [post] is at the fore-part of the sacrifice; therefore it has eight corners. 3.7.1.
[29] The gods used to throw him [the sacrificial post] along after [the animal].
"Just as even now some follow this practice, so did the gods act; then the *rakṣas* followed after and drank up the sacrifice.
3.7.1 [30] Those gods said to the *adhvaryu*:

"Offer the very splinter of the sacrificial post; then it will have been offered with the *svagā* call, and thus the *rakṣas* demons will not spring up after the sacrifice, thinking, 'This is indeed the raised thunderbolt! 3.7.1 [31].
Thus spoke the Adhvaryu.

He offered up the very splinter of the sacrificial post; then it was as if this [post] had been made *svagā* (well-offered), and thus the Rakṣases did not drink after the sacrifice, thinking, "This is indeed the raised thunderbolt.
And so it is with this one now.

He offers only a chip from the sacrificial post; thus it becomes consecrated with the *svagā* call, and so the *rakṣases* do not follow after and drink up the sacrifice. "This is indeed the raised thunderbolt," he thinks, and so he offers: "May your smoke go to heaven, your light to the sky; fill the earth with ashes, *svāhā*! 3.7.2.1.
As great as the altar is, so great is the earth.

The sacrificial posts are indeed thunderbolts; thus, by means of these thunderbolts, he secures this very earth and excludes his rivals from it. Therefore, there is a set of eleven sacrificial posts, and the twelfth is the *upaśaya*.
When it has been fashioned, he places it to the south. As for why there are twelve *upaśaya* (spare) stones:
once, the gods, while performing the sacrifice, were afraid of an attack by the *asura*-rakṣases. That which... [3.7.2]

Just as an arrow that has been shot may or may not strike its mark, and just as a staff that has been struck may or may not strike its mark, so it is with those; but this twelfth *upaśaya* stone which remains is like an arrow drawn back but not yet released, or like a weapon raised but not yet hurled— this very thunderbolt is raised on the right side against the destructive spirits (*nāṣṭrā*).
For the sake of driving away the *rakṣases*, there is therefore a twelfth *upaśaya* (supplementary post).
He sets it down [with the formula]:
"This is thy place on earth; thy animal is the wild one. For the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) is indeed an animal; thus he provides him with that.

He assigns the wild animals specifically to the forest; thereby he becomes possessed of cattle. Regarding this, they say that the erection of the eleven sacrificial posts (*yūpaikādaśinī*) takes place on the same day.

However, some indeed erect them on the day before the Soma-pressing (*śvaḥsutyā*), both for the sake of preparation and because they say, "On the day before the pressing, they erect the sacrificial post. 3.7.2. [4]
One should not do it in that way.

One should erect the post closest to the fire (agniṣṭha). For having erected this [post], the Adhvaryu does not go beyond it until the encircling; indeed, these [other posts] remain for that night unencircled. That is a reproach regarding the cattle.

They indeed erect the sacrificial post in the morning, for they immolate the animals in the morning; therefore, one should erect it in the morning itself. That which is to the north of the *agniṣṭha* [the central post]—that one he should erect first, then the southern one, and then the northern one.
The southern half is the best, and likewise the northern. 3.7.2.[6] Now, they say otherwise:
one should first raise the southern [post] from the *agniṣṭhā* pillar, and then the northern.
"The southern [post] is the northernmost, and thus his rite is completed toward the north. 3.7.2.
[7] That which is the tallest should be the southernmost;
then the next shorter, and then the next shorter for the northernmost.
Likewise, the northern [post] is the shortest. 3.7.2.
[8] Then they erect the wife’s post for the wives;
indeed, the wife’s post is erected for the sake of completeness.
He immolates an animal for Tvaṣṭṛ; for Tvaṣṭṛ indeed transforms the emitted seed, and thus he (the sacrificer) now transforms that emitted seed.

It has testicles, for he who has testicles is a procreator; therefore it has testicles. One should not let it complete its ritual course; one should release it after the fire has been carried around it. For if one were to let it complete its course, it would be detrimental to offspring.
It would go to its destruction; he abandons that offspring. Therefore, one should not complete [the sacrifice]; one should release it while it has only been carried around with fire.
For the victim and the sacrificial post are one and the same.
Indeed, they never immolate a victim without a sacrificial post. Thus, if it were otherwise, it would not be so.
From that time on, the animals became capable of enduring whatever food they were to consume; just as this two-footed human now moves upright, so too did those two-footed creatures move upright.
Then the gods perceived this thunderbolt.
When they raised that sacrificial post (yūpa), they were struck with fear and cowered;

from that they became four-footed, and from that food came into being—just as this food exists for living beings today. For indeed, they stood in opposition to him; therefore, they immolate the animal victim at the sacrificial post alone, and never apart from the post. 3.7.3. [3]

Then, having brought forward the victim and churned the fire, he binds it. As for why it is done in this way: truly, the animals did not at first consent to becoming the sacrificial offering; therefore, they now offer them in the fire as sacrificial offerings once they have become such.
The gods hemmed them in, and being hemmed in, they did not come forth.
They said, "These [beings] do not know his course—that which one offers as an oblation in the fire;
let us, having hemmed in these very cattle, churn out a fire and offer fire into that fire."

"They will surely perceive that this is indeed the path of the oblation, this its foundation, thinking, 'They are indeed offering the oblation into the fire'; then they will descend, and then they will be well-disposed toward the sacrifice. Thus, having restrained the animals...

Having churned the fire, they offered fire into the fire; they understood: "This indeed is truly the path of the oblation, this is its foundation; it is into fire that the oblation is offered. Then they descended [into the water], and thereafter they became joyful in mind for the sake of the sacrifice. 3.7.3. [6]
In the same way, having immolated the animal and churned the fire, he offers fire into the fire; for he knows:
"This indeed is the course of the oblation, this is its foundation; they say that the oblation is indeed offered into the fire. Thereupon he descends from there.
He becomes delighted for the sake of the sacrifice; therefore, having brought forward the animal and churned the fire, he binds it.

Regarding this, they say: "One should not bring the animal forward, nor should one churn the fire; rather, taking only the rope, one should go straight up to it, fasten it, and bind it. One should not do it in that way, for it would be as if one intended to perform the rite in a manner contrary to the sacred law.
Therefore, one should walk around this very [altar] in that manner.
Then, taking a blade of grass, he performs the *upākaraṇa* rite with the formula:
"Possessing a companion, may I restrain [the victim]," for one who has a companion is indeed powerful.
He takes up a blade of grass.
"Thou art the assistant," he says, for a second person indeed assists; therefore he says, "Thou art the assistant.
"The divine subjects have approached the gods," he says; for these cattle are indeed the divine subjects, as they stood by for the sake of the gods.
When he says, "O gods, the divine hosts have come forth," he says this very thing.
When he says, "The eager ones, the best of bearers," it is because the gods are indeed wise; therefore he says, "The eager ones, the best of bearers."
"O divine Tvaṣṭṛ, rest in the wealth!

Tvaṣṭṛ indeed rules over cattle, and cattle are wealth. When the gods found him not remaining still, they said to Tvaṣṭṛ, "Come near and respond! This is what he means when he says, "O divine Tvaṣṭṛ, rest in the wealth. (3.7.3)
"May the oblations be sweet for thee," he says.
For when they submitted themselves to him, thinking, "We shall become the oblation," therefore he says, "May the oblations be sweet for thee. 3.7.3 [13]
"O Revatīs, rejoice!
For cattle are indeed rich (revant); therefore he says, "O Revatīs, rejoice. "O Bṛhaspati, hold fast the riches! Bṛhaspati is indeed the Brahman, and cattle are the riches; these the gods [bestowed].

They enclosed those who were not standing firm on the far side by means of the *brahman* itself; they did not pass beyond it. In the same way, this [priest] now encloses them on the far side by means of the *brahman* itself; they do not pass beyond it. Therefore he says, "O Bṛhaspati, maintain the treasures.
Having made a noose, he fastens it. Now, therefore, regarding the very act of binding: 3.7.4.1. [1]
Having made a noose, he fastens it with the formula:

"O divine oblation, I fasten thee with the noose of *ṛta*. For this rope belongs to Varuṇa; thus he fastens him with the very noose of *ṛta*, and so this [noose] does not belong to Varuṇa [in its effect upon him].
"The rope does not injure him" (3.7.4.2), [and] "Be bold, O human! For indeed, in the beginning, no human could overpower this; that which belongs to *Ṛta*...
With a noose he binds this offering for the gods; then a human dares to seize it. Therefore he says, "Be bold, O human! Then he fastens [the animal].
"By the impulse of God Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, I bind you,
acceptable to Agni and Soma"— thus,
just as when taking the oblation for a deity he assigns it, so now he assigns it to these two deities; then he sprinkles it, for there is indeed one [deity].
The significance of the sprinkling is that it makes this [the sacrificial post] pure.
He sprinkles it with the formula, "For the waters, for the plants! Thus, he makes it pure from the very source from which it originated.

For when it rains, this [sacrifice] performs its function; then the plants are born. Having eaten the plants and drunk the water, this sap comes into being from that. From sap comes semen, and from semen come animals. Thus, he makes it pure (*medhya*) from that very source from which it originates and from which it is born. 3.7.4. [5]

"May your mother permit you, may your father permit you"—for he is born from both his mother and his father; thus, from the very source from which he is born, he makes him pure (*medhya*). "May your uterine brother permit you, may your companion of the same herd permit you"—this is what he [says] regarding those who are yours.

"By that, I undertake you with your approval"—this is what he says. "I sprinkle you, acceptable to Agni and Soma"—by means of those two deities for whom he undertakes [the sacrifice], he thereby makes you fit for the sacrifice.
Then he holds [the water] close.
"Thou art the drinker of waters," he says; thereby he makes him pure within.
Then he sprinkles [him] from below with the words, "May the divine waters make it palatable; may the oblation for the gods be well-tasted. Thereby he makes him pure on all sides. 3.7.4. [7]
Then he says, "Recite for Agni as he is being kindled.

Having poured the northern libation (āghāra) and having moved around without letting the two ladles touch, he anoints the victim with the *juhū* ladle. The northern libation is indeed the head of the sacrifice; and here, the victim is the sacrifice—thus, he places the head upon the sacrifice itself.

He replaces it; therefore, he anoints the animal with the *juhū* ladle. He anoints it on the forehead with the words, "May your breath unite with the wind"; with the words, "May your limbs [unite] with the sacrificial objects," he anoints it on the two shoulders.
"O Lord of the Sacrifice, [grant] the blessing!"—this he says regarding the two hips; "attain that desire for which they immolate the animal"—this is what he thereby says.
Indeed, when the animal is being slaughtered, its breath merges into the wind; "attain that which is your breath."

"May he attain the wind," by this he says this; "with the limbs, O worshipful one," for they worship him with his limbs; "attain that which they worship with their limbs for thee"—by this he says this; "he is the lord of the sacrifice, [granting] the blessing," for by this he invokes a blessing for the sacrificer;
"attain that which they shall invoke as a blessing for the sacrificer through thee"—by this he says this.
He sets down the two offering-spoons; then, for the *pravara*, he causes the announcement to be made—the significance of this is exactly as before.

Then he causes the second announcement to be made, for there are two *hotṛ*s here. 3.7.4 [10] He causes the second announcement to be made, for there are two *hotṛ*s here. Sa... [text fragment] ...bhavataḥ sa.
He calls for the *śrauṣaṭ* to Mitrāvaruṇa, but he chooses the sacrificer as the Hotṛ. For Agni is the leader of the divine clans;
Agni is indeed the mouth of the deities. Therefore he says, "Agni is the leader of the divine clans.
[And he says], "This sacrificer is [the leader] of men," for he is the one who corresponds to that [role] in the very place where he sacrifices.

"Therefore he says, 'This sacrificer [is one] of men. 'May their household-fire shine with undivided [flames], may you two [shine] for two winters,' he says; by this he means, 'May their household-fires be unharmed for a hundred years.
'May your blessings be united, but your bodies remain ununited.'"
"Let the rays alone be joined together, not even the bodies"—this is what he thereby says. For if their bodies were also to be joined together, Agni would burn the sacrificer beforehand.
When he offers into the fire, he thus gives this [oblation] to Agni; then, as for that which the officiating priests [perform] here...
They invoke a blessing for the sacrificer; Agni fulfills all of that for him.
Thus they unite only their wealth (*rādhāṃsi*), but not their bodies (*tanū*); therefore he says, "Uniting our wealth, not uniting our bodies.
Now, at this point, when the *hotṛ*, having been chosen, sits down upon the *hotṛ*'s seat.
Having sat down for that, he gives the impulse; being impelled, the Adhvaryu takes up the two offering-spoons.
Then they proceed with the *āprī* verses.

Now, when they perform with the Āprī verses, it is because he who is consecrated (dīkṣita) gathers the sacrifice together with his whole mind and his whole self, and desires to carry it out; his self, as it were, becomes depleted. They replenish him with these Āprī verses. Because they replenish him, they are called Āprīs.
Therefore, they perform the Āprī offerings. These indeed become eleven fore-offerings (*prayāja*);
for there are these ten vital breaths in a person, and the self (*ātman*) is the eleventh.
In that upon which these vital breaths (*prāṇas*) are established—so great indeed is the person (*puruṣa*), and all this constitutes his self—they cause it to swell.
Therefore, there are eleven *prayāja* offerings.
Having called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he says:

"Prompt for the kindling-sticks!"—saying "Prompt! Prompt! at every fourth fore-offering, while pouring together [the butter], he performs ten fore-offerings. Having offered the ten fore-offerings, he says, "Bring the *śāsa*!
Indeed, they call the sword the *śāsa*. 3.8.1. [5]
Then he takes a chip from the sacrificial post (*yūpa*).
Having first anointed it with the *juhū* ladle, he touches the forehead of the animal with it, saying:

"Anointed with ghee, protect the animals! For the chip of the post is indeed a thunderbolt, the *śāsa* is a thunderbolt, and the clarified butter is a thunderbolt; he thus makes that [thunderbolt] complete.

Having fashioned the *vajra*, he makes it a protector for that [post] in the darkness, thinking, "Lest the destructive *rakṣas* should harm it. He again buries a chip of the sacrificial post, saying, "May this be your recognized splendor (*aśri*)," as he hands over the *śāsa* (the sharp-edged axe).
He sets down the two *sruk* ladles. 3.8.1. [6]
Then he says, "Recite for the fire being carried around!

Taking a firebrand, the Āgnīdhra carries the fire around it. Now, as to why he carries the fire around: he thus encloses it with fire so that no opening remains, lest the destructive spirits and demons [should harm it].
"Touching it," he says, for fire is the repeller of the *rakṣases*; therefore, he carries the fire around it.
He carries it around it at the very spot where they cook it.
Regarding this, they say: "One should bring back that same brand; then, having churned out another fire right here, one should [cook] it upon that."

"They should cook [the oblation] on the Āhavanīya fire; for this [fire] is indeed not [suitable] for that which is uncooked, since they would cook it upon it; nor is this [fire] for that which is cooked, since they would offer it upon it. One should not do so. 3.8.1. [8]
Just as something that has been swallowed becomes so [internalized], so does this become for him when he carries the fire around it (paryagni).
Just as one might take back what was swallowed, pick it out, and hand it over to another, so it is in this case.
Therefore, they should crush the embers from this very firebrand (ulmuka) and cook it upon them. 3.8.1. [9]
Then, taking a firebrand, the Āgnīdhra goes forward in front;
he thus places Agni in front so that Agni, driving away the destructive spirits and demons from the front, proceeds, and they lead the animal along a path free from danger and destruction. Him—
The Pratiprasthātṛ takes hold of the two omentum-spits; the Adhvaryu takes hold of the Pratiprasthātṛ; and the sacrificer takes hold of the Adhvaryu.
Regarding this, they say: "This [Adhvaryu] should not be taken hold of by the sacrificer, for they lead him to death; therefore, he should not take hold of him."
Immediately after that, he should take hold [of the sacrificer]; for they do not lead him to death whom they lead to the sacrifice;
therefore he should take hold immediately. If he were not to take hold, he would exclude himself from the sacrifice;
therefore he should take hold immediately. Thus, by means of the two omentum-spits, he takes hold of it indirectly.

The Pratiprasthātṛ [takes hold of] the Pratiprasthātṛ, the Adhvaryu [takes hold of] the Adhvaryu, and the sacrificer [takes hold of] the Adhvaryu; thus, this constitutes an indirect taking hold of one another. Then, from the strewn Veda-grass mat—

The Adhvaryu takes up two blades of grass; having called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he says, "O Hotṛ, give the precept: 'Offer the oblations to the gods! This is the formula for the Vaiśvadeva at the animal sacrifice. Then he makes [the sacrificer] recite.
"O Revatī, O sacrificer!"—Revatī is indeed speech; because speech speaks much, therefore speech is "possessing wealth" (revatī).

"Enter with what is dear," he says; this means, "enter with safety. "From the wide atmosphere, in harmony with the divine Vāta"—for along the atmosphere a Rakṣas roams, rootless and severed on both sides, just like this [wind].

"The person, rootless and cut off on both sides, moves through the intermediate space; by being in harmony with the wind, protect him from the intermediate space"—this is what he means when he says, "From the wide intermediate space, in harmony with the divine wind.
"Sacrifice this oblation in its own self."
He thus says this to Speech: "Sacrifice with your own self for this uninjured oblation; be united with his body.
He thus says this to Speech: "Be united with the body of this uninjured oblation.
Now, when they dismember him...

He throws down a blade of grass in front of it with the formula, "O most abundant one, place the lord of the sacrifice in the most abundant sacrifice. He thereby strews sacrificial grass for him so that the oblation may not be spilled. Whatever of his spills here while he is being dissected, that settles upon this [grass]; thus it does not go to ruin. 3.8.1. [15]
Then, having returned and turned toward the Āhavanīya fire, they sit down, thinking, "Lest we be witnesses while he is being slaughtered.
They do not strike him with a blow from behind, for that would be human; rather, [they strike] from behind the ear, for that belongs to the Pitṛs.

Taking that [heart], they either thrust it into his mouth or make it a neck-halter for him. He does not say, "Slay! Kill! because that would be human; rather, he says, "Make him conscious! You have gone after [the gods]! For in the world of the gods (*devatrā*), he has indeed followed after the gods; therefore he says, "You have gone after. 3.8.1. [16]
When they pierce him [the victim], he offers before the immolation, saying, "Svāhā to the gods!
Then, when he announces, "The animal has been immolated," he offers, saying, "To the gods, Svāhā! For some [offerings] have the *svāhā* uttered first.

The gods who have the *svāhā* call above them are others; he thus gratifies them. Both these classes of gods, being gratified, carry him to the heavenly world. These two oblations are indeed for the sake of looking around (*paripaśavya*). If he should desire [to look around], let him offer them;
if, however, he should not desire it, let him pay no heed to them. 3.8.2.1.
When he has declared, "The animal has been consecrated," then the Adhvaryu says to the Neṣṭṛ, "Lead up the wife! and the Neṣṭṛ leads up the wife,
carrying the water for washing the feet.
He makes her recite:

"Homage to thee, O Ātāna! For the sacrifice is indeed the Ātāna, for they stretch out the sacrifice; thus the sacrifice is the Ātāna. Now, she who is the wife is the hind part of the sacrifice; he thus intends to propitiate the sacrifice by making her face the east.
He thus makes amends to this very sacrifice; so indeed, this sacrifice does not harm him. Therefore he says: "Homage to thee, O stretcher-out! "Go, unhindered! 3.8.2. [3]
"Go forward with no rival," he thereby says; "along the streams of ghee, along the paths of Truth," he thereby says, "go straight forward";
"O divine waters, carry us pure, well-served among the gods; may we be well-served as those who serve," he thereby purifies the waters. 3.8.2. [4]
Then the wife touches the vital breaths of the victim with water.
As to why she touches the vital breaths with water: the oblation of the gods is indeed living, and that of the immortals is immortal; yet they slay the victim when they quiet it.

In that he sprinkles water—water being indeed the vital breaths—he thereby bestows those vital breaths upon him; thus this very living person becomes the oblation for the gods, as the immortal for the immortals. Now, as for why the wife touches [it].
The wife is indeed a woman, and from a woman these creatures are born;
thus he causes him to be born from this woman. Therefore the wife touches [the water].
She touches it.
"I purify your speech," [he says] for the mouth; "I purify your breath," for the nostrils; "I purify your sight," for the eyes;
"I purify your hearing," for the ears; "I purify your navel," for that breath which is undefined;
"I purify your penis," or "I purify your anus," for that which is this.

Afterwards, he bestows breath upon it; he causes it to breathe. Then, having gathered together the tracks and the footprints, he says, "I purify these.
