For one stands firm by means of the feet; thus, for the sake of stability, he establishes it therein. 3.8.2. [7] Now, as for the waters that remain over...

With half of them, or as many as there are, the sacrificer and [the other] sprinkle him first from the head; they thereby bestow the vital breaths upon him and impel him forward from that state. 3.8.2.
[8] Now, as for the fact that they make it harsh.
When they establish [the fires], saying, "The waters are peace; with those waters, through peace, appease them! With those waters, join them together!"—at that moment they sprinkle along [the path].
"May your mind swell; may your speech swell; may your breath swell; may your eye swell;
may your ear swell"—thus he bestows the vital breaths upon him and sets them in motion. "That which is cruel in you, that which is settled, may that swell; may it expand"—so [he says]. 3.8.2. [10]
Now, when they make it harsh and when they settle it—water is peace; therefore, with water, by means of peace, you two appease it; with water, you two join it together;
"may that be purified for you," thus they make it pure; "for strength and days," [they do this] behind the animal.
As they lead [the horse] away (ninayataḥ), 3.8.2.[11]: "In that they make it fierce and establish it, it is so that these days and nights shall not remain unappeased."
With the verse, "From those great waters," they lead the animal behind [the sacrificial post].
Then they turn the animal over so that it lies on its back;
he places a blade of grass between [it and the post], saying, "O herb, protect! For the post is indeed a thunderbolt.
Thus, this thunderbolt-sword does not injure him; then he places it down with the sword, saying, "O Svadhiti, do not injure him!
For the sword is indeed a thunderbolt; thus, this thunderbolt-sword does not injure him.
Now, that which is the well-known edge—

With that [blade of grass] he places [the head of the horse]; for it is consecrated by the *yajus* and thus fit for sacrifice. He holds the tip of the grass in his left hand at the level of the vital breaths, and he takes the base with his right hand. When he throws it away—
From where this blood spurts up, he smears both sides [of the blade], saying, "Thou art the portion of the Rakṣases," for this blood is indeed the portion of the Rakṣases. Having cast it away,
he stands upon it.
"Here I trample upon this Rakṣas; here I crush this Rakṣas;

here I lead this Rakṣas into the lowest darkness. Thus, by means of the sacrifice itself, he crushes the destructive Rakṣases. And as for the fact that it is rootless and cut off on both sides—it is because it is indeed rootless.

This Rakṣas, cut off on both sides, wanders in the intermediate space, just as this man, rootless and cut off on both sides, wanders in the intermediate space; therefore it is rootless and cut off on both sides. 3.8.2.[16]
Then they extract the omentum.
With it he covers the two omentum-roasting spits, saying, "O Heaven and Earth, may you be covered with ghee!
Thereby he causes these two, Heaven and Earth, to partake of strength and sap; he bestows strength and sap upon them.

These creatures subsist upon this *rasavatī*, which provides the means of livelihood. 3.8.2.[17] There are two omentum-spits made of *kārṣmarya* wood. For it was there that the gods, in the beginning, immolated the animal victim.
As he was being dragged toward the north, his sacrificial wood fell downward; that became this *vanaspati* tree.

Because it fell downward as he was being dragged, it is called *kārṣmarya*. With that very essence, he thus provides him with nourishment and makes him complete. Therefore, the two omentum-spits are made of *kārṣmarya* wood. 3.8.2. [18]
He lets it soak;
he heats it over the animal-cooking fire, and thus it becomes cooked here as well.
The Āgnīdhra takes up a brand, and they go along behind the pit (cātvāla); they come and arrive at the Āhavanīya fire.

The Adhvaryu throws this blade of grass into the Āhavanīya fire with the formula, "Vāyu, indeed, [is the fuel] for the drops," for this is the kindling-stick for the drops. Then, standing to the north, he heats the omentum;
for he is about to pass beyond the fire from the south.
Going around it with the intention of cooking it, he thus offers this expiation to Agni; so indeed Agni does not harm him as he passes by.
Therefore, standing to the north, he heats the omentum.
They carry it between the sacrificial post and the fire.
Now, as for why they do not carry [the oblation] along the middle line by which they carry other offerings:
it is so that we do not extend the sacrifice with something uncooked. And as for why they do not carry it outside along the front of the sacrificial post:
they would thereby place it outside the sacrifice. Therefore, they carry it between the sacrificial post and the fire, having gone around to the south.

The Pratiprasthātṛ cooks [the omentum]. 3.8.2. [21] Then, having taken up clarified butter with the *sruva* spoon, the Adhvaryu makes an offering over the omentum, saying: "May Agni enjoy the clarified butter; *svāhā*! And so it is.
"These drops, having been cooked and consecrated with *svāhā*, become oblations and reach Agni.
Then he says, "Recite for the drops. He recites verses addressed to Agni for the drops; as to why he recites verses addressed to Agni for the drops...
"Rain indeed has its offering from here, for from here Agni wins the rain; he wins these drops by means of those [verses];
thus these drops rain down. Therefore, he recites verses addressed to Agni for the drops.
When [the oblation] is cooked, the Pratiprasthātṛ then says, 'It is cooked; proceed!'"
Having taken up the two offering-ladles, the Adhvaryu steps across, calls for the *āśrāvaṇa*, and says, "Prompt [the Hotṛ] for the offerings accompanied by the *svāhā*-utterances.
When the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered, he makes the oblation.
Having offered, he first pours clarified butter over the omentum itself.
Now, as for the speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*): the Caraka-Adhvaryus indeed sprinkle the speckled butter first, saying, "The speckled butter is the breath.
While he was doing so, a Caraka-Adhvaryu challenged Yājñavalkya, [saying], "Is this not the breath?"
"This Adhvaryu priest has gone inside; the vital breath will desert him," [he thought].
He would look at his own arms and say:
"These two arms are grey; where indeed is the word of a Brāhmaṇa?"
One should not pay heed to the thought "it happened thus," for this is indeed the final fore-offering (*prayāja*).

In this sacrificial offering (*haviryajña*), at the final fore-offering, one first bastes the *dhruvā* ladle; for it is from that [ladle] that he is about to offer the first two portions of clarified butter (*ājyabhāga*).
However, here he is about to offer the omentum (*vapā*) first; therefore, he should baste the omentum first, and then—

Now, as for the speckled butter: the reason he does not baste the animal with it is so that he shall not baste what is uncooked. In this way, his entire animal becomes basted when he bastes the omentum; therefore, he should baste the omentum first, and then [the rest].
The speckled butter (pṛṣadājya) [is used]. 3.8.2.
[26] Now he spreads a layer of clarified butter;
then he places a piece of gold; then...
While cutting off the omentum, he says, "Recite for Agni and Soma the omentum and fat of the goat.
Then he places a piece of gold [upon it], and then he pours clarified butter over it twice from above.
As for why there are pieces of gold on both sides:

They indeed kill this animal when they offer it in the fire; gold is immortal life. Thus he establishes himself in immortal life; thus he rises from there, and thus he comes to life. Therefore, there are two pieces of gold on both sides. Having called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he says: "To Agni and Soma, the omentum and the fat of the goat."
Having said "Send forth," he does not say "It has set out"; when the *prasava* has been given, he says "It has set out," and he offers the oblation when the *vaṣaṭ* has been uttered.
Having offered the omentum, having made the two omentum-spits meet and thrown them after [the offering], he makes the offering to the upward-moving sky with the cry of *svāhā*.
"Go to the wind; let these two not be thus deprived of their testicles by those two through which we have offered the omentum. 3.8.2.
[29] Now, as for why they proceed with the omentum:
it is to that very deity for whom they immolate the animal that they thereby gratify.
He gratifies with the fat; this deity, being gratified by this fat, remains calm while the subsequent oblations are being cooked.
Therefore, they proceed with the omentum. Then they purify themselves at the *cātvāla* pit.

They indeed do something cruel when they quiet the animal and when they dissect it. Water is the means of pacification; therefore, they appease it with water as a means of pacification, and they heal it with water. That is why they purify themselves at the *cātvāla* pit. Now, whatever deity the animal belongs to—

He subsequently prepares a sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) dedicated to that deity. As to why he subsequently prepares the sacrificial cake: rice and barley are indeed the essence (medha) of all animals; by means of that very essence, he thus provides him with completion and makes him whole. Therefore, he subsequently prepares the sacrificial cake. 3.8.3. [2]
Then, having proceeded with the omentum, he proceeds with this cake. For they extract this omentum from the middle; verily, he satisfies him from the middle with this essence and makes him complete.

Therefore, having performed the offering with the omentum, he performs it with this cake; for wherever this animal cake is offered as a subsequent oblation, that indeed is its proper connection. Then he dissects the animal.
"Make it move three times; make the heart of that which has moved three times the most excellent," for the sacrifice is threefold. Then he instructs the slaughterer:
If anyone should ask you, "Is the oblation cooked, O Śamitr? you should simply say, "It is cooked.
[If they reply,] "O venerable one, it is not cooked; it is indeed not cooked," [then... 3.8.3.
[5] Then, having taken a portion of the speckled butter with the *juhū* ladle...
The Adhvaryu, having gone out, asks, "O Śamitṛ, is the oblation cooked?
"It is cooked," he replies. "That belongs to the gods," the Adhvaryu says in a whisper. As for why he asks: it is because [he desires to know] that. 3.8.3. [6] Thus, as for his questioning.
The oblation of the gods is indeed cooked, not uncooked; for the slaughterer knows whether it has been cooked or not.
That is why he asks.
"One should proceed with what has been cooked," he says. Now, even if it is not cooked, it becomes a cooked oblation for the gods;
it becomes cooked for the sacrificer, and the Adhvaryu does not become a sinner through that act. That sin falls upon the slaughterer.
He asks three times, for the sacrifice is threefold. And when he says, "That belongs to the gods," it is indeed that which is cooked which belongs to the gods.
Therefore he says, "That of the gods" (3.8.3). He first sprinkles clarified butter upon the heart;
for the heart is indeed the self, the mind, and the vital breath.
He thus places the speckled butter—the vital breath—into his own mind; in this way, he becomes the very life of the gods as their oblation, and the immortal among the immortals.
He then pours [the butter] over it.

"May your mind unite with the mind, may your breath unite with the breath," he says; he does not utter "svāhā," for this is not a *āhuti* offering. They carry the animal between the *cātvāla* pit, the sacrificial post, and the fire. 3.8.3. [10] They carry it behind the *cātvāla*.
Now, as to why they do not carry it along the middle:

[it is] so that they may carry the other oblations; for if it were cooked, one might think, "Lest we should tear it limb from limb and make it cruel by cutting it up, and thus join it with the sacrifice in the middle. And as to why they do not carry it outside along the front of the sacrificial post: [it would be] excluded from the sacrifice.

Therefore, they should perform [the ritual] from the sacrifice; hence they carry [the oblation] between the sacrificial post and the fire. Having placed it to the south, the Pratiprasthātṛ makes the offering. The Plakṣa branches serve as the northern under-layer; he makes the offering upon them.
Now, as to why the Plakṣa branches serve as the northern under-layer... 3.8.3. [11]

When the gods first immolated the victim, Tvaṣṭṛ vomited it out from its head, thinking, "They shall not immolate it thus. For animals belong to Tvaṣṭṛ; this very thing is the brain in the head and the marrow in the spine.
Therefore, like one who has vomited, Tvaṣṭṛ indeed swallowed him; for this was what had been vomited by Tvaṣṭṛ.
Therefore, one should not eat it, for it is the vomit of Tvaṣṭṛ.
His vital essence fell downward.

This very tree was born; the gods beheld it, and therefore it is called *prakhyas*—for "plakṣa" is indeed the same as "prakhyas. By means of that very essence, he thus causes him to prosper and makes him complete; therefore, it is a branch of the *plakṣa* tree.

The northern sacrificial grass is spread out (3.8.3.13). Then he makes an under-layering of clarified butter in both the *juhū* and the *upabhṛt* ladles, as well as in the *vasāhomahavanī* vessel and the *samavattadhānī*. Then...
He places pieces of gold into both the *juhū* and the *upabhṛt*.

Then he recites the invitatory verse (*anuvākyā*) for the *manotā* deity regarding the oblation. Now, as to why he recites the invitatory verse for the *manotā* regarding the oblation: it is because [the *manotā*] encompasses all [the deities].

Indeed, all the deities approach the animal being sacrificed, thinking, "He will utter my name; he will utter my name. For the animal is the oblation for all the deities; the minds of all those deities are woven into the animal. It is these very [minds] that he thus gratifies, and so it is not in vain for the deities.

The minds become united; therefore, he recites the invitatory formula for the *manotā* portion of the oblation. 3.8.3.[15] He first cuts a portion from the heart. Now, as to why he first cuts a portion from the heart even though it is situated in the middle: the vital breath (*prāṇa*) indeed...

For from the heart this vital breath (*prāṇa*) moves upward; the vital breath is indeed the animal. For as long as one breathes with the vital breath, so long is one an animal. But when the vital breath departs from him, then having become like a block of wood, he lies useless. 3.8.3. The heart, indeed, is the animal.

He first cuts a portion from this very self; therefore, if any one of the portions should be omitted, he need not heed it, for he has already made an offering of that entire animal by cutting the heart first. Therefore, although [the animal] is in the middle, he cuts the heart first, and then [he proceeds] according to the previous order. 3.8.3. [17]
Then for the tongue;
for it stands forth from the fore-part. Then for the breast; for that is from there.
Then for the single-moving arm; then for the two sides; then for the thin part; then for the two kidneys. 3.8.3. [18]
He divides the rectum into three parts.
Having set aside the thick part for the *upayaj* offerings, he cuts the middle portion into two pieces and places them in the *juhū* ladle;
he then places the thin part among the three limbs (*tryaṅga*). Then, from the buttock for the one who wanders alone (*ekacarā*), he cuts this much into the *juhū*. 3.8.3. [19]
Then, regarding the *upabhṛt* [ladle]:

having divided the rectum of the three-part foreleg into two parts, he makes the offering; then, from the three-part hindquarter, he makes the offering; then he places two chips of gold upon it; then he pours clarified butter over the top. 3.8.3. [20]
Then he takes the fat-oblation.
He says, "Thou art gladdening," for the fat indeed moves as it were; therefore he says, "Thou art gladdening.
"May Agni prepare thee," he says, for Agni indeed prepares this; therefore he says, "May Agni prepare thee. "May the waters mingle with thee," [he says], for the waters...
For they extract this sap from the limbs; therefore he says, "The waters have carried thee.
[With the words] "Thee with the rush of the wind," for he who blows here blows along the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*); indeed, it is for the sake of the intermediate space.
He takes it; therefore he says, "With the speed of Vāta, for thee.
[3.8.3.22] "With the rush of Pūṣan. This indeed is the rush of Pūṣan, for he takes it for him; therefore he says, "With the rush of Pūṣan."
Thus [it is said]: "3.8.3 [23] 'He shall suffer from heat. This indeed is the heat; for it is from this that he draws [the draught], therefore they say, "from the heat."
Thinking "May it tremble," he then pours clarified butter over it twice from above.
Then he stirs it with the edge of the razor or the blade, saying, "May hatred be driven away"; thereby he drives away the destructive *nāṣṭrā* demons from here.
[They] strike [the victim].
3.8.3.[25] Now, if there remains any broth, he pours it into the *samavattadhānī* (the vessel for the portions); he then throws the heart into it, and the tongue.
Having cut the thin part of the chest and the vaniṣṭhu, he then twice pours clarified butter over them from above.
As for the two pieces of gold being on both sides:
they indeed strike this animal when it is offered in the fire.
Offering up gold—which is immortal life—he becomes established in that immortal life; thus he rises from it, and thus he lives.
Therefore, there are two pieces of gold on both sides.
Then, as for why he cuts the portions crosswise:

From the left foreleg and from the right hind leg, and from the right foreleg and the left hind leg; therefore this animal strides its steps crosswise. For if he were to cut portions straight on, this animal would stride its steps straight on; therefore he cuts the portions crosswise. And as for why he does not cut a portion from the head:

Not on the shoulders, not on the spine, nor on the thighs. 3.8.3 [28] In the beginning, the Asuras indeed sacrificed animals; the gods did not approach them out of fear. Then this earth spoke to them.
"Do not disregard this; I shall be the overseer for you all, according to how they proceed with this," [said the goddess].
She said: "They have offered one oblation and left the other remaining. Those which they left remaining are these very portions (*avadāna*); from them, the gods [offered] to Sviṣṭakṛt.
They assigned three parts [of the victim] to the gods; therefore, one should cut portions from three parts. Then the Asuras ate [the remaining parts]:
from the head, from the two shoulders, and from the lower back and the two hind thighs; therefore, one should not cut portions from those.
Furthermore, because Tvaṣṭṛ gnawed at the lower back, one should not cut a portion from the lower back. Then he says, "To Agni and Soma, of the goat..."

Having called for the *āśrāvaṇa* with "Recite the invitatory verse for the oblation," he says, "Prompt [the Hotṛ] for the offering of the oblation to Agni and Soma"; he says "it is not yet set forth" before the *prasava*, and "it is set forth" once the *prasava* has been given.
3.8.3. [30] Between the two half-verses of the *yājyā*, he offers the *vasā-homa*.

Or rather, this sacrificial essence (medhas) has risen upward from here; by means of this essence, the creatures subsist upon the sap of Yama. This essence is from below the sky; the fat-oblation is indeed essence, and the sacrificial essence is essence.
By means of essence, he thus makes the essence intense. Therefore, this essence is not exhausted even while being consumed. 3.8.3. [31]

Now, as for why he offers the *vasā* oblation between the two half-verses of the *yājyā*: this [earth] is one half-verse and yonder sky is the other half-verse; between heaven and earth is the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*). It is indeed for the intermediate space that he offers.
Therefore, between the two half-verses of the *yājyā*, he offers the *vasāhoma* (the fat-oblation).
He offers it with this Vaiśvadeva formula: "O drinkers of ghee, drink the ghee; O drinkers of fat, drink the fat!
You are the oblation of the intermediate space, *svāhā*! For the intermediate space belongs to the All-gods (*vaiśvadeva*); since by means of this [space] these [beings] exist...

The creatures, both those that breathe out and those that breathe up, move about in the intermediate space; therefore, he offers at the *vaṣaṭ*-call what belongs to the All-Gods (*vaiśvadeva*)—namely, those portions which are in the *juhū* ladle.
Then, while stirring the clotted butter (*pṛṣadājya*) with the *juhū*, he says:
Having called for the *āśrāvaṇa* with "Recite for Vanaspati," he says, "Prompt for Vanaspati," and offers the oblation when the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered.
As to why he offers to Vanaspati: he thereby makes this very sacrificial post (*yūpa*), which is a thunderbolt, a sharer in the sacrifice.
Vanaspati is indeed Soma; he thus makes the animal itself into Soma. And as to why [he offers] between the two...
He offers two oblations; he thereby pervades both. Therefore, he offers the two oblations between them.
Now, as for those portions that are in the *upabhṛt* ladle, while bringing them together, he says: "To Agni Sviṣṭakṛt..."
Having called for the *āśrāvaṇa* with "Recite the after-offering," he says, "Prompt [the Hotṛ] for Agni Sviṣṭakṛt," and offers when the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered. 3.8.3.
[35] Then, with what remains of the fat-oblation (*vasāhoma*), he sprinkles the quarters: the quarters, the intermediate quarters, the directed quarters, and the sub-quarters.
"To the quarters, Svāhā!"—the fat-offering is indeed essence; thus he places essence in all these quarters.
Therefore, this essence is found coming from every direction. Then he touches the animal.
Now is the time for the touching; however, if he touches it beforehand, fearing that those who approach it will crush it, he should touch it right here if he does not fear such crushing. 3.8.3. [37]
The out-breath belongs to Indra;

"May Indra’s out-breath settle in every limb," he says, for when [the victim] is cut limb by limb, he thereby unites it with the out-breath and the in-breath. "O divine Tvaṣṭṛ, let much come together for thee."
"In that he becomes of different form while possessing the same mark, he thus makes it complete in its entirety.

"May his friends, his mother, and his father rejoice after thee as thou goest to the gods for help"—in that he has offered him [the oblation], he thereby makes him whole and unites with him; thus his self becomes whole in yonder world. 3.8.4.1.
There are indeed three sets of eleven in the sacrificial animal:
eleven fore-offerings (*prayāja*), eleven after-offerings (*anuyāja*), and eleven concluding offerings (*upayaja*).

There are ten fingers of the hands, ten toes of the feet, and ten vital breaths—namely, the out-breath (*prāṇa*), the up-breath (*udāna*), and the through-breath (*vyāna*). Such is the extent of the person (*puruṣa*).
"The most excellent among animals, after whom all other animals follow.
Regarding this they say: "What is performed in the sacrifice by which the vital breath (*prāṇa*) becomes auspicious for all the limbs?
It is when he divides the rectum into three parts.
The anus is indeed the vital breath (*prāṇa*); this very breath extends forward, and it moves along with that [anus]. When he divides the anus into three parts—
A third part [is for] the *upayaj* offerings, a third part in the *juhū* ladle, and a third part in the *upabhṛt* ladle;
by that, the vital breath becomes auspicious for all the limbs. 3.8.4.
[5] But indeed, one should sacrifice an animal.

If he should bring this sacrificial essence (medha) [to the victim] while it is emaciated, he should squeeze into the rectum whatever remains of the abdominal fat. The rectum is indeed the vital breath (prāṇa); this breath extends forward, and along it the vital breath moves. The animal is indeed the vital breath; for as long as one breathes with the vital breath, so long is one an animal. Now...

When the vital breath departs from him, he then lies like a piece of wood, senseless. 3.8.4. [6] The animal is indeed the rectum; the sacrificial essence is the fat; thus he brings it to the state of sacrificial essence. And if it is fleshy, [he does so].
"In that case, intelligence comes to him spontaneously.
3.8.4.[7] Then he takes the speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*).
This world consists of two things: clarified butter and curds; it is indeed a pair.
A pair is procreation; thus, this procreative pairing is brought about. Therefore, he proceeds with the *anuyāja* offerings.
The *anuyājas* are indeed cattle, and the speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*) is milk; thus, he places that milk into the cattle.
He places it; thus this milk is placed within the cattle, for the speckled butter is breath, and the speckled butter is food, and breath is indeed food.
With that, he proceeds at the fore-offerings (anuyājas).

That which is this breath in front, it is that he thereby places; with it he offers the after-offerings (upayaj). That which is this breath behind, it is that he thereby places. Thus these two breaths are placed on both sides—both that which is above and that which is below. 3.8.4. [10]
Now, one of these two offers the *vaṣaṭ* call for both [the Adhvaryu and the sacrificer];

it is for the Adhvaryu and for him who performs the secondary offerings (*upayaj*). And because he performs the secondary offerings while the sacrifice is being performed, they are called "secondary offerings" (*upayaja*); furthermore, in that he performs the secondary offerings, he thereby causes [the offspring] to be born.
He offers the *upayaj* oblations from behind, for from behind offspring are born of a woman.
He offers them thus: "Go to the ocean, svāhā! The ocean is indeed water, and water is semen; he thus pours forth semen.
"Go to the intermediate space, svāhā!
Indeed, offspring are born following the intermediate space; thus he causes them to be born following the intermediate space. 3.8.4 [13]
"Go to the god Savitṛ, svāhā!"—Savitṛ is indeed the impeller of the gods; thus, impelled by Savitṛ, he brings this [offspring] forth. "Go to Mitra and Varuṇa, svāhā!"
Mitra and Varuṇa are indeed out-breath and in-breath; he thus places out-breath and in-breath among the creatures.
"Go to day and night, Svāhā! he says.
"Go to the meters, svāhā!"—verily, offspring are born in accordance with day and night; he thus causes them to be born in accordance with day and night. 3.8.4. [16]
"There are indeed seven meters, seven domestic animals, and seven wild animals; it is these two groups that he thus causes to propagate. "Go to heaven and earth, svāhā! [3.8.4.17]
Prajāpati, having created the creatures, enclosed them within heaven and earth; these creatures are thus enclosed by heaven and earth.
In the same way, this [sacrificer], having created the creatures, now encloses them within heaven and earth. 3.8.4. [18]
Then he performs the secondary offerings (*atīṣṭi*).
For if he were not to perform the secondary offerings, there would be only as many creatures as were created in the beginning, and they would not procreate;
but because he performs the secondary offerings, he causes them to be born. Therefore, these creatures [procreate].
They are born again as they turn back toward him. 3.8.5.
He performs the *atyupayaj* sacrifice, saying, "Go to the sacrifice, svāhā! Water, indeed, is the sacrifice; water is seed; thus he pours forth seed. 3.8.5.2.
"Go to Soma, svāhā!"—Soma is indeed seed; he thus pours forth seed. "Go to the celestial ether, svāhā!"
The waters are indeed the celestial sky; the waters are semen; he thus pours forth that very semen with the words, "Go to Agni Vaiśvānara, Svāhā!
For this earth is indeed Agni Vaiśvānara; it is she.
He thus causes this very foundation to be reproduced.
Then he wipes his face with the words, "May my mind be in my heart. In this way, the sacrificer preserves himself.
It does not follow after [the sacrifice]. 3.8.5.[6] Then they perform the *saṃyājana* of the wives with the tail (*jāghanī*).
The tail is indeed the hind part; from the hind part, indeed...

From a woman offspring are born; therefore, he causes this very thing to be born when they cause the wives to perform the *saṃyājana* sacrifice with the tail. He cuts portions for the wives of the gods from the interior;
for from the interior of a woman offspring are born.
Above [the offering to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt], he offers to Agni Gṛhapati; for from above, the male indeed mounts upon the female. 3.8.5.
[8] Then they go to the purificatory bath (avabhṛtha) with the heart-spike.
For of the animal being sacrificed, the heart—

The spit enters from the heart; therefore, it is a "heart-spit" (*hṛdayaśūla*). Now, that part of the omentum which they cut around, that is the *alaṃjuṣ*. Therefore, one should indeed roast it after cutting it around. When the animal has been moved three times, he pulls out the heart and places it on top [of the omentum]. 3.8.5. [9]
Then he offers the heart-spike.

He should not throw it away on the earth, nor into the waters. For if he were to throw it away on the earth, it would enter the plants and the trees; and if he were to throw it away into the waters, it would enter the waters.
Therefore, one should not discharge it on the earth nor into the waters. Having entered the water,
one should bury it at the junction where the dry and the wet meet, if indeed...

If he should become weary before reaching the water for bathing, he should pour out a vessel of water in front of the sacrificial post; where the junction of the dry and the moist occurs, he hides [the post] there with the formula:
"Do not harm the waters, do not harm the plants. Thus he does not harm the waters or the plants.
With the verse, "From every bond, O King Varuṇa, release us; when they say 'O inviolable one,' we swear by Varuṇa," he releases himself from the bonds of Varuṇa.

Then [he recites], "Release us from Varuna. Thereby he releases him from every bond of Varuna, from everything pertaining to Varuna. 3.8.5. [11] Then he addresses [the waters]: "May the waters and plants be friendly to us; may they be unfriendly to him who..."

"He hates us, and we hate him"—at that moment when they proceed with this [offering], the waters and the plants indeed withdraw from him and stand apart; however, by means of those [plants], he establishes a bond of friendship, and so they enter him again. This is the expiation performed therein; it is certainly not [the expiation] for the Agniṣomīya.
He performs [the rite] for the animal, but not for the Agni-related one; rather, it is for the barren cow (*vaśā*) as the *anūbandhyā*. For the entire sacrifice concludes with her.
Indeed, this constitutes the performance of the heart-spit (*hṛdayaśūla*) rite for both his Agni-Soma animal and the Agni-related animal, when they perform the rite for the barren cow. 3.9.1.1.
Prajāpati, having created living beings, felt as if he were depleted. Therefore, his creatures turned away; they did not remain for his prosperity or for the eating of food. 3.9.1 [2]
He reflected:
"I am the intermediate region; I have been emitted for this desire of mine, yet that desire of mine has not been fulfilled.
My offspring have turned away from me; my offspring have not remained for the sake of prosperity and the eating of food. (3.9.1)
That Prajāpati reflected: "How indeed might I replenish myself again, so that my creatures may return to me and remain for my glory and for the sake of food? 3.9.1 [4]
Desiring offspring, he performed worship, exerted himself, and practiced austerities.
He beheld this set of eleven offerings; having sacrificed with this set of eleven, Prajāpati replenished his own self, and offspring returned to him and remained with him.

For the sake of prosperity and the eating of food, he became more prosperous after having sacrificed. Therefore, one should sacrifice for him with the Ekādaśinī; thus indeed he increases in offspring and cattle, and offspring come to him.
His offspring return to him and remain for his prosperity and the eating of food; having sacrificed, he becomes more prosperous.
For this purpose he sacrifices with the set of eleven victims.
He first seizes a victim for Agni.
Agni, indeed, is the mouth of the deities, the progenitor;
he is Prajāpati, and he is also the sacrificer. Therefore, the offering belongs to Agni. Then follows the offering to Sarasvatī.
Sarasvatī is indeed speech; by means of speech, Prajāpati thereby replenished himself again.
Speech returned to him; he made speech subject to his own will. Verily, this sacrificer now replenishes himself by means of speech;
speech returns to him; he makes speech subject to his own will. 3.9.1 [8]
Then [he offers] to Soma. Soma is indeed food; by means of food, Prajāpati thus nourished himself again, and food turned toward him, following after him from his own self.
"Let him prepare food; thus he causes this [sacrificer] to swell with food, and food turns toward him; he makes food subject to himself.
[9] Now, as for why it follows that of Sarasvatī:
Sarasvatī is indeed speech, and Soma is food; therefore, he who is well-disposed toward speech becomes truly an eater of food. 3.9.1.
[10] Now follows the offering to Pūṣan.
Pūṣan is indeed cattle; by means of cattle, Prajāpati then replenished himself.
Cattle turned back toward him; he made cattle subject to his own self. Verily, by means of cattle, he now replenishes himself;
cattle turn back toward him; he makes cattle subject to his own self. 3.9.1 [11]
Now follows the offering to Bṛhaspati. Bṛhaspati is indeed the Brahman;
by means of the Brahman, Prajāpati thereby replenished himself again, the Brahman turned back toward him, and he made the Brahman his own follower.
This [offering] of his is thereby nourished by the *brahman*; the *brahman* turns toward him; he makes the *brahman* favorable to himself.
Now, as for the fact that it follows the offering to Pūṣan.

Pūṣan is indeed cattle, and Bṛhaspati is the Brahman; therefore, the Brāhmaṇa is the most audacious regarding cattle, for they have been placed within him and deposited in his mouth. Therefore, having given away all that, he goes about clothed in a skin. 3.9.1. [13]

Then follows the Vaiśvadeva offering. All indeed are the Viśvedevas; with everything, Prajāpati thereby replenished himself again; everything turned back toward him, and he made everything subject to himself.
In this way, he causes all this to swell; everything turns toward him, and he makes everything subject to himself.
Now, as for why it follows that which belongs to Bṛhaspati:

Bṛhaspati is indeed Brahman; the All-Gods are this entire universe. He thus makes Brahman the mouth of this entire universe; therefore, the Brāhmaṇa is the mouth of this entire universe. 3.9.1. [15] Now follows that for Indra.

The sense-organ (*indriya*) is indeed vigor (*vīrya*); it belongs to Indra (*indra*). By means of that very sense-organ and vigor, Prajāpati nourished himself again; the sense-organ and vigor returned to him, and he made the sense-organ and vigor part of his own self.
In this same way, by means of that very sense-organ and vigor, he now nourishes himself; the sense-organ returns to him.
Vigor returns to him; he makes the sense-organ of vigor conform to himself. 3.9.1.[16] Now, as for the fact that the Vaiśvadeva offering follows [the Āgneya]:
Indra is indeed the nobility (*kṣatra*), and the All-gods (*viśve devāḥ*) are the common people (*viś*); it is thus food-eating (*annādya*) that he provides for him.
He performs this first;
then the Māruta [offering].
The Maruts are indeed the subjects (viś), and the subjects are the foundation (bhūman); by means of that foundation, Prajāpati [established it].
He further nourished himself; abundance returned to him; he made abundance his own.
Verily, he is thus nourished by abundance; abundance returns to him; he makes abundance his own. 3.9.1 [18]

Now, as for the fact that it follows the one addressed to Indra: Indra is indeed the nobility (*kṣatra*), and the All-gods are the common people (*viś*); the Maruts are indeed the common people. Thus, by means of the common people, he makes this nobility firm on all sides; so this nobility is made firm on both sides by the common people. 3.9.1. [19]
Then [the offering] for Indra and Agni:
Agni is indeed brilliance, and Indra is sensory power and vigor;
by means of both these powers Prajāpati nourished himself again, and both powers returned to him, both powers.

He makes two joints for himself; by means of both these powers he is indeed strengthened. Both powers turn toward him; he makes two joints for himself as both powers. 3.9.1 [20] Then follows the Sāvitra offering.
Savitṛ is indeed the impeller of the gods; thus, all these desires of his are fulfilled, impelled by Savitṛ.
Then he immolates the animal for Varuṇa at the end; thereby he [releases him].
He releases [the victim] from every noose of Varuna, from everything belonging to Varuna.
Therefore, if there should be a set of eleven sacrificial posts (*yūpaikādaśinī*), one should offer the animal dedicated to Agni at the post standing nearest the fire.

Then he should employ the others; they should initiate them in the same manner as before. 3.9.1.[23] If, however, there should be a set of eleven victims, they should immolate the victim for Agni at the sacrificial post, and then the others in the same manner as before. 3.9.1.[24]
They lead them northward here;
they lead the one dedicated to Agni first, then the others in their proper order. They fix them here.
They first pierce the southernmost [post] dedicated to Agni, then, having led the others toward the north, they proceed as before.
At that point where they perform the ritual with the omenta of those [animals], [the following occurs].
They proceed first with the omentum of the offering to Agni alone, and then with those of the others in their proper order. 3.9.1. [27] Wherever they proceed with them...

They proceed first with the offering to Agni alone, and then with the others in their proper sequence. For when the head of the sacrifice was cut off, its sap flowed away and entered the waters; it is with that very sap that they [now] enter the waters.
They think that this very essence is flowing as it flows.
When he goes for the *vasatīvarī* waters, he thereby brings back that very essence and places it in the sacrifice, making the sacrifice full of essence.
Therefore, he brings the *vasatīvarī* waters.
He distributes them at all the pressings; thus, he places essence into all the pressings. All...
He makes the pressings flavorful; therefore, he distributes [the water] among all [of them].
3.9.2.[4] He should indeed take [the water] from those that are flowing;
for that is the essence of the sacrifice; therefore, [he takes it] from those that are flowing.
One should take [the draughts].
3.9.2.[5] Indeed, these are taken for protection;
for everything else here, whatever it may be, dissolves away, even this [person] who is here.
It purifies; therefore, these [waters] do not flow away. For that reason, one should take [the water] from flowing streams.
One should take it by day, thinking, "May I take the essence of the sacrifice while seeing it. Therefore, one should take it by day. Indeed, for this purpose...
He draws [the cup] for him who shines yonder; for he draws it for all the gods, since his rays are indeed all the gods.
Therefore, one should draw it during the day; for he is indeed like the day, and for that reason also one should draw it during the day. This, indeed, is what all the gods [do].

They go to the house of the sacrificer. He who takes up the Vasatīvarī waters before the setting of the sun—just as one would wait upon a superior person who is about to arrive with a prepared dwelling—so do these oblations enter him. They enter him.
They fast upon these *vasatīvarī* waters; that is the *upavasatha*. 3.9.2.
[8] If the sun should set while they have not yet taken [the water], then an expiation is performed there, provided it is one who has previously performed the sacrifice.
One may take them from the *nināhya* (the stored supply). For previously, during the day, those [soma-plants] have already been taken by him.
However, if he has not yet performed a sacrifice, or if someone who has performed a sacrifice has either arrived at his place or is staying nearby, one may take them from that person's *nināhya*;
for previously, during the day, those [plants] have already been taken by him. 3.9.2. [9]

If he should not find either of these two, he should go out carrying a firebrand; holding it above him, he should take [the earth], or holding gold above him, he should take it. Thus, that form of his is produced.
This one shines. 3.9.2.[10] Now, therefore, he draws [the water]:
"These waters are rich in oblation," for the essence of the sacrifice entered into them; therefore he says this.
"Rich in oblation are these waters," [he says]; "the one rich in oblation desires to win them," for the sacrificer, being rich in oblation, indeed desires to win them;
therefore he says, "the one rich in oblation desires to win them.
"The god rich in oblation, the sacrifice... [he says].

The sacrifice is indeed the *adhvara*; thus, for whichever sacrifice he draws [the cup], he makes that one possessed of the oblation (*haviṣmat*). Therefore he says: "May the divine sacrifice be possessed of the oblation. "May Sūrya be possessed of the oblation."
Verily, he takes them for him who shines yonder; for he takes them for all the gods, since all the gods are his rays. Therefore he says, "May Sūrya be possessed of the oblation.
Having brought them, he places them behind the Gārhapatya fire.

"I place thee in the seat of Agni Vapanagṛha"—by this he means to say, "I place thee in the seat of Agni Anārtagṛha. Now, when the animal sacrifice to Agni and Soma is completed, he carries [the fire] around, saying, "Step aside! The sacrificer sits down in front of the two *havirdhāna* sheds.
He takes it up (3.9.2.14). He goes out by the southern door.
He places them on the southern hip [of the altar], saying: "Ye are the portion of Indra and Agni."
For he draws them for all the gods, since Indra and Agni are indeed all the gods; having brought them back again, he places them in front of the wife.
Having gone around behind the wife, he takes them up.
He goes out by the northern way.

He places them on the northern hip [of the altar], saying, "Ye are the portion of Mitra and Varuṇa. He should not place them thus; for that would be excessive, and in that way the ritual perfection (*sampad*) is not achieved. He should say instead, "Ye are the portion of Indra and Agni"; thus it is not excessive, and in that way the ritual perfection is achieved. 3.9.2. [16]
These [bricks] are carried around for protection.

Agni is in front, and then these are laid down on all sides, driving away the destructive spirits and demons; he places them in the Āgnīdhra fire-hall with the formula: "You are the portion of the Viśve Devas."

Then he causes all the gods to settle therein; these indeed are the best of those who dwell, therefore they are called *vasatīvarī* (dwelling waters). He who knows this becomes the best of those who dwell. These, moreover, are seven sacrificial formulas (*yajus*). 3.9.2. [17]

With four [formulas] he takes [the fire]; with one he sets it down at the Gārhapatya; with one he carries it around; with one [he places it] at the Āgnīdhra. These are seven. For the meters born of speech are seven, and among them the Śakvarī is the most excellent, consisting of seven feet. It is for the sake of this correspondence that there are seven sacrificial formulas (yajus).
They awaken them.
Having touched water, they approach the Āgnīdhra fire-shed; there they take up the portions of clarified butter.
Having taken the clarified butter (ājya), they go forward and set down the ājyas. Then he brings down the King (Soma);
this earth is indeed the foundation, the birthplace of these [waters].
He brings it down toward this very support of creatures; he extends it for her, he procreates it for her.
He brings it down between [the pressing stones];
for the sacrifice is breath—thus he does not place the sacrifice outside of breath, [but] upon the pressing stones.

He places them facing each other. Soma is indeed the nobility (*kṣatra*), and the pressing-stones are the common people (*viś*). He thus places the nobility above the common people. As for the fact that they face each other, he thereby makes the common people face the nobleman, so that they do not speak in opposition to him. Therefore, they face each other. 3.9.3 [4]
He brings it down with the formula, "Thee for the heart, thee for the mind! He says this for the sake of the sacrificer's desire;
for by means of his heart and mind, the sacrificer desires that very desire for which he performs the sacrifice. Therefore he says, "Thee for the heart, thee for the mind! (3.9.3).
"To the sky thee! To Sūrya thee!"—by saying "To the sky thee! To Sūrya thee," he says, in effect, "To the world of the gods thee!
And when he says, "To the gods thee! Raise this sacrifice upward to the gods; may the Hotr-offerings reach them," [he means that] the sacrifice is indeed...
"O Sacrifice, place this sacrifice upward for the gods in heaven"— this is what he says. "O King Soma, descend among all these subjects"—
he thus [places him] for the sovereignty over these subjects.
He brings [the king] down for the sake of the kingdom (rājya). Then, having released him, he worships [him], saying:
"May all subjects descend unto you," as if in a manner that is not quite orderly.

When he says, "Descend unto all thy subjects," Soma is indeed the nobility (kṣatra), and thus he makes it a reversal of the natural order; accordingly, this world is made a reversal of the natural order. But here he acts rightly and as before when he says, "Let all thy subjects descend unto thee"; thereby he causes him to descend together with these very subjects.
Therefore, when a Kṣatriya approaches, these subjects, the commoners, descend before him; they wait upon him from below.
Having sat down, the Hotṛ priest becomes one who is about to recite the Prātaranuvāka.
Then, placing a fuel-stick on the fire, he says:

"Recite for the gods who come in the morning! The meters are indeed the gods who come in the morning, and the after-offerings (anuyājas) are the meters. "Prompt the gods! Sacrifice to the gods!"—with these words they proceed with the after-offerings. 3.9.3 [9]

Regarding this, some say, "Recite the invitatory verses for the gods. But one should not speak thus; for the gods who come in the morning are the meters, and the after-offerings are the meters. They proceed with the after-offerings [thinking], "Prompt for the gods! Sacrifice to the gods!"—thus they act with the after-offerings.
Therefore, one should say: "Recite for the gods who come in the morning.
Now, when he places a fuel-stick on the fire, he thereby kindles the meters; and then, when the Hotṛ—

He recites the Prātaranuvāka; he thereby causes the metres to swell again and makes them fresh. For the metres have indeed become exhausted by the gods; for by means of the metres the gods attained the heavenly world. Now, here they neither chant nor recite; it is thus that he causes the metres to swell again and makes them fresh.
With those [verses] that have not yet been exhausted, they perform the sacrifice; therefore, the Hotṛ recites the Prātaranuvāka. Regarding this, they say:

"What is the response (*pratigara*) for the Prātaranuvāka? The Adhvaryu should remain awake and wait; whenever he blinks, that indeed is his response. However, one should not do it in that way; even if he should fall asleep, let him do so at will.

He should sleep wherever the Hotṛ priest concludes the Prātaranuvāka; there the *pracaraṇī* ladle is located. Having taken four portions of clarified butter into it, he offers an oblation. 3.9.3.[12] For at that point, indeed, the head of the sacrifice was severed.
Its essence, having flowed, entered the waters;
therefore, on the previous day, he brings them as the *vasatīvarī* waters. Now, whatever essence of the sacrifice remains there, that very thing he thereby seeks out.
Indeed, it is for this reason that he offers this oblation.
He thus spreads out this very essence of the sacrifice and secures it;
and those deities for whom he offers this oblation, he thereby gratifies them. Satisfied and gratified, they bend this essence of the sacrifice toward him. 3.9.3 [14]
He offers: "May Agni hear my call with the fuel-stick"—by this he means, "May Agni hear this; may he acknowledge it for me.
"May the Waters and the divine Dhiṣaṇās hear"—by this he means, "May the Waters hear this; may they acknowledge it for me.
"May the pressing-stones hear, like those who know the sacrifice"—by this he means, "May the pressing-stones hear this; may they acknowledge it for me."
"May they know me"—this is what he says; "not the sacrifice of the ignorant," for the pressing-stones are wise.

"May the god Savitṛ hear my call, svāhā!"—he thereby says, "May the god Savitṛ hear this of mine; may Savitṛ acknowledge me. Savitṛ is indeed the impeller of the gods; thus, impelled by Savitṛ, he partakes of the essence of the sacrifice. 3.9.3. [15]

Then, having taken another fourfold portion of clarified butter and moving toward the north, he says, "O Hotṛ, seek the waters! By saying "seek the waters," he means this very thing; for when the Hotṛ recites from this point onward, he thereby spreads out that very essence of the sacrifice.
He held it back, and he likewise follows this [practice] so that the destructive *rakṣas* demons do not harm them in the interval. 3.9.3.[16] Then he gives the direction:
"Come, O Camasādhvaryu of the Maitrāvaruṇa; O Neṣṭṛ!"
"Bring forward the wives, the Ekadhana pitchers, and these Vasatīvarī waters; you shall attend upon the Āgnīdhra at the Cātvāla pit with the Hotṛ’s cup"—this is the formal direction (saṃpraiṣa).
They then go out toward the north.

They go by way of the *cātvāla* and in front of the *āgnīdhra*. They go in whichever direction water is located. They go together with the wives; as for why they go together with the wives—when indeed the head of the sacrifice was cut off.
Its essence, having flowed, entered the waters; these Gandharvas, the guardians of Soma, guarded it.
Then those gods said:
"This Gandharva here is surely a destroyer; how can we bring this essence of the sacrifice to a place free from fear and destruction?
They said, "The Gandharvas are indeed fond of women; let us go with their wives, for the Gandharvas are [attached] to their wives. 3.9.3 [20]
"Then they will covet this essence of the sacrifice, thinking, 'We shall bring it here where there is no fear and no danger.
They went together with their wives;
but the Gandharvas seized them right among the wives, so that [they could not reach] this place where there was no fear and no danger.
They took away the essence of the sacrifice.
And so it is here:
he goes forth with his wives as a great power; those Gandharvas are indeed in the wives.
Then, while they are still coveting it, he brings this essence of the sacrifice into a place that is fearless and free from danger.
He offers an oblation of water;
for when this oblation has been offered, this essence of the sacrifice approaches it.
He rises up; having thus revealed it, he seizes that very [essence]. And as to why he offers this oblation: he thereby spreads out the very sap of the sacrifice and secures it.
He asks for darkness; and those very deities to whom he offers this oblation, he thereby gratifies.

Satisfied and pleased, they bend this essence of the sacrifice toward him. 3.9.3. [25] He offers: "O divine waters, O Apāṃnaptṛ. For the waters are divine; therefore he says, "O divine waters, O Apāṃnaptṛ. He who...

"Your wave that is worthy of oblation"—by saying this, he means "your wave that is fit for sacrifice. "Powerful and most intoxicating"—by saying "powerful," he means "possessing heroism"; by saying "most intoxicating," he means "most delicious.
"Give that to the gods among the gods"—in saying "give that to the gods among the gods," he has thus entreated them.

"To those who desire the *śukra* (pure/white)," he says; "to those who desire the truth," is what he thereby means. "Of whomsoever you are the portion, *svāhā*!"—for this [oblation] is indeed their portion. 3.9.3.
[26] Then, with the cup of the Maitrāvaruṇa, he pours this oblation over [the *śukra*].

With the words "Thou art a furrower," just as a coal might be consumed by fire, even so this oblation becomes consumed by this deity. Indeed, with these waters he is about to sprinkle the King; for the clarified butter in the Maitrāvaruṇa’s cup is a thunderbolt, and it is seed.
"May I not injure Soma with the thunderbolt, with the clarified butter; may I not injure the seed, Soma"—thinking thus, he therefore causes it to float away.
Then he draws [the water], saying:
"I draw thee for the stability of the ocean. The ocean, indeed, is the waters; he thus places this [Soma] in the waters for the sake of its stability.
He places it; therefore, when water is used for such enjoyment, it is not exhausted.
Following that, they draw out the *ekadhanas*; following that, the *pānnejana* waters.
Now, as to why he draws [the water] with the cup of the Maitrāvaruṇa.

When the sacrifice indeed departed from the gods, the gods made it go forward by means of the *praiṣas* (calls), they caused it to shine forth with the *puroruks*, and they announced it with the *nivit*s;
therefore, he draws [the cup] with the Maitrāvaruṇa’s goblet. 3.9.3. [29]
They come forward. The Agnīdh stands opposite at the *cātvāla* pit with the *vasatīvarī* waters and the *hotṛ*'s cup;
he makes them touch one another over the *cātvāla*, [reciting]:
"The waters have united with the waters, the plants with the plants," and [he takes] that essence of the sacrifice which was brought on the previous day.
And he thus unites both that which was brought on this day and that which was brought yesterday.

Now, some indeed pour the *vasatīvarī* waters into the *maitrāvaruṇa* cup, and from the *maitrāvaruṇa* cup they pour them back into the *vasatīvarī* waters—both that essence of the sacrifice which was brought on the previous day and [that which is brought today]. 3.9.3. [30]
Saying, "We shall now mix together both that which was drawn today and that [which was drawn previously]," they do so; however, one should not do it in that way.

For when he pours [the Soma] into the Ādhavanīya vessel, then the essence of both parts of the sacrifice is mixed. Then he takes the Vasatīvarī waters into the Hotṛ’s cup from the Nigrābhya waters; as for why he makes them touch over the Cātvāla pit, it is from there [that they come].
The gods ascended to heaven; thus he causes the sacrificer to follow that very path leading to the heavenly world.
They come back. The Hotṛ asks him: "O Adhvaryu, have you found the waters? By this he means: "Have you found them? He [the Adhvaryu] says to him: "I have found them."
"He has bowed down to me as it were," he says; "and then he has bent low for me"—this is what he thereby declares. 3.9.3.
[32] Now, if it should be an Agniṣṭoma, if there should remain a residue in the *pracaraṇī* ladle sufficient for an oblation, that—
If there should not be enough for the oblation, he takes another fourfold portion of clarified butter and offers it with the verse addressed to Agni:
"O Agni, the mortal whom you protect in battles, whom you impel in the contests for booty—he shall be the master of perpetual nourishment, svāhā!
Thus he offers with a verse to Agni; for the Agniṣṭoma is indeed Agni, so he establishes the Agniṣṭoma in Agni by means of a verse containing the word "mortal."
The Agniṣṭoma is indeed commensurate with a man; he should offer in this manner if it be an Agniṣṭoma.
If it be an Ukthya, he should touch the middle enclosing-stick; [there are] three.

There are three enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*); by means of these, the sacrifice is established at that time. However, if it should be an *atirātra* or a *ṣoḍaśin*, one should neither offer the oblation nor touch the middle enclosing-stick; rather, having risen and gone silently, one should enter [the hall].
Thus he distinguishes the sacrificial rites according to their proper order. 3.9.3. [34]
The odd and the even become a single unit;
three or five, five or seven, nine or eleven,
eleven or thirteen, thirteen or fifteen— this is a pair.

They are a pair for the sake of procreation; yet this one remains in excess. He exceeds over the prosperity of the sacrificer. Now, he who exceeds over the prosperity of the sacrificer is their "single possession" (*ekadhana*).
Because that is their single possession, they are called *ekadhanas*. 3.9.4.1.
Then they sit down around the two pressing-boards.
Then he ties gold to this [pressing-board]. For this world is twofold, indeed, there is no third: truth and untruth. The gods are truth, and human beings are untruth. It is indeed the seed of Agni.
"May I touch the shoots with truth; may I drive away Soma with truth"—therefore, indeed, he ties gold to this [sacrificial post].
Then he takes up the pressing-stone.
Now, these pressing-stones are made of stone; for Soma is indeed a god, and Soma is in heaven.
Soma was indeed Vṛtra, and those mountains and stones are his body. By means of that very body he thus completes him, making him whole; therefore they are made of stone.
They either become [the slayers] or they slay him—namely, that which they press; they slay him with this [pressing]. Thus he rises from there, and thus he returns to life.
Therefore, the pressing-stones are made of stone.
He takes it up [with the formula]: "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, I take thee."
"Ravāsi"—the Sun is indeed the impeller of the gods; thus, impelled by the Sun, he takes it up with this.
"With the arms of the Aśvins"—the Aśvins are the two Adhvaryu priests; thus, he takes it up with their very arms, not with his own.
"With the hands of Pūṣan"—Pūṣan is the distributor of portions; thus, he takes it up with his very hands, not with his own.
This [soma] is indeed a thunderbolt; man is not its master. He takes it up with these deities:
"I take thee, O giver of wealth.
For when they press him with this [pressing], then he becomes an oblation; and when he offers the oblation, then...

"He gives the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*); for he bestows these two things—the oblations and the sacrificial fees. Therefore he says, 'O giver' (*rāvāsi*). "Make this sacrifice profound. The sacrifice is indeed the *adhvara*; [he means] "make this great sacrifice..."
"Make [it]," he thereby says; "well-pressed for Indra," for Indra is indeed the deity of the sacrifice, therefore he says, "for Indra";

"well-pressed most excellently," that is what he means by "well-pressed most excellently"; "with the highest stalk," for Soma is indeed the highest stalk, therefore he says, "with the highest stalk"; "full of vigor, full of sweetness, full of milk."
By saying "full of sap," he means exactly this when he says, "full of vigor, full of sweetness, full of milk.
Then he restrains his speech.
For the gods, while performing the sacrifice, were indeed afraid of an attack by the Asuras and Rakṣases.

They did so and said, "Let us sacrifice in a whisper; let us restrain our speech. They sacrificed in a whisper and restrained their speech. 3.9.4. [7] Then he brings the *nigrābhya* waters. He makes him recite over them: "You are the *nigrābhya*s, heard by the gods; satisfy me!"
"Satisfy my mind; satisfy my speech; satisfy my breath; satisfy my eye; satisfy my ear; satisfy my self; satisfy my offspring;
satisfy my cattle; satisfy my attendants; may my attendants not be thirsty. Water is indeed essence; it is upon these that he invokes this blessing.
"May you satisfy my whole self; satisfy my offspring; satisfy my cattle; satisfy my hosts;
may my hosts not be parched with thirst. That which is this *upāṃśusavana* [stone] is, by its underlying principle (*nidāna*), Vivasvat Āditya; it is his *vyāna* breath. 3.9.4. [8]
He measures it out.

For they indeed slay him when they press him; they slay him with this [measuring], and thus he rises from there, and thus he comes to life. And again, as to why he measures it out: therefore there is measure among men, and whatever else there is that has measure.
He measures it out, saying, "For Indra, accompanied by the Vasus and the Rudras. Indra is indeed the deity of the sacrifice;
therefore he says, "For Indra. By saying "accompanied by the Vasus and the Rudras," he [measures] for Indra along with the Vasus and the Rudras.

With "For Indra thee, accompanied by the Ādityas," he thereby assigns the Rudras to Indra; with "For Indra thee, the slayer of the arrogant," the arrogant one is indeed the rival, so he says this for "For Indra thee, the slayer of rivals. This is his special portion (*uddhāra*); just as there is a special portion for the chief, so is this his, apart from the gods. 3.9.4 [10]

"For thee, O Soma-bearing hawk!"—with these words he measures out for the Gāyatrī; "For Agni, thee, the bestower of the increase of wealth"—Agni indeed is the Gāyatrī, so he measures it out for the Gāyatrī.
Because the Gāyatrī, having become a hawk, brought the Soma from heaven, by that [act] she [is the hawk].
The falcon is the carrier of Soma; by that very power of his, he measures out this second [portion].
Now, as to why he measures five times:
the sacrifice is commensurate with the year, and there are five seasons.
One obtains that [soma] by means of five [fingers] of the year; therefore, he measures it five times.
He touches it, saying:
"O Soma, with that light of yours which is in heaven, which is on earth, and which is in the wide mid-air, with that [light], for this [man]..."

"O Sacrificer, grant wide space for wealth; speak in favor of the giver. For when he first became the sacrificial offering (*havis*) for the gods, he reflected: "May I not become the offering for the gods with my entire self.
He then deposited these three bodies in these three worlds. 3.9.4 [13]
The gods indeed desired to win him back;

by means of this very [offering], they obtained these bodies of his, and he became entirely the sacrificial food (*havis*) for the gods. In the same way, this sacrificer obtains these bodies of his by means of this very [offering], and he becomes entirely the sacrificial food for the gods.
The oblation becomes [ready]; therefore he touches it thus. Then he pours in the *nigrābhya* waters. For the waters indeed slew Vṛtra; it is by that very power that the waters [are used].

Therefore they flow; as they flow, nothing at all can withstand them. They indeed moved according to their own will, thinking, "For what purpose should we stand still, we by whom Vṛtra was slain? Indeed, everything here that exists—whatever there is, even this wind that blows—was standing still for Indra. 3.9.4. [15]
Indra said, "All this which exists is indeed mine; stay here with me.
They asked, "What would be ours from that? He replied, "The first draught of King Soma shall be yours. "So be it," they said.
They stood up against him; he seized them with his chest. Because he seized them with his chest (*uras*), they are called *nigrābhyās*. In the same way, the sacrificer now seizes them with his chest.
This is the first draught of King Soma for him: that he pours [the water] together with the *nigrābhyās*. 3.9.4. [16]
He pours it out [with the words]:
"Ye are refreshing, conquerors of Vṛtra. For the waters are auspicious; therefore he says, "Ye are refreshing.

"Conquerors of Vṛtra," for these [waters] indeed slew Vṛtra. "Willingly bestowing bounty, wives of immortality," for the waters are indeed immortal. "O goddesses, [lead] this [sacrificer] to the gods..."
"Lead the sacrifice"—there is nothing hidden here in this [formula]. "Invited, drink of the Soma"—thus, having been invited, they consume the first portion of King Soma. 3.9.4.
[17] Now, about to strike [the post]:

One should meditate in one's mind upon whomsoever one hates, thinking: "I strike this one, not you. For they indeed despise even him who kills a human Brahmin; how much more so him who kills this divine one? Indeed, Soma is divine; they kill him when they press him, and they kill him with this [act]. Thus it is.

In that way he rises, in that way he lives, and in that way he becomes sinless; even if he should not hate anyone, were he to meditate in his mind upon a mere blade of grass, in that way he becomes sinless. He strikes out. 3.9.4 [18]
"Do not fear, do not tremble"—by this he says, "Do not be afraid, do not tremble;
I strike at that one, not at you. "Bestow strength"—by this he says, "Bestow sap.
"O two bowls, being firm, be firm; bestow strength"—some say this refers to these two pressing-boards; what [is the meaning]?

Now, even if one were to split these two boards here, they are indeed heaven and earth; these two tremble at this raised thunderbolt. Therefore, he pacifies it by means of these very two, heaven and earth, so that being pacified, it does not harm him. "May you two bestow vigor," he says; by this he means, "may you two bestow sap. [The word] *pāpmā*...
"O Soma, you have not been slain"—by this he destroys all his evil.
He presses three times;
he collects three times; he undergoes the fourfold *nigrābha* (water-sprinkling); that makes ten. Ten syllables indeed [constitute a *virāj*].

Virāj is Vairāja, and Soma; therefore, he prepares it ten times. Now, as for why he approaches the *nigrābha*: when he first became the sacrificial oblation (*havis*) for the gods, then these quarters [were established].

"May I touch him with these quarters, with my beloved mate, with my own abode"— it was for this purpose that the gods touched him with these quarters, with their beloved mate, when they took hold of the *nigrābha*; and in the same way,
this [sacrificer] now touches him with these quarters, with his beloved mate, with his own abode.

That which he approaches as the "grasping" (nigrābha), he approaches with [the formula]: "From the east, from the west, from the north, from the south—let the quarters run toward you! Thus he causes him to come into contact with these quarters, with his mate, with his dear abode. "O Mother, come forth! (amba niṣpara).
"May they find one another," he says. The mother is indeed a woman, and the quarters are women; therefore he says, "O Mother, come forth.
"May they find one another," he says; offspring are indeed *arīḥ*; thus he says, "May they recognize one another. Therefore, even those offspring who are as if far apart recognize one another;
that is why he says, "May they find one another. 3.9.4. [22]
Now, as for why he is named Soma:
when he first became the sacrificial offering for the gods, he reflected, "May I not become the offering for the gods with my entire self. That which was his most beloved body...
He set it down. The gods indeed desired it; they said, "Pull this out for us, so that we may prepare the oblation together with it.
He pulled it out as if from afar, saying, "This is truly mine. Therefore, its name is *soma*.
Now, as to why it is called *yajña*.
They indeed kill him when they press him; then, when they bring him forth, he is born as he is being performed.
Because he is born (*jāyate*), therefore it is called *yañjaḥ*, for *yañjaḥ* is indeed the same as *yajñaḥ*. At that point, he also uttered this speech: 3.9.4 [24].

"O most powerful god, you indeed shall praise the mortal; O bounteous Indra, there is no other comforter than you. Thus I speak these words to you. "Indeed," he said, "being a mortal myself, 'you alone, and no other than you, shall be my progenitor from here. 3.9.4 [25]
Then they draw the cups from the *nigrābhya* waters.
Indeed, the waters slew Vṛtra; it is by that very power that the waters flow. From those flowing waters he takes the *vasatīvarī* waters, and from the *vasatīvarī* waters, the *nigrābhya* waters.
They draw the cups from the *nigrābhya* waters; it is by that very power they draw the cups. From the *hotṛ*-cup [they draw];
for the *ṛc* is a woman and the *hotṛ* is a man, and from a woman these creatures are born; thus he causes him (the sacrificer) to be born from this woman, the *ṛc*, the *hotṛ*.
Therefore, [he draws] from the *hotṛ*-cup.
